items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I wish to advise the House that I have
received a letter from Mike Sabin resigning his seat with effect from Friday, 30 January
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House express its
confidence in the National -led Government and  commend its programme for 2015 as
set out in the Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament. Mr Speaker, can I take this
opportunity to welcome you and other members back to the House for the parliamentary
year and to remind the House that New Z ealand went to the polls on 20 September
2014. For the third time the New Zealand public delivered a clear mandate to this

items.speaker: National-led Government. The message was pretty simple
items.text: carry on. Carry on making
the country wealthier, carry on making this a more vibrant country, carry on making this
a more multicultural and globally connected country, and carry on making New Zealand
a successful little nation we can all be proud of. That is what they said. And for the third
time the public allowed us to work with our friends in the ACT Party, United Future,
and the Māori Party. I want to take this opportunity to thank them for being part of what
is a strong and stable Government. It has been for the last 6½ years and will be for a
further 2½ years for the 9-year period, and then beyond, hopefully, in the years ahead.
We went into the election campaign last year with a pretty simple slogan: “Working
for New Zealand”. Working for New Zealand. We went there because this is a
Government that is working for New Zealand. Growth last year was at 3.2 percent; on
average, it will be 3 percent or more for the next 3 years. Wages have gone up 15
percent over the last 5 years. Employment: 80,000 new jobs were created in the last 12
months and 217,000 more New Zealanders are in work than 5 years ago. When it comes
to Kiwis and the decisions they make, very, very few of them are going over the
Tasman to Australia —in fact, we had the smallest net loss across the Tasman since
1994. It has got to the point where the Government is now  running job fairs to make
sure that New Zealanders in Brisbane and in Melbourne who left under the previous
Labour Government know to come back to New Zealand because there are jobs here for
them. On the weekend we had the Sevens here in Wellington. They could not fill that
stadium, but Helen Clark could—every single year she could fill the Westpac Stadium
with Kiwis wanting to leave.
The cost of living is good for New Zealanders. Inflation is at 0.8 percent —it is low.
Interest rates are half of what they  were when this Government took over. The balance
of payments deficit at 2.6 percent is a third of what it was under the previous
Government. We are getting close to surplus, and when it comes to the debts that this
nation has, by 2020 they will be under 20 percent of GDP. That is a third of what they
were projected to be when we inherited those terrible policies of the free-spending, free-
wheeling Helen Clark administration of 1999 to 2008.
So how can we summarise all this? Quite simply. New Zealand is a c ountry of
people who now live longer, earn more, are better educated, have better health, and are
less likely to be victims of crime. That is why the New Zealand public, when they went
1364 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
to the polls, resoundingly asked us to come back and to be the Governme nt for a further
3 years, and that is the programme that I want to lay out for you today.
But just before I do that, let me make the contrast that is on display between this
active, busy Government and the do- nothing Opposition over there. Andrew Little ha s
been the leader of the Labour Party for 84 days —84 days. In 1873 Jules Verne thought
you could get around the world in 80 days. Well, in 84 days Andrew Little has not even
got around his caucus let alone the world. He has not even got around the four people
who voted for him. He is not Andrew Little; he is Dr Dolittle. This man does absolutely
nothing. Granted, his predecessors whom I faced managed to stagger from gaffe to
crisis and back again  in 84 days, but this is a man who has done absolutely nothing .
No—I am wrong. He has had two ideas—two ideas—in 84 days.
No. 1 has been to give Māori sovereignty. Under Andrew Little they can write laws
only for themselves, but they are not allowed to buy an ex -State house. They are not
allowed to buy a State house but under Andrew Little they will be allowed to write laws
only for Māori. The other great idea he has had in 84 days is to hold a workshop about
what a job is. That is a novel concept for a Labour MP —I am prepared to admit that —
but it is hardly the stuff that sets the electorate on fire. No, this is it. This is the summary
of 84 days of Andrew Little. It is a success. Why? Because he is not David Cunliffe.
That is it. That is the reason why “Project Little” is working. But we are a busy
Government; they are a do-nothing Opposition.
So let us move on to what the Government is planning to do over the course of 2015
and the years ahead. Resource Management Act reform: this is a House that so often
talks about the cost for New Zealanders of buying houses. Let us see how many of them
are prepared to stand up and back the Government’s agenda to make the Resource
Management Act work better for our country and for New Zealanders.
The Business Growth Agenda—350 initiatives that make it easier to do business with
the Government, that see more money invested in science and technology, that see our
export markets grow. It will see a Food Safety Science and Research Centre established
at Massey University to educate young New Zealanders. It will see four additional
centres of research excellence and three information and communications technology
graduate schools there for young New Zealanders.
When it comes to the workplace, this is a G overnment that will be advancing
legislation that will balance the need for the creation of jobs with the safety of those
who go to our workplaces each and every day. In those critical areas of  forestry,
construction, and agriculture, t his will be a Government that will champion legislation
over the course of the next 12 months to make it safer.
When it comes to wages, this is a Government that will raise the minimum wage in
2015, as it has done every single year that we have been in Government —every single
year. We already have the highest minimum wage to average wage ratio of any country
in the OECD, but in 2015 the minimum wage will rise.

items.speaker: Infrastructure
items.text: when you want a country that operates efficiently and effectively, you
need infrastructure. That will mean more roading projects. The Waterview Connection
in Auckland—Alice, that massive, big machine that is digging the tunnel through there
at Waterview, has already turned around and is heading back towards Auckland. That
will see that $1 billion -  plus project completed over the course of the next few years.

items.speaker: The Waikato Expressway
items.text: my friends in Hamilton there talk so wonderfully about the
commute from Hamilton to Auckland  now. Christchurch motorways are being built.
Northland, that place we love so much; Northland, those people we respect so much—
they need to get to Auckland on the road, and this Government will be supporting Pūhoi
to Wellsford, not just with planning but with a road. That is on top of the 11 regional
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1365
roading projects I unveiled last year and the $100 million going into urban cycleways,
because we know that people want to get around their cities on their bikes.

items.speaker: Ultra-fast broadband
items.text: this is a Government that is getting New Zealand wired for the
world. Five hundred and s eventy thousand homes can already connect to ultra -fast
broadband—69,000 of them have taken it up. And if you live in Whangarei or Te
Awamutu or Ōāmaru, your city or place has been fully fibred under a National -led
Government. Labour was opposed, yet National is getting New Zealand wired up.
We on this side of the House know we are not going to get rich selling things to each
other. We are, as a nation, getting rich if we sell things to the world, and our trade
agreements will reflect that. In a few months’  time there will be the signing of the free -
trade agreement with Korea—a very important partner for New Zealand. The Gulf
States are looking much more closely at a free- trade agreement. And the Trans-Pacific
Partnership—what does the Opposition actually think? Does it want a free -trade
agreement with the United States, a $17 trillion economy? Dr Dolittle does not know.
Half the caucus says yes; half the caucus says no. You would not have a clue. Its
political support partners, the Greens, do not want a bar of it. They do not want to sell
goods and services on an unrestricted basis to the United States. The active, busy,
National-led Government says yes; the Opposition says no.
Climate change—an issue that this House cares about. This is the Government that
will be taking to Paris later in the year a target that New Zealand can adhere to when it
comes to climate change, along with solutions in science and technology when it comes
to agriculture.
Housing is an issue of considerable concern to New Zealanders. Who does not want
to own a home? But this is the Government that has not sat around and done nothing.
Under this Government, 100 special housing areas have been approved —100 special
housing areas; 84 of them in Auckland. Last year 2,000 new homes per month w ere
constructed under a National -led Government —24,000 homes in the last 12 months.
That is double the rate from when we took over, and you can see it in the GDP and
employment activity. In 2014 residential construction alone was $10 billion, and there is
plenty more of that to come.
And when it comes to social housing, this is not a Government that thinks Housing
New Zealand has to own every home; this is a Government that is prepared to go out
there with community housing providers, as I announced earlier  in the year, and say to
people: “We will supply more income -related rents. We will allow iwi to actually own
homes. We will allow the Salvation Army and Presbyterian Support  and other
community groups to have the homes. There will be more homes available. The
bottleneck and logjam that are there will be unblocked with a far more sensible
scheme.”
New Zealand has voted in the Government because it does things for them and their
families. And foremost in that is the creation of jobs. No one is more proud tha n when
their youngster gets a job or when they make sure they can keep their job or get another
job. Two hundred and seventeen thousand jobs have been created under this
Government in the last 5 years. And what the effect of all of the stronger economy
means is that the Government has more money, even in these very challenging
conditions, to spend on things that matter to New Zealanders.  This year—free doctors’
visits for 400,000 New Zealanders under 13 years of age. This year there will be an
extension of paid parental leave from 14 weeks to 16 weeks, and a year after that, on 1
April, an extension from 16 weeks to 18 weeks, and for those who are not eligible for
paid parental leave, the parental tax credit will increase from $150 a week to $220 a
week.
1366 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
When it comes to ACC, with good management we have sorted out the mess we
inherited from Labour, and we will see motor vehicle ACC costs drop by $130 per car,
and the levies on employers and the self -employed will also drop. When it comes to the
most deprived kids in New Zealand society, look to the Budget of 2015 for some ideas
on what the Government will be doing in that area.

items.speaker: Education
items.text: we all know that nothing is more important than helping young New
Zealanders to get an education. This is the Government  that is putting $359 million this
year into a series of initiatives that will keep good teachers in the classroom for longer,
that will mento r teachers and principals. W hen we see a failing school, we will not do
what Labour and the Greens and others in t his House have done and turn a blind eye
and imagine it does not matter; we will attract a good principal to go to that school and
turn it round. And this is the side of the House that supported national standards and the
roll-out of technology to our schools. We see more kids in early childhood education
and more Māori and more Pacific students coming out. Education is working under
National, but there is a lot more to be done.
When it comes to our corrections facilities, Wiri prison will be opened, I think, in
2015, and by 2017 every prison in New Zealand will be a working prison where our
prisoners will be expected to get skills and get the opportunity to take a job when they
ultimately leave prison.
When it comes to Māori, this is a Government that is ac tually doing something for
Māori in New Zealand —46 deeds of settlement signed under this Government; under
the previous Labour Government, one to two a year were signed. At the rate that Labour
was going, it would have taken until 2060 to achieve what I think National will achieve
by 2017. This will be a Government that will reform and rewrite the Te Ture Whenua
Māori Act, which will see 1.4 million hectares of land available for development, $8
billion worth of value to the economy, and thousands of jobs. The Government will not
forget those who are vulnerable in our communities. There will be more work done on
child abuse, domestic violence, community security and safety, and on using technology
to enhance the police.
In 2015 there will be a review of the intelligence agencies to ensure that our laws are
fit for purpose and that we have intelligence agencies that can keep New Zealanders
safe. When we have seen intelligence legislation in this House that makes New
Zealanders safer, far too few political part ies have been prepared to step up and support
it, but when we saw the crises in countries like France, recently, in Canada, and in
Australia, we did not hear a word from the Opposition. They are not prepared to support
legislation to make New Zealanders safer, but they are as quiet as little lamb chops
when things happen outside of that.
It will be a busy year for foreign affairs. We are on the Security Council in 2015 and
2016. Issues like Ukraine and Iraq and Syria, the Middle East, and the war on Islamic
State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) will be all important for us, as a good participant on the
Security Council, to debate and discuss. This will be a Government that will take
seriously its responsibilities when it comes to standing up to ISIS. As I said in Waitangi,
I will not, as leader of New Zealand, stand back and see Jordanian pilots burnt to death,
I will not see young children beheading soldiers, I will not sit back when people are
thrown off buildings because of their sexuality, and then be lectured b y the left about
human rights. They do not care enough about human rights to do something about it. No
wonder they are looking down in shame.
When it comes to Christchurch, the big job of the rebuild of Christchurch will
continue. The Canterbury Earthquake  Recovery Authority will become a departmental
agency.
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1367
This is going to be a busy year for the Government. We were elected by the people
of New Zealand and were given the biggest mandate in the history of MMP to carry on
the work we have done in the past and want to do in the future. We are not here to fill in
the green seats; we are here to do a lot for New Zealand. It is a pretty simple message: it
is a lot over here, and it is a little over there. And I tell you what, New Zealand is
hungry for a lot, and only four people over there wanted “a Little”.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I move, That all the words after
“That” be deleted and replaced with “t his House express no confidence in this
National-led Government because this is a government that has lost its moral compass
and turned a blind eye to the deplorable actions of its MPs;  that is fixated on selling off
our state houses rather than building m ore homes; that is leading us into a war with no
clear goals and no exit strategy;  that has more Kiwis out of work and in poverty t oday
than when it came to power;  and that now has no greater ambition for New Zealand
than changing our flag while leaving the real issues to fester. ” Apparently, that was the
speech of a leader of a nation. Apparently, that was the sort of speech that we are all
meant to be inspired by, rise up to, and feel good about. But it was typical of this Prime
Minister—nasty pettifoggin g, with no direction and nothing to offer. He has had 2
months on the beaches and he has come back with nothing more to offer.
Before I go any further I want to say how pleased I am to be back, and to wish you,
Mr Speaker, and all my colleagues a happy Ne w Year. It has been a great summer
break. Some have had a good holiday. Todd Barclay went on a voyage of discovery. He
discovered his electorate —“Oh yes, there is a deep south!”—after years of living in
Wellington. Chris Bishop went kayaking in the Hutt Ri ver and he wound up a bit like
his political career: hard up on the rocks, with no future. Amy Adams spent her holiday
going around and unpicking everything that Judith Collins did not do. So it has been a
very successful summer for some.
This is a Government that has mastered the art of something very, very special.
Kirkcaldie and Stains and Smith and Caughey’s would be very proud of them. This is a
Government of window dressing. This is a Government that has mastered the art of
window dressing: giving the appearance of doing something —giving the appearance of
doing something—even though what it is doing is something completely different; or
repeatedly promising something that it never delivers on, like the fiscal surplus. How
many years now, Mr English, has the Government promised a surplus and not
delivered? How many more years are we to go? What is it now —2017 before the
surplus, before the great fiscal managers of the National Government produce
something, produce a tangible result? That is the window dressing.
Let us talk about housing and housing affordability. Those members talk about
housing affordability. Their plan, their magic plan, for housing affordability—get this—
is to sell State houses. Not a single extra house, but the selling off of State houses.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: What about Homestart?

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Poor old Nick Smith, the “Dr Strangelove” of the National
Cabinet. Poor old Nick Smith, with his great plan to help housing. He is going to reform
the Resource Management Act in ways that we do not know about —because he cannot
tell us. There is great talk about section 6 and great talk about section 7, but we do not
know what it is. What is the change? And if he does have change, what difference is it
going to make to the people trying to get into a house? What difference is it going to
make? Not a single difference. Not a single new house will be built because of their
policies on that side of the House—not a single new house.
Low-income and middle -income A ucklanders are struggling to get into a house. I
heard a story this morning about a professional Auckland couple in their 30s —probably
a little younger than Simon Bridges. They have done their OE and they have come back.
1368 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
They have done very well on their O E, because they could afford a deposit. That was
one thing. They had no help from their parents. But they now have a mortgage. They
have a modest Auckland house with three bedrooms, and do you know what the
mortgage is? It is $750,000—$750,000 for first -home buyers in Auckland, a young
professional couple. That is what the National Government has given us when it comes
to housing. And it will talk about: “Oh, we want more houses. Oh, we’re going to
change the law to give us more housing.” It is just more window dressing —just more
window dressing from the “Dr Strangelove” of the National Cabinet, Nick Smith.
The Government has done nothing to add housing supply. Oh, that is not quite true.
It has the special housing areas.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How many houses?

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Fifteen houses—

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: —or 50? Am I over-estimating it? I might be—15 houses. Oh,
that will help. That will help the poor old Aucklanders trying to get into their hous es.
That will help the Aucklanders who can no longer live near where they work and who
have to live in the far north, north of Auckland, or even down in Hamilton now if they
want to work in Auckland. That is the product of this Government: just more window
dressing. No idea, no plan, no policy, and no plan to do anything that is going to make a
difference. It says that selling 8,000 State houses will make the difference. And it says,
and here is the other bit of window dressing in selling the 8,000 State houses: “Oh, they
will all go to the community housing groups.” There is not a single community housing
group that can afford 8,000 State houses. The community housing groups cannot afford
to buy up those 8,000 State houses.
John Key knows that when he make s that promise he is promising thousands and
thousands of State houses to his mates, the property developers, because that is what
this plan is about. It is not about adding houses. It is not about making housing more
affordable. It is not about helping those who cannot afford to buy or cannot afford to
rent in the private rental market. He is about just flogging them all off, because that is
what National did last time it was in Government, and John Key is no different to the
last lot. This mob just sells State houses because that is what it does —looks after its
mates. More window dressing.
And then we come to unemployment. You know, the weird thing is this. You look
around the rest of the world—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: 80,000 new jobs.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: You look around the rest of the world, Dr Smith, and
unemployment is going down. Unemployment is coming down. We all got through the
global financial crisis. We all got through it. At the time at the start of the global
financial crisis, we were No. 1 in the OECD in terms of our unemployment —the lowest
level of unemployment at the beginning of the global financial crisis. When I gave my
state of the nation speech 2 weeks ago, we were ninth. Two weeks on, we are now 10 th.
We have slipped when it comes to employment. Unemployment in this country is going
up. Unemployment in this country is going up because this Government has no plan.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: You left it at No. 11.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It has got Paula Bennett. She will massage the numbers and
she will shove people off the unemployment queue, but the Government has got no plan
to create jobs, to add jobs, to reduce unemployment, and to get people living in dignity.
Unemployment has gone up. Unemployment has gone up by another 3,000 people  in
the last 3 months. You know, these are the spring and summer months, when employers
take people on. These are the good months, and unemployment has gone up by 3,000.
That is why the Reserve Bank is holding interest rates. It has no confidence in the future
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1369
of this economy under this Government. That is what is happening in this country, and
that Government gives us more window dressing. It will spin the numbers. It will spin
the numbers, but the people who are living it know what it is like. They cannot afford to
make ends meet. They cannot get a job. The families are struggling. That is New
Zealand today for far too many New Zealanders, and that Government does not care,
because that is the nature of it.  It will just dress it up. It will just make it up as it goes
along and hope that nobody notices. Well, I have got news for John Key: people are
noticing. People are noticing because they are hurting. When unemployment goes up in
the prime months when empl oyers take people on, then they know something is wrong.
When people are struggling to make ends meet, they know there is something wrong,
and there is—and there is.
Has this Government given us anything? Is there a single measure it can point to that
is going to add more jobs?  You see Steven Joyce sitting there, and his single biggest
contribution as Minister in charge of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment is zero -hour contracts —the nastiest, most brutal form of employment,
which only ever happened in the time he was the Minister. Even employers come to me
and say: “This is appalling. We can’t have this. We shouldn’t have it —zero-hour
contracts where people can be obliged to turn up to work, and work not be given and no
pay be given.” What  an appalling state of affairs that Steven Joyce has led the
employment market into. People look at it and they are horrified, their parents look at it
and they are horrified, and their grandparents look at it and they are horrified.

items.speaker: Employers come to me a nd say
items.text: “How is it that a Government could allow this to
happen?” The good, responsible employers who are looking for good, responsible
people say “We would never touch zero-hour contracts, but those people down the road,
they are doing it, and this Government shows no interest in doing anything about it.”
Well, we will in Labour, and you will see our member’s bill that will actually deal to
that issue. Steven Joyce’s single biggest contribution is zero-hour contracts.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Then there’s Skycity.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: And then there is Skycity. I am glad you asked, Mrs King,
because the convention centre is very important. Remember how important it was to
New Zealanders? We must have a convention centre —we must have one , because the
market for international conventions down at the bottom of the world is so big ,
apparently. They are falling over themselves to come down here —never mind that
Rotorua and Hamilton cannot fill their convention centres. Pay that no mind, becaus e
the National Party knows best and they went off and did a deal—they went off and did a
deal. Who did the deal? Oh, John Key. He had a dinner with the Skycity executives, and
here were all these other people lining up, all these other people thinking it was going to
be a fair process, an open tender, and they thought they would have a chance to put up
their proposal and say: “Yes, we can build a convention centre.” But no. Not under the
National Government, not under the masters of the universe. The master s of the
universe, John Key and Steven Joyce —oh dear, not them again. They got around the
negotiating table, and what a deal —what a deal. The masters of the universe, John Key
and Steven Joyce, negotiated the deal of the century. Well it sure was if you are Skycity.
But for the taxpayer, what have they done? What have they given us? What have they
given us?
This is what Treasury said when it looked at it. Treasury said that it had “strong
concerns that the private benefits to Skycity will exceed public ben efits to New
Zealanders.” Whoops! The masters of the universe did such a fantastic deal that their
own officials have trounced it —their own officials have trounced it. What did the
Auditor-General say about the process and about John Key’s negotiating skil ls and
Steven Joyce’s negotiating manner? What did they say about that? They said “we do not
1370 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
consider that the evaluation process w as transparent or even -handed.” B ut that is all
right because when you are the Prime Minister promising the nation a free convention
centre, there are no bounds.
But whoops! It is not free. Oh no! The free convention centre is going to cost us.
Will it be just a little bit? Oh, we can afford the odd million here and there, just a little
bit, just to get it over the line. How mu ch do they want to squeeze out of us? It is $140
million—$140 million for the casino, for the gambling experts in Auckland who have
had this exclusive licence for so long. The deal that John Key and Steven Joyce, the
masters of the universe, negotiated —the free convention centre —is going to cost us
$140 million. Well, that is what they call economic development. That is what they call
a plan for the future. Well, it is a plan for Skycity’s future. It is doing very well. It has
got the licence for 2048 and, mark my words, that mob will not walk away from it.
They have put too much into it. There is too much at stake —there is too much at stake.
Those are the economic issues.
What about the standards of the Government? What about the promise of 2008 that
“The Government I lead will be a Government of good standards.”, and its chance to do
something, its chance to demonstrate that National actually is a party of standards in
Government? It was confronted with it at the end of last year. One of National’s MPs
was under a police investigation. One of its MPs—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I invite members throughout this debate to be very careful.
We know that there was a court case, and we know that all details were suppress ed.
[Interruption] Order! There is Standing Order 115. Should any members think I should
consider this matter differently, I invite them to use that Standing Order and write to
me. At this stage no member has done so. I invite Mr Little to continue.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I understand and appreciate the
caution you are expressing. I make no reference at all and make no comment beyond the
fact that it is on the record that a MP was under a police investigation. He is not the
first. That Government well knows, because it has drawn the attention of the public to
other MPs under a police investigation—a police investigation that led to no outcome at
all.
But here is the point. We had an MP under investigation, who was then allowed by
this Government to chair the parliamentary committee—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I have given a ruling that I had given
considerable consideration to. If the member continues in this vein, I will have no
choice but to terminate his speech. I have given a ruling whereby we acknowledge there
is a court case of which all details were suppressed. [ Interruption] Order! This is a time
when this Parliament has a responsibility, a duty, to respect the jurisdiction of the court,
and I expect that to occur today. I invite Mr Little to continue.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I absolutely understand the principle of comity between
Parliament and other branches of g overnment. That is absolutely crucial. I have made
no reference to any core process. I just want that to be on the record—none
whatsoever—but standards of public life are important. Standards of public life are
important, and the way we, as MPs in this House, conduct ourselves is important.
Whether or not we are party to a conflic t of interest and whether or not our parties and
our party leaders know we are subject to a conflict of interest —that is important to
every citizen in New Zealand. Every single one of us is required to exercise proper and
appropriate standards of conduct, including, when we are in conflicts of interest, to
declare that and act appropriately. If our leaders know that we are in a conflict of
interest, it is incumbent on the leader to act appropriately and properly. I just say this to

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse and Anne Tolley
items.text: the truth will set you free. We will come back to
this. The truth will set you free.
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1371
I want to go on to this very important issue that the Prime Minister has correctly
raised, although in rather an unfortunate manner, and that is the challenge t hat the world
faces in dealing with an outfit like Islamic State, or ISIS  as it is known. It is brutal, it is
horrific, it is ugly, it is revolting, and it has appalled every single citizen who has seen
it. Every person who respects democracy is appalled by it. The challenge is this: after 10
years of training of the Iraqi army by the best -trained, best -equipped, best -resourced
army in the world, what is it that we can do now that is going to make a difference?
After US$25 billion of training for the Iraqi army, what is it that our people and those
around the world who are invited to join might do? Let us not be panicked. Let us not be
panicked into a response to deal with the most brutal and the worst outfit, which does
not operate to any rules, does not op erate with any borders, and does not observe any
conventions, but is nasty and brutal. Japan tried it and dealt with them, and their
hostages were killed brutally. Jordan tried to deal with them, and their pilot was brutally
killed in the ugliest, most app alling fashion. What is it we are going to do? What is the
mission, Mr Key? What are you asking New Zealanders to agree to —to put our people
in harm’s way—that is going to make the difference? That is the question.
New Zealanders are sensible, practical p eople. We all see it. We all feel the urge to
do something, but we want to know that what we do is going to make a difference. That
is the challenge that the world faces: not to rush in there, hoping that we might find out
what to do when we get up there, but to know what it is before we get there and to
understand that the most and only effective measure so far has been air strikes by other
forces, which is something we cannot do.
Labour’s focus is very clear. We are about an economy that is going to gene rate
jobs—real jobs, good jobs, jobs that mean good living standards and good incomes for
people. The right laughs at us. The members laugh at us because they do not care about
the people who are struggling to get jobs at the moment. They do not care about  those
who are on the unemployment queue because it is going up because this Government
does nothing about it. We will take that challenge on. We will work with the sector that
is generating the most jobs at the moment, the small business sector —the most ignored
business sector in the country. It is funny how you talk to members of that sector and
they say: “This Government has done nothing.” What do they want? They want access
to easy, readily available education—stuff that tells them how to get started an d what to
do. For those who have been in business for a while and are wondering how to take
advantage of better economic conditions and how to expand, they want some assistance
to do that readily accessible. Those dealing with the multitude of Government a gencies
want to know how to do that efficiently —to have one point of contact to do it. It is all
possible. It is all achievable. This Government does not care. It does not care about the
small business sector, because that is not where its mates and the donations come from.
That is the truth of it.
We will be a party that is serious about housing, about affordable housing, and about
adding to housing—10,000 houses a year over 10 years. That is our policy. That is our
measure. That will make a difference. T hat young professional couple in Auckland are
now saddled with a $750,000 mortgage and are terrified if either of them loses their job,
because that will be it, that will be their lives gone. But no one else will be put in that
position.
We will address the single biggest issue that New Zealanders are concerned about:
the growing inequality. If the Prime Minister wants to talk about separatism, I will talk
about it to him. I will talk about those who are being kicked out of the housing
market—obstructed—and those who are living in palatial residences. That is the
separatism that I am concerned about: those whose incomes are getting less and those
1372 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
whose incomes are getting stratospheric. That is the separatism I am concerned about,
not the stuff that the Prime Minister is concerned about.
New Zealand deserves better. New Zealand deserves leadership, a real leader who is
prepared to confront the real issues, prepared to deal with the issues that New
Zealanders have, with respect and with dignity, and to deal with them in a way that is
going to make a difference, generate jobs, and give dignity to people who need it most.
That is the challenge facing New Zealand, not what this Government is talking about:
fiddling and faddling and more window -dressing, which is what we have got under this
mob.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Before I begin my formal speech, I
would just like to acknowledge the death of Dr Apirana Mahuika. This is a moment of
great sadness for the Green Party, and we would like to join with Ngati Porou in sharing
their sadness at the passage of Dr Mahuika. He was a leader like no other. He was
unashamedly ambitious for his people, as well as for all Māoridom, and he had friends
right across the political spectrum. In my own dealings with him, I always found he had
an amazing capacity to take on new ideas. He was interested not only in the Māori
economy but also in how the Māori economy could benefit from the  growing green
economy. We will miss him very much.
It has been an extremely hot summer in Wellington. All over the country it has been
hot—even in Wellington. All across the country green fields have been turning brown,
rivers have dried up or slowed to a  trickle, and, unfortunately for our farmers as well as
for our native plants and animals, the threat of drought now hangs heavy over the land.
Will 2015 be another record year for the climate?
Last year was the warmest year on record around the world. Nin e of the 10 warmest
years on record have occurred since 2000. I hear the Prime Minister making jokes about
it because he is a science- denier. This is the 38 th consecutive year that the average
annual temperature has been above the long -term average—38 cons ecutive years. The
trend is pretty clear: our climate is heating up, and we are facing, in the words of the
climate change Minister, Tim Groser, “the great challenge of our age”. He is right;
climate change is the greatest challenge of our age. Runaway glo bal warming hangs
over us like the threat of a nuclear winter did during the height of the Cold War. Just as
they did during the height of the Cold War, parents are looking into the eyes of their
children and are asking: “What kind of a world are we leaving behind for you?”.
But I am not going to focus this speech on the dire consequences of doing nothing on
climate change. I am sure all of us have heard the science— at least most of us have. We
have read about the wicked storms, the wild fires, the droughts , the risks to agriculture
and forestry, and the threats posed to our homes and wildlife. We have probably even
seen some of the changes firsthand in our own backyards.
We have known about climate change for some time. Margaret Thatcher gave
speeches about  climate change in the 1980s. Simon Upton, as part of a National
Government no less, came close to passing a climate tax in the 1990s. And the Kyoto
Protocol came into force in the 2000s, promising concerted and coordinated global
action on the climate. We have had a few more false starts since then, but we have seen
how a polluting industry can organise powerfully to secure its own short -term interests
at the expense of our children. As a result, carbon emissions have continued to grow
unabated around the world, but particularly here in New Zealand.
As a people we have one of the highest carbon footprints in the developed world, and
the Ministry for the Environment has stated in its annual report that our country’s net
emissions will continue to go even hig her—up a further 50 percent by 2020. People
often think that I have made a mistake when I say this. They say: “Oh, you mean to say
New Zealand’s emissions are going down 50 percent by 2020.” —but sadly, no. The
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1373
actual truth is that since John Key has been P rime Minister, New Zealand’s net
emissions have increased by 20 percent, and according to the Ministry for the
Environment climate pollution will increase by 50 percent by 2020 under the current
policy settings —because, of course, the current policy settin gs subsidise climate
emissions.
If climate is war, the New Zealand Government is fighting on the wrong side. It is on
the side fighting for global climate catastrophe. Two decades after Simon Upton’s
courageous, but ultimately failed, attempt to get action  on climate change, it is time we
changed sides and joined those trying to cut greenhouse emissions, instead of
continuing to dramatically increase our own emissions.
In New Zealand one does not have to look very far to find conscientious objectors to
the Government’s war to accelerate climate change. We are a can -do country. New
Zealanders generally look forwards, not backwards. We are a people who do not fear
the future. When faced with a challenge New Zealanders protest, we invent, we forge
ahead with pr actical solutions. I am thinking of people like the New Zealander Ian
Wright, co- founder of Tesla Motors, an electric vehicle manufacturer, who is now
developing electric drivetrains for trucks in California. I am thinking of people like
Dayle Takitimu, an  indigenous rights and environmental lawyer, who has led her iwi,
Te Whānau -a-Apanui, in their struggle against deep- sea drilling off the East Coast,
working alongside Dr Apirana Mahuika. And I am thinking of people like Mike
Bennetts, who is taking liquid fuel company Z Energy from being in the middle of the
problem to at least the start of the solution by investing millions of dollars in the
development of sustainable biofuels here in New Zealand. And there are many, many
more.
Some of our best and bright est are realising that our prosperity relies on a thriving
environment and that the threat of climate change brings opportunities to be smarter
about how we do business, smarter about how we can create and conserve energy, and
smarter about how we organise to create social change to mobilise in the face of climate
change—smart green economics and smart green thinking in action.
And then there are those in Government who are stepping up to the climate threat.
Dunedin City Council has taken the first steps to divest from fossil fuels, realising that
dirty energy has no place in our prosperous future. At an even smaller level, the
community board in Eastbourne, Wellington, is pushing its local council to fund a
cycleway around the bays —one that will double as a  protective sea wall to help repel
increasingly severe, climate change -  driven storm events and storm surges, which
threaten to close the only road in and out of Eastbourne. Victoria University has
divested from fossil fuels.
Overseas an increasing number of corporations have taken up the challenge. They are
recognising both the threat that is climate change but also the opportunities of a low -
carbon economy. The massive Norwegian pension fund, worth over a trillion New
Zealand dollars—yes, that is $1,000 billion—has recently divested from 32 coal mining
companies as well as tar sands producers. The fund argues that these companies face a
grim future as action on climate change limits their future production. Stanford
University in the United States has div ested from coal, and, my personal favourite, the
Rockefeller Brothers Fund, established by the heirs to the famous oil magnates the
Rockefeller brothers, is getting out of oil and fossil fuels.
Having understood that change is inevitable and that first movers have the advantage,
companies like Walmart, Mars, and Procter and Gamble are helping to create a
revolution in the power sector by switching to 100 percent renewable energy. Forty -
three percent of Fortune Global 500 companies now have clean energy targets, and
some corporations have even set an internal price on carbon to drive innovation, despite
1374 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
the fact that Governments have not set one. Unilever’s chief executive office, Paul
Polman, a global leader in sustainability, recently said: “Our share price is up 25 percent
in the past 4 months alone, showing the world that you can address tough issues without
touching the economic viability of your business model.” However, no one person or
business—not even one the size of Unilever, a €50 billion company —can win this
climate war alone. Business relies on clear signals from Government about the long -
term price path of carbon before it can reasonably be expected to commit the large
amounts of capital needed to shift to a low-carbon future.
It is now time for this House to play catch-up and to work with those who are helping
the transition that the New Zealand economy needs to make to a low -carbon future. We
need a partnership approach linking individuals, communities, non- governmental
organisations, businesses, and Governments across the globe. Dealing with the threat of
climate change is not only  going to define us as a people, it is going to define the very
nature of leadership.
This House’s record on climate change has been weak. The last two New Zealand
Prime Ministers of our times —Helen Clark and John Key —will be remembered as
expert political managers, as indeed they are, but neither really got on top of the big
one: runaway climate change. To be fair, towards the end of the Clark Government it
did manage to get an emissions trading scheme implemented despite significant
resistance, but the Key Government immediately weakened the scheme.
When you look at New Zealand’s actual emissions over the course of the 21st century
they have consistently increased. And when you understand that New Zealand’s
emissions are set to increase by 50 percent in the next decade, you realise that there is a
huge historical cost to the managerial style of politics that has dominated New Zealand
politics for the last decade. How wi ll we manage the sea when it is lapping at our
doorstep?
The enemy of climate change will not be defeated by coal -driven political
management and business as usual. Abraham Lincoln, Kate Sheppard, and Michael
Joseph Savage achieved remarkable victories for  slaves, women, and the poor, in
moments of great political courage and conviction. Our great leaders —the ones we
remember—stepped outside the current of history and showed how we could live better,
how seemingly impossible hurdles could be overcome with e ffort and ingenuity. They
defined the spirit of the age and expanded the definition of what it means to be human.
Their inspired leadership was a gift of love—no less.
When it comes to the war against climate change we can no longer live in denial by
saying we are so small that we do not matter —the mantra of this Government. That is
not the Anzac spirit. That is not the spirit of the Māori Battalion. If you excuse the
sporting metaphor, imagine if the All Blacks believed that when they ran on to the pitch
to face a country ten times as large as theirs . The climate crisis is a universal call to
arms, and we in this House need to play our part.
In John Key’s post -election interview with John Campbell on TV3, he said: “I will
lead a Government that leads for all New Zealanders. I don’t want to pass everything 61
votes to 60. It’s a really bad place to end up as a Government, just passing everything
with the barest of majorities. I don’t think that’s the right way to govern.” I was
heartened by his statesmanship, his sense of inclusion, and his offer of good will. Surely
climate change, the greatest challenge of our times, is one issue above all of them that
we need to find a way to work on across the House. Our children’s livelihoods are too
important to play partisan politics over.
National plus the Greens plus Labour plus New Zealand First plus the Māori Party —
if we voted on legislation that halted our growing carbon emissions and made polluters
pay, it would send the strongest political signal that we mean busi ness on the climate.
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1375
To whom, besides ACT, could the climate science deniers’ lobby turn to look after its
interests? It sounds deceptively simple to choose collectively an energy -efficient, low-
carbon path for our economy rather than the Government’s curr ent choice of an energy-
intensive, high- carbon pollution economy, one that at some point —we do not quite
know when—is going to end catastrophically. Once we get the price on carbon right and
we have the supporting incentives in place, we have the dynamic m arket economy, the
scientists, the business people, and the social innovators that can do the rest.
This century will be the century of sustainability. The countries and the businesses
that lead the shift to sustainability will dominate this century. How much harder could
New Zealand push in crucial climate negotiations if we could show the world that we
have our own house in order, instead of it being in a mess, and that we are beginning the
necessary transition and the world has not collapsed? But if this  Government continues
with the business -as-usual, pollution-economy approach to the climate, we will fight it
all the way. Our children’s future demands that we do so. The Green Party will work
with the Key Government if this Government changes course and introduces policies to
actually cut emissions, but we will fight it with everything we have got if it continues
down the current path of increasing emissions.
This climate fight should unite us in this House against a common enemy, climate
change, rather t han divide us between the lines of short -term expediency versus long -
term prosperity for our children and for our country. The Greens remember which side
we were on in the battle over apartheid in 1981, and we know which side of the climate
fight we are on in 2015.
Ban Ki -moon, the Secretary -General of the United Nations, said at the World
Economic Forum in Davos that we are the last generation that can take steps to avoid
the worst impacts of climate change. But he also said we are the first generation that can
end poverty. Alongside climate change, tackling inequality is the Green Party’s other
main priority. Like climate change, inequality denies our children the opportunity of the
prosperity that they deserve. Inequality denies our children their health, their education,
and the simple hope for a better future.
We have been waiting 30 years under economic orthodoxy —the spell that economic
growth will deliver us out of inequality and poverty. How many times have we heard
from this Government and Governments past that we just need to grow the economy
first to enable us to address inequality and child poverty? Well, per capita GDP has
grown by 40 percent since the late 1980s, while child poverty rates have doubled. New
Zealand went from a child poverty rate of 11 percent in the late 1980s to 24 percent
today. There are 35,000 more children in severe poverty in New Zealand today than
there were when this Government —this National Government —came to power. That
makes a total of 205,000 New Zealand children living in severe poverty. One in four
Kiwi kids lives in poverty. Somewhere we have gone terribly wrong. These are children
going without the basics like fresh fruit and veges, raincoats, and medicine. These are
kids three times more likely to be admitted to ho spital, five times more likely to die of
cot death, and 27 times more likely to have rheumatic fever. They are likely to stay sick
for much of their lives and die young. Our rates of child poverty are unconscionable.
They are immoral.
The costly interventi ons and wasted potential also have a dramatic impact on
economic performance. In what is likely to be a seminal finding, the OECD, the
Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, the world’s leading
economic thinktank, found late last year that inequality hurts economic growth
significantly. The OECD showed that New Zealand —one of a handful of developed
countries where inequality has grown fastest since the mid- 1980s—has experienced the
biggest loss of economic growth as a result of inequality. T he OECD estimates that
1376 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
New Zealand lost 10 percentage points of growth over the last 20 years due to our
record levels of poverty and inequality. No country besides Mexico has had a worse
record than us.
The OECD has found that “The gap between rich and poor is at its highest level … in
30 years.”, that “inequality has a negative and statistically significant impact on
medium-term growth.”, and that “Policies that help to limit or reverse inequality may
not only make societies less unfair, but also wealthier.” Put positively, policies that limit
or reverse inequality in our society will not only make people’s lives fairer,  they will
make New Zealand, as a whole, wealthier. Doing the right thing about inequality will
reward us economically. And why is it like that? It is pretty straightforward. The OECD
and many others have confirmed that income inequality undermines educational
opportunities for disadvantaged people, especially children, lowering their chance to
upskill and break out of the poverty cycle. We are not talking just about 1 percent or 5
percent of p eople missing out on the basics,  this is about the bottom 40 percent of
families.
The Green Party’s “Feed the Kids Bill” is having its first reading in the first weeks of
Parliament. It is a small, possibly imperfect, response to the fact that hungry kids cannot
learn at school. Let us govern in the interests of all New Zealanders and vote to send
this bill to a select committee, to turn it into the kind of legislation that will leave a
significant legacy for our children.
In 2015—in this year —we can end child poverty and take steps to avoid the worst
impacts of climate change. Are we going to see in this political term a resumption of
business as usual, a style of political non- leadership that manages its way through the
next 3 years doing whatever it takes to stay in power? Or can we escape the trap of the
perfectly human instinct to protect our short-term interests, and provide real leadership?
We have done it in the past. The year 1981, with the anti  - Springbok Tour protests,
was the defining year in which many New Zealanders provided leadership on racial
equality and opposed apartheid. In 1987 the passage of the nuclear -free New Zealand
Act was the culmination of years of leadership by many New Zeal anders on going
nuclear-free. The year 2015 is the year for leadership on climate change and inequality.
The Greens are ready to provide that leadership, and we look forward to working with
many other New Zealanders who also are providing leadership on the se critical issues.
We sincerely hope that the New Zealand Government is one of them.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Mr Speaker, Happy New Year
to you and all other colleagues. Our respects from New Zealand First to Api Mahuika —
it is indeed the end of an era; he was an outstanding Māori leader and a great New
Zealander—and also to Rex Pollock, who recently, sadly, passed away in Tauranga.
To begin this parliamentary t erm let us ask three seriously pertinent questions. What
condition are we in as a country? Are we moving in the right direction?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Yes, we are.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: We will leave Gerry out of that because any answer
Gerry gives is not worth the air it passes on. And are we building a fair, stable, and
prosperous society? Right now the backbench members of the National Party are
beginning to have their knees knock be cause they know we are not. First of all, what
about the quality of public discourse in New Zealand? You see, National is about
shutting down public debate. One of our most brilliant literary people wins the Man
Booker Prize, makes a comment about her country, and what happens with this highly
educated, liberal National Party? Well, it comes out and attacks her, not because of what
she said but her right to even say it. How shallow is that? And that goes for the political
debate as well, because what those members want is the kind of blind obedience that
certain in the financial sector love if it is serving their minority interests. And of course
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1377
the types like Gerry Brownlee are only too happy to serve them because that is what
they have always done. That is what they have always thought of—themselves and their
own privileges. And we have got public sector—
Simon O’Connor: Name the book, Winston.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The Luminaries. Do you want me to read it to you?
[Interruption] See what I mean? Tell me. That is the kind of arrogance that the
backbench of the National Party is going to have to deal with very shortly because it is
going to be sent a message. The message will come with great clarity, and it will know
that not long after that it may be doing what the backbench of the Australian Liberal
Party is doing—standing up for itself for a change, apart from being wanton puppets.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Oh, like yours do.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, New Zealand First is a party of dynamism, as
you can see—of experience, of youth. Which other party went up by 62,000 votes at the
last election?
Denis O’Rourke: We did.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I know. That party had millions of dollars and went
up 72,000, and we had nothing and went up by 6 2,000. That tells us that when it comes
to efficiency of spending money, New Zealand First is the party to back. But then I
know that about 30 or 40 percent  of the National Party supporters are themselves
beginning to think that now. We get the correspondence. They are beginning to get
worried, especially the farming sector, especially the dairy farmers of this country.
But the point is that National members  are about creating a myth —and using
Government departments —that all is well. And the sad thing is that so many in the
commentariat have gone along with them and this mainstream myth that New Zealand
has been doing exceptionally well. When you look at our growth in GDP, exporting —
no, that is down; manufacturing, no, that is collapsing. No, but, apparently —
[Interruption] Oh, there is the lady from Christchurch. She looks at me with a curious
look. I know she is very wealthy, but when manufacturing goes from 33 percent of GDP
and is now heading towards 26 percent, I think you in Christchurch should take notice,
not nod your head as though you do not know anything about it. And what is the export
imbalance with imports right now? Got any idea? Is it heading to $12 billion? Well,
where are you going to be when that happens, when you are coming to getting a job and
keeping your business sustainable?
Now back to reality here. The idea that you have got a competent Government when
inequality and poverty are growing at a greater rate than in nearly every other developed
nation, and homeownership is now being denied to a whole generation of Kiwis —
before the election there was no housing crisis; after the election: “We’ve got the
solution. We’ll change the Resource Management Act and all of a sudden we’ll have all
these houses. We’ll change the Resource Management Act and all of a sudden, by some
miracle, the housing crisis will be settled.” What has happened to public debt? Well, our
debt is up six times now to $65 bil lion under those people who claim to be managers of
the economy. The truth is that the National Party —if you want to really u nderstand the
National Party—no longer works for ordinary New Zealanders; it works for a well -off,
moneyed bunch of cronies both he re and overseas. And, boy, does it pour the money
into propaganda. I mean, for every dollar that we had at the last election, it had $40. It
sprayed it around like confetti and just got home. We have got to take our own
responsibility for that, because we could have stopped it. It is not our fault, of course.
We did our best —make no bones about it —but the reality is that this expenditure from
here and overseas to buy elections is going to come to an end. What we have seen is the
wholesale transfer under National of New Zealand’s wealth into the hands of the few —
and many offshore. Whether selling power generators, flogging State houses now, or
1378 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
decimating the Resource Management Act, the underlying agenda is always the same:
the favoured few will benefit at the expense of the many.
But sooner or later New Zealanders will wake up. Sooner or later in Northland you
will see them respond. Sooner or later they are going to send you a message. Mr Foster -
Bell, are you in or are you out? Come on, put your hand up and tell us. Are you going to
run, son? Tell me, are you going to run? This will be fascinating. Oh, I know he is
keen—I know he is keen. Do not worry, gentlemen and ladies over there, if there is one
party that is thinking seriously about it, it is New Zealan d First. I know that numerous
comments have been made by the Prime Minister. He is getting a bit nervous himself.
He had the audacity to talk about a thing like age. Well, Mr Prime Minister, we do not
dye our hair and we are not losing it —we do not dye our  hair and we are not losing it.
And if I was you, I would just get on with trying to run the country.
Whilst we are at it, he is also giving away the country’s birthright. Look, 95 percent
of the banking sector is owned by Australia. That is the Ned Kelly  policy. A torrent of
profits and dividends and other payments every year go offshore to foreign -owned
banks and you have got not one single policy from National to stop this outflow. The
media is massively owned offshore —Fairfax and APN are both Australian. Insurance
companies are nearly all overseas owned. And farmland and business and residential
property are being sold like confetti.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who wrote this disappointing rant?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Unlike that member  over there, we are able to write
our own speeches. We do not need a dumb researcher to write it. We can do it
ourselves—always have done, always will be able to. Do not ask questions about who
wrote this speech. What you are trying to say is: “Who will ha ve the brains to interpret
it for me?”. That is what you should be asking: “Who on my side has got the
intelligence to interpret it for me, because, clearly, sitting over here and putting my
hands up for somebody in the Mafia will not do any more.” Nationa l members, of
course, do not want to know the truth. National members do not want to know where
the sales are going to. They do not want to know how many of our houses are being
sold. They do not want to know how many houses Bayleys are selling in China every
day now. They do not want to know whether the buyers are coming from Luxembourg,
United States, Canada—they just do not want to know.
Meanwhile, we have got people struggling with stagnant wages in a now growing
high-cost economy. Ask any person comin g back from London or elsewhere, and they
are quite shocked to find how expensive it is—[Interruption] No, not for Gerry, because
Gerry has always had it good. Gerry has always been on the pig’s back —he has always
been on the pig’s back and it shows. I am talking about ordinary New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Must be a very big pig.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, actually, it is a hippopotamus. It is not a pig; it
is a hippopotamus. But the reality is that I am talking about ordinary people struggling
to make families work in this country. Overseas buyers have an insatiable appetite for
our land. Do you know why? With the world’s massively growing population, they
know that arable land is g oing to be more and mor e a high-price product. Do not blame
them; blame the dumb people in politics who do not get it. Look, even Michael Field,
who used to write for the New Zealand Herald—here it is: “NZ farms eyed as
‘boltholes’ for world’s super rich”. It is all there on 20 January in the New Zealand
Herald. Then you go to the next one, on 7 February, 1 week on. Here is Bayleys putting
out its press release saying —this is just what is happening, according to Bayleys real
estate, in Canterbury —that a bevy of foreign landlords is now at the Overseas
Investment Office, and that is what New Zealand wants. We hav e enough landlords of
our own overseas investment and talking about creating jobs, but it goes go on to say
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1379
that they are snapping up properties in Canterbury and all over the country because
rentals are going through the roof. The member from Christchurch over there, of course,
will not do a thing about it because he is in their league. Exploitation of ordinary
people’s needs, desires, and wants is what National members are  about, by their silence,
because in failing to act, they are saying: “This is good enough for us.” There are those
two articles, and we are saying that we need a register. We need to know what is going
on, just like Australia, which has one, and so many other countries.
And then, on immigration, over 50,000 a year came last year, in the last 12 months.
All where to? Auckland. Needing housing? Most desperately. What is my Samoan
friend who is now the Minister for Pacific Peoples doing about that? He knows that the
people who are missing out are his people, that they are being squeezed out everywhere,
but no, no; he is probably like the Māori Party. He wants to go to the airport and give
them a pōwhiri  and make them all welcome. Well, you know, charity begin s at home,
and it begins with the Māori Party recognising that the biggest losers in all this
argument are the people they purport to represent. That is why the Māori Party’s vote is
in decline. That is why it is all over, Rover, because when it had a chan ce to put its
people first, it decided to go for the baubles of office. How tragic is that —how tragic is
that?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: That’s a bit rich.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I know, son. I have resigned and walked out of office
more often than you have had hot dinners. So do not say that it is a bit rich for me. Only
an ignoramus would say that. Learn some history, righto? What sort of Government
would allow an influx of that many —over 54,000 a year —with no jobs, no
accommodation, or  say, as Mr Key did today, that 81,000 is a record for new
employment in New Zealand? How stupid is that? We have had record employment
every year for the last 55 years, because it is axiomatic, is it not? If you increase the
population, you might just get  more and more employment, but what is the level of
unemployment? It is 140,000 who cannot get 1 hour of work a week because when you
get 1 hour of work a week, you are off the register. Well, invite that sort of deceit into
your own mental processes, but we think it is a fraud on the population and we think it
is repugnant in our society. Incomes are stagnant. There is a chronic housing crisis —
140,000 cannot get 1 hour of work a week, and the health system is straining at the
edges. There is massive immigration and growing inequality.
And then, of course, a key issue, mentioned by my colleague Mr Norman in the
previous speech, is climate change. Well, you know, we were the first party to say that
the emissions trading scheme is a rort, and it is.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: You voted for it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: We said that the emissions trading scheme was a
rort. Yes, son, we voted for it when it was $25 per unit. We did not drive it down to
$2.35. That is what Mr Nick Smith did. So do not make that stupid statement, because
some of us remember what we voted for, and he destroyed the forestry industry all at
the same time. Mr Smith, of course, is famous for running with the hares and hunting
with the rabbits. That is what he is famous for. This is the guy who said: “ACC is in
absolute crisis. I must do all this and this and this.” It was a total public relations f raud
of course, and then, of course, ACC found it was in serious surplus.
But back to the point. Today we learn that Skycity is going to be an eyesore. Second
question—how is Skycity going to improve it? The Prime Minister says that the
taxpayers of New Zealand will, and the ACT Party wants to support that.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Absolutely.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, absolutely. No doubt about it. The ACT Party is
so dumb, of course, that when it announced that it was going to change the Resource
1380 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
Management Act, it did not wait to find out what the details were; it just said it would
support it. This is meant to be the most intelligent party in Parliament, with all this
experience, and that member is asked: “What do you think about the Resource
Management Act changes?”, and he said he will support it. Do you know what is in it?
No. Do you know what its content is? No. “But then again, I don’t have to because I am
a puppet.” That is what he really said. “I’m there because the N ational Party put me
there.” Oh, we know that. Even New Zealand First got more party  votes in Epsom than
they did. True—we got more party votes in Epsom than they did. Look, how can you
possibly predicate a political career when you are a puppet and when, every time John
Key says “Jump” you say “How high?”. He is now in charge of the alternative school
system and yet he knows nothing about education. He knows exactly nothing about
education, but, then again, his predecessor was one John Banks and he knew even less.
So that is the ACT Party’s contribution.
Then we have the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS). In June last year we were all
told, 3 months out from the election, that we were not going to the Middle East. The
election was hardly over and all of a sudden the Prime Minister is concerned at these
massive breaches of human rights. Did you see his posturing in the House today? He
went into a fit of concern about human rights abuses by ISIS. What did he say about
Boko Haram? Not a murmur, not a mutt er, not a syllable, not a sound. His concern, and
the Government’s concern, is to be in the club —the club that says that if you go to
Australia and you work there for 21 years and you get tipped out of your job you do not
get the dole any more, you do not get fundamental rights any more. Or if you are in the
UK they have changed all our privileges there. Is that the club he is talking about? Or is
it the club that belongs to  the United States, which says: “We’ll give a free trade
agreement to Chile and Morocco but we won’t give one to New Zealand.” —this great
democracy for the last 155 years. Only nine of us have that great, proud tradition, and
that is the club he wants to suck up to every day?
Prime Minister, we need somebody to stand up for our country’s  interests and our
values. The Prime Minister should not think he can walk on to the stage of New Zealand
politics and, with no parliamentary debate and no consensus, send people into danger,
and maybe imperil this country as well without the decency of a democratic decision by
this Parliament. On the issue of the two flags —we have got Hone’s flag and we have
got the Prime Minister’s flag, until, of course, it looked a bit like the ISIS flag, and now
the Prime Minister has changed his mind and he wants the silver fern. What a diversion
that is! And as for separatism, well, who signed the UN Declaration on the Rights of
Indigenous Peoples? Who has got the two- prison system, the two flags, and race -based
local government now sweeping throughout New Zealand, and Whānau Ora? They are
policies based on race. That is the National Government’s legacy. That is what it has
done, and to criticise Mr Little —well, I cannot use the phrase, but it is a bit like some
utensil calling the other one black. It is pretty sad, is it not, really?
Then, of course, we have a $1 million by -election in Northland that should not be
happening. It was avoidable, because the Prime Minister and many of his colleagues
knew the circumstances well before 20 September  2014. They knew the circumstances,
and the Prime Minister is going to be found out. Anybody who knows Northland knows
it is a rumour mill, and if they know the National Party they know it is an even bigger
rumour mill, and the very idea that the Prime Minister did not know until D ecember
2014 is utterly preposterous. When the police commissioner says he did not drop the
ball, well, whom did he tell? Anne Tolley? I think so. I know Northland. You know
Whangarei. News gets out there before it even gets to the court. News gets out the re
before it even gets to the police station. If you get picked up on a driving charge at 1
o’clock, and at 1 minute past 1  everybody knows. But the only person who does not
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1381
know is this inveterate Minister famous for, as Enid Blyton would say, “forgettery ”.
The Prime Minister, the No. 1 Minister, does not know about all the great serious crises
happening in this country. Whether it be the Coatesville raid, the SIS, the Government
Communications Security Bure au, he just does not know. O n this issue, which w ill be
extremely embarrassing to the National Party —and its hypocrisy will know no bounds
when it comes to fundamental human rights—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I am not concerned about the sub judice issue. I am
talking just about the political issue.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No—the word that member
used.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Yes, that is right. Thank you very much. I am glad
you grasped that, Mr Assistant Speaker. That is very important, because the sub judice
rule does not mean that this Parliament is constrained in a way that I fear we might be.
But it is g oing to be deeply embarrassing, and our message to the people up north is:
“Hang on, because help’s on its way.” Our message to people up north is: “Had
enough? Send them a message. You won’t change the Government but you sure will
make them listen for the  very first time.” And to  the people in Kaipara paying all those
rates for the disaster on the Mangawhai Heads, and Kaikai, Kaitāia, Kaeō, Kawakawa,
and all those forgotten territories, our message is: “Don’t give up. Hang on. Help’s on
its way, and the campaign will start soon.” Thank you very much.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: E Te Mana Whakawā, nei rā te mihi
mahana ki a koe, otirā, ki Te Whare katoa. Ā, te tihi o Hikurangi Maung a, te pāpā,
Tākuta Apirana Mahuika, whārikihia ngā kupu ātaahua o Tākuta Hōhepa Tamehana, ka
mātānawe te manawa, ka haehae taku kiri. Ka noho nei mātou, ka tangi , kua hinga he
tōtara haemata. E  te pāpā, waiho mā mātou āu mahi whakahirahira e kawe, āu wawat a
kia tutuki. Haere atu rā koe ki tōu Kaihanga, ki ngā ringa mahana o Te Atua. Ā, i a koe
e takoto ana kai tō marae o Tikitiki, ka rere ngā mihi whakanui i a koe, ka tika. E te
pāpā, moe mai rā, moe mai rā!
[Mr Speaker, warm greetings to you and indeed to the entire House. To the summit of
Mount Hikurangi, fatherly figure Dr Apirana Mahuika, I lay out the beautiful words of
Dr Hōhepa Tamehana. The heart is scarred and I am lacerated. We sit here and lament
that a strong growing tōtara has fallen. Oh fatherly figure, leave your magnificent work
and your aspirations for us to address and fulfil. Go forth to your Creator and to the
warming arms of the Lord. And while you lie in state upon your courtyard of Tikitiki,
tributes extolling you fly about, and rightly so. Rest, fatherly figure, rest!]
As we mourn the loss of a great leader of our nation, I rise today in quiet reflection
on the work of this significant man. The calibre of this man will not be seen again in Te
Ao Māori. He belonged to the ilk of a  grand and noble generation. His legacy reminds
us of our very foundation as a nation. In this 175 th year since Te Tiriti o Waitangi was
signed, it is right to formally acknowledge the sacred covenant that our nation is built
on and that he and his kind fought so hard to uphold. With the week of celebrations and
commemorations complete, this is our moment to dream big, to dream loud, and to be
proud. This is our time to honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the founding unification
document of our modern nation, a nd to consider the partnership between Māori
astangata whenua and the Crown.
What does it mean to live up to the promise of Te Tiriti? When Te Tiriti o Waitangi
was signed we had a strong and vibrant community based around our marae and our
culture. We were developing a robust economy, trading with early tauiwi visitors and
settlers, and traversing the Pacific to trade on foreign soil. The Māori Party challenges
this Government —indeed, every Government —to honour the obligation it has in
1382 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
exercising kāwanatanga to support partnership with iwi and ensure that Māori
retainrangatiratanga, or self-determination.
In 2014 we heard a lot about the rock star economy. The Prime Minister has outlined
much about that rock star status today. The thing about a rock star is that they build
their success on their fan base. In order to keep it at the top of the charts, a true rock star
must keep the fans happy. In essence, they must be accountable. Some here may
remember Sid Vicious—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who?

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: —Sid Vicious—who once said: “You can’t arrest me, I’m a rock
star.” But in real life, his status meant nothing. When it came to doing what was right,
he should have been doing the right thing. And so when I compare our economic status
as Māori 1 75 years ago, and I look at all the posts that flood our Facebook accounts, I
have to wonder who constitutes the fan base being propped up by the rock star
economy. The thing is if we are to dream big and live up to the aspirations of those who
invested in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, we have to insist on doing all that we can to restore our
communities to the state of relative prosperity they enjoyed at first encounter in 1840.
We owned 100 percent of Aotearoa. Māori were compared by health standards to the
richest of European royals. We must restore our fan base. We must take decisive action
to tackle poverty and its insidious effects. We must leave no stone unturned, and in this
I welcome the opportunity to work with the Government to tackle the crippling effect s
of poverty.
We can start with putting greater income in the hands of those who need it.
According to statistics, between 2009 and 2014, a couple with children had their benefit
increased by a mere $31 a week over that period, while a single superannuitant had their
