income increased by $56 per week. We absolutely agree with the Children’s
Commissioner that we must take a wide lens to this issue. Targeting benefit levels to
bring them in line with the cost of putting healthy food on the table is a start. L et us be
clear: the establishment of a ministerial committee on poverty —the Budget packages
the Māori Party has consistently negotiated since 2008—has established that the
elimination of poverty is our top priority. We are duty -bound to take poverty seriously,
to make poverty a thing of the past, and to avoid getting distracted by token simplistic
approaches. It is evident to us that poverty of the hand is in fact surpassed only by
poverty of the mind and poverty of the spirit. It is simply not sustainable to say all our
answers will come when we have school cafeterias in place to feed the kids. We need to
raise benefit levels and extend the in -work tax credit to families living on a benefit. We
need to create ongoing employment and to continue to support th e amazing initiative
established by the Māori Party for Māori and Pacific trade training, cadetships,
apprenticeships, building school scholarships, and recruitment incentives for teachers.
We are thrilled that trade training schemes like He Toki ki te Rika in Christchurch
are producing fantastic results. Graduates are in paid employment or are undertaking
further study. Partnerships between iwi, industry, and training providers are game -
changers, resulting in industry and training providers reviewing the way they work with
Māori. Ninety-six percent of the graduates from the Māori Affairs cadetship programme
have remained in paid employment or have gone on to further studies. All this leads to
the Māori unemployment rate being the lowest it has been in 7 ye ars. Do not get me
wrong. We are utterly delighted with the investment we have been able to create in
successful futures for so many of our young people through these schemes, but there are
two areas of ongoing priority we cannot ignore. We must increase benefit levels and, at
the same time, we must continue to lift the minimum wage.

items.speaker: The Māori Party asks the question
items.text: what gain is there by retaining the income abyss
between life on a benefit and life in work? Professor Jonathan Boston suggested that the
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1383
gap between those in work and those on a benefit has increased by 25 percent in a
generation. What we want to know is why the gap needs to be so huge in order to
incentivise people to work. We have to remember that two out of five families in
poverty are also in work, so simply getting into work is not in and of itself the answer.
Both benefits and wages are too low, and more direct, immediate action is required.
The Māori Party is not afraid to ask the hard questions. We do not want any
piecemeal solutions.  We do not need any tokenistic apologies or suggestions of
constitutional change without sound policy or strategy to make sure that it is not just
media-grabbing rhetoric. We believe in a value -added future —a future where the
investment we make today will create optimism for tomorrow. We welcome the
difference being made in social housing. So many poor families are paying far too much
for their housing. We are pleased that those with high housing needs who live in
properties run by approved community housin g providers can get the same support that
people in Housing New Zealand properties do.
There is more to do. A warrant of fitness on social housing will ensure the
Government does not abdicate its responsibility to protect the most vulnerable whānau.
I was  grateful to attend the launch of the Te Tai Tokerau economic development
strategy, working to build on the development of the Northland area for Māori. That
strategy recognises that $2.4 billion was the contribution that Māori in Northland made
to that ec onomy every year. Māori in the Northland area, in Te Tai Tokerau, are the
highest numbers of Māori entrepreneurs in the country. We must recognise that there is
value added in Māori strategy. Working with iwi, as the Government has agreed to do,
will ensur e that we can bring to pass the actions of those strategies and not just the
dreams.
If the promise of Te Tiriti o Waitangi is to come together in a unifying way, we need
to uphold its principles. It is time to make a tangible difference to the lives of o ur
tamariki mokopuna; to recognise that we need to do so to ensure, instead of flinging
abuse from the cross benches, that we can work together with the Government tirelessly
and relentlessly to recognise Māori as value added to this country through real
recognition of Te Tiriti o Waitangi; to find ways to enable all of our tamariki to thrive
without fear of abuse, without embarrassment of disparity, and without hunger; and to
ensure they and their whānau are housed in warm and safe homes.
E Te Mana Whakawā,  n e i  r ā  m ā t o u  o  T e  P ā t i  M ā o r i  e  t ū  n g ā t a h i  k i  t e  t a h a  o  te
Kāwana i runga i te wawata o Te Tiriti, hei hiki i aua wawata o ngai tātou te iwi Māori,
hei hāpai i ngā hiahia. Tēnā koe, tēnā tātou.
[Mr Speaker, we of the Māori Party stand in unison with the Government upon the
desire that the Treaty will raise those aspirations of ours, the Māori people, and elevate
the needs. Thank you and us.]

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: One of the benefits of being a younger
member of the House is that sometimes you can learn a thing or two from some of the
older members of the House, and from one, who may be the oldest of all, we got three
very good questions.
What state is the country  in? Well, it is an interesting fact that if you look at the
polling data across the world and you look at Canada, the United Kingdom, the United
States, Australia, and New Zealand, and you ask the people in each country: “Is your
country heading in the right direction or the wrong direction?”, New Zealand is the only
one of the five where people persistently have said the country is heading in the right
direction, for the last 6 years straight. When the member asks the question: “Are we
heading in the right direction?”, the people have answered the question. Maybe he
thinks they are stupid. What he will find out —what he will find out if he stands in
Northland—is that the people there have moved on too. That place has changed since
1384 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
the 1960s. If he stands there it will be a very sad political death. However, I have heard
that he may be leaving me a couple of backbenchers in his will, so it may not be all bad.
Are we getting towards a fairer society? That is a question that I would like to
address in this spe ech. The country is in a good state, and we are heading in the right
direction. I learnt this on the 175 th anniversary of our nation’s founding, up at Waitangi
just last week. I probably speak for many New Zealanders when I say that I had stayed
away all of my life because of the acrimonious pictures on the TV screen that put me off
visiting Waitangi on 5 and 6 February. What a warm and pleasant experience. I had to
say a prayer on a marae—almost two new experiences in one day.
What I found when I watched the TV at the end of that day was something
astonishing and surprising. I thought Andrew Little had wanted to be the Prime Minister
of New Zealand —I really did. All his behaviour up until that point had suggested that
he wanted to be the Prime Minister of New Zealand. We heard from the co-leader of the
Green Party that he knew which side of apartheid he was on in 1981. But does Andrew
Little know the answer to that question, or is he actually trying to bring it back right
here in New Zealand? Perhaps he agr ees with Sir Tīpene  O’Regan, the normally
sensible and respectable man, who said that Pākehā New Zealanders do not know their
history. Well, let me remind Andrew Little, and anyone else who has any doubt, of what
some of our history is.
Perhaps we should start about 400 years ago when Martin Luther challenged the
Inquisition and nailed his theses to the door of Rome. Perhaps we should talk about
William Wilberforce, who campaigned valiantly for years to end slavery in England, or
Abe Lincoln, who did it ac ross the Atlantic, in the US. Perhaps we should talk about
Kate Sheppard, who said that both women and men should be able to vote equally here
in New Zealand. Perhaps we could come forward a little way, to Fran Wilde and Louisa
Wall, who said that people s hould be treated equally before the law, regardless of their
sexuality.
Our heritage and our history is the creation of a free and equal society where
everybody is equal under law, and that is one of the greatest achievements any country
has ever made. If Andrew Little really wants to be the Prime Minister of New Zealand,
he had better back -pedal quickly on the idea that we should be backing down on the
wonderful achievements that our country has managed in becoming one of the most
diverse, free, and harmonious societies that this world has ever seen.
When we come to the question of housing affordability, it is worth thinking how far
we have come on that topic. The Demographia index has been comparing median
household incomes with median house prices every  year for 8 years. When it started
doing it, Helen Clark used to say: “If only they would put some unaffordable European
countries in, New Zealand’s housing affordability might look a little bit better.” Well,
how far we have come —we now have a Government that accepts there is a housing
affordability problem in New Zealand. We have a Government that is actually
addressing the root causes of housing unaffordability in New Zealand. What are those
causes? If you study the phenomena, it is not the tax system. S ydney, Vancouver, and
Los Angeles have much more unaffordable housing than us and they also have a capital
gains tax. It is not the banking system or the interest rates. Many, many markets across
the United States and Canada all have the same banking system. They all have the same
interest rates, but only some markets are deeply unaffordable.
We now have studies of the approach of hundreds of urban housing markets to urban
planning. What do we discover? It is those that take on constrictive urban planning
regimes, and say: “Thou shalt not build there.”, that find themselves with a shortage of
land on which to build, and, as a result, a shortage of houses. It does not matter, as the
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1385
Labour Party would have it, if the Government builds the houses, because eve n builders
working for the Government cannot build houses on no land.
The initiative that this Government will take up is to clean up the Resource
Management Act, take out the vagaries, and make the Resource Management Act about
science—science: physics, chemistry, and biology. The Resource Management Act
should be about biodiversity. It should be about air, water, and soil. It should be about
the physics of noise, of traffic, of shading. But it should not be about vague concepts
that lead to ephemeral goals pursued by urban planners denying an entire generation of
New Zealanders the opportunity to own a home. How far we have come —we are now
reforming the root cause of housing unaffordability. I give the support of the ACT Party
to National on reforming the Resource Management Act at its roots, at sections 5, 6, and
7, and focusing them on science rather than the kind of ephemera that we hear from the
other side of the House. The first step towards building more houses is to free up land
upon which to build them.
Another thing that happened over the last couple of months that I would like to add
to the Prime Minister’s address is that a number of partnership schools have opened. I
have got bad news for the Opposition: boy, are they performing off the charts. The
number of students enrolled is going through the roof. It is 440, up from 360 last year.
The Post Primary Teachers’ Association is terrified of the ongoing success of these
schools. Vanguard Military School —96 and 100 percent pass rates at level 1 and 2.
[Interruption] The member there should go and visit, and see what it does for the kids
who choose to attend this school. But her ideology is more important than those kids
getting skills, getting qualifications, getting jobs, and feeling good about the mselves.
That is why she is going to be staying over there. You could visit any of the other
schools where the results are outstanding, in particular for the context of some of the
challenges that they face.
Next month we are going to see Sir Michael Jone s and Willie Jackson opening
partnership schools. This policy has momentum. It is diverse. It is unstoppable. You
wonder why the Labour Party is in so much trouble in this House. It is because the ACT
Party is now doing its job for it. We are delivering what Peter Fraser promised as
education Minister in 1949. I know it is hard, Tracey Martin, but you need to accept
this. If you really care about—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I beg your pardon, Mr Assistant Speaker. If the member really
cares about delivering on the promise that every child will develop to the full extent of
their powers by our education system, then we must be able to let in new methods. I
actually agree with one of the things that Eleanor Catton said. She said that when you
have success, too many people are there to beat up on you unless they can collectivise it
for themselves. Imagine a world in which the approach of the teachers union, in whic h
the approach of the Opposition, and in which the approach of even Tracey Martin, was
such that we admired people who have taken risks, gone out on a limb, been creative,
and enrolled their kids in order to find ways to address one of New Zealand’s most
urgent problems.
Would it not be nice to live in a country where Eleanor Catton’s concern about tall
poppy syndrome was addressed and we could actually try new things to make kids’
lives better without such negative wailing from all over the Chamber. But,
unfortunately, we fight on, and I am very proud to do so with my colleagues from the
Māori Party, from United Future, and from the National Party. We are going to deal to
the Resource Management Act because when you see that child poverty numbers rise
from 130,000 to 285,000 as soon as you include the figures for housing affordability —
or the effect that has on family budgets —then you know the No. 1 thing we can do for
1386 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
child poverty is expand the supply of housing for New Zealand families, and have we
not come a long way in addressing that?
We know that we are coming into a world and a century when the premium on skills
will be larger than it has been at any previous time, and it is going to be more important
than ever that all New Zealanders have the skills.  We are unleashing social
entrepreneurship in order to achieve that goal. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I am pleased to support a large
proportion of what is contained in the Prime Minister’s statement, and generally to work
with my colleagues in National, ACT, and the Māori Party towards its attainment. But
there is one area that my predecessor, David Seymour, outlined that I could not disagree
with more, and that  is his argument about changes to the Resource Management Act.
The suggestion that that is a silver bullet to our housing crisis is risible, fatuous, and
unbalanced, and those that proclaim it deserve that title as well.
I think that before people put the Resource Management Act into its grave they ought
to think about what it replaced. No one wants to go back to the days of 54 different
pieces of planning law and of the Town and Country Planning Act, which was derided
up and down the country as cumbersome, ineffectual, inconsistent, and chaotic. There is
a majority in this House, I believe—a clear majority—for making sure that the Resource
Management Act is fit for purpose in terms of its procedures and practices. That can be
achieved, and it could have be en achieved as long ago as 2013, when the National
Government first proposed changes, if there had not been the intention at the same time
to change the purpose and principles clauses —particularly, clauses 6 and 7 —of the
Resource Management Act. There is no need to tamper with those provisions to achieve
the efficiencies in the legislation that the vast majority of the members in this House
would seek.
I say to the Minister for the Environment that he should look to every editorial writer
in New Zealand; h e should look to everyone who has expressed impartial concern on
this—not the developers and the commercial interests, but people who have expressed
an impartial concern. They have all urged him to move with caution. I say to the
Government that if it chooses to do as the Prime Minister himself said last year and
proceed with moderate and pragmatic changes, it could well attain significant support in
this House. But if it continues with the attitude that it has shown to date on this issue, it
will get it through at the very best by one vote. That would be a travesty and that would
be a mark of inconsistency, because all of the case law built up over the last 20- odd
years of the Resource Management Act would go out the window. The certainty that is
being proclaimed for change would be replaced by the uncertainty of having to start all
over again. It is a simple nonsense, and yet the Government could resolve the matter
fairly quickly were it not prepared to want to have its cake and eat it too.
I want to talk about a couple of other measures that were contained in the Prime
Minister’s speech that I think deserve the House’s paying some attention to. In the
statement there was a reference very late in the day to the appalling situation now
developing as a result  of the barbarous activities of the Islamic State of Iraq and the
Levant. No one can condone what has been occurring. No one can say that it is in any
way acceptable or meets any reasonable standard of human behaviour. The difficulty
comes in what an effective solution is. When one looks at the Middle East generally, the
immediate conclusion to be drawn is that Western intervention over the last century, be
it from the time of the Balfour Declaration right through to now, has had one universal
outcome: failure, division, and more intense bitterness and rivalry than was in place
before it started. So when we determine as this country what our response to that
appalling situation should be, we need to be guided by the history. Maybe Sir Tīpene
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1387
was right and Pākehā often do not know their history if we seem determined to blunder
in and repeat the mistakes of the past.
We need to be working alongside responsible Governments in the area, encouraging
them first off to seek solutions to their own issues and to seek their own solutions, not
have them imposed upon them by us acting in a “We know best” sense from the outside.
It is a difficult balance because we cannot stand by and let barbarism continue, but at
the same time we cannot act in a way that is simply going  to fuel those fires more
strongly for the future. One of the challenges that New Zealand faces is to draw that
responsible line.
I must say in this regard that the intervention last week of the British Foreign
Secretary on his visit here was anything but  helpful. This Chamber carries the plaques
that remember the consequences of the last time the family acted together: Gallipoli,
and the mindless slaughter of Australian and New Zealand troops in the pursuit of a
British objective; Passchendaele; and the S omme. So to come here and say to New

items.speaker: Zealanders today
items.text: “We love having you on board. You’re part of the family, but you’ve
still got to queue up at the aliens gate at Heathrow.” is unacceptable in the extreme.
I would have thought that a well -briefed visi ting politician would understand the
sensitivity of New Zealanders  on these issues. After all, in the 1980s the more the
United States administration of Ronald Reagan told us what our anti -nuclear policy was
not to be, the more we embraced the stand that t he New Zealand Government was
taking. We are like that as a people. Here is this patronising figure from abroad loftily
telling us that we are in the club, that we are part of the family, and that it would be
lovely to have us along for the next round of unmitigated slaughter. It is simply
unacceptable. New Zealand should draw the line very strongly when it comes to that.
There is one other area that the Prime Minister touched on that is also extremely
important, and I think we can actually start to make s ome progress. There is to be a
review this year of our security legislation. I think that is good. It is proper. But it needs
to be conducted in a transparent and open way. There are two steps that I think need to
be taken sooner rather than later. The review has to be established by 30 June this year.
I think the form of the review needs to be made public well before its establishment, and
I think the draft terms of reference need to be published and socialised around this
House, in the first instance, and more broadly before they are adopted.
This is not a political issue; this is a New Zealand issue. We are talking about New
Zealand’s security interests —New Zealand as a nation, our domestic security, and our
international security. It is not a game of political one -upmanship but a game of
ensuring that those who operate in that very peculiar world are accountable, are
transparent, and have very clear lines of operation that Parliament has ordained for
them. Last year the then -director of the Government Communications Security Bureau
gave an extraordinary speech where he spelt out the objectives of his agency as he saw
them. One of them was advising the Government on military strategy. That is not the
role of an intelligence agency. It might be the belief of those who like wearing trench
coats and walking around in the shadows and what they think is the role of an agency,
but it is not the role of a responsible agency today, particularly against the backdrop of
the revelations that people like Edward Snowden have made and that various other
whistleblowers around the world have shown about the way in which these
organisations operate. No one is actually saying you do not need them, but everyone
seems to be saying they need a more open and accountable environment.
The review this year provides that opportunity, and I sincerely hope that the
Government takes the chance to ensure that what arises is a robust, credible set of
organisations that can meet both the test of public scrutiny and the test of time, because
increasingly, as tensions grow, the challenges that they will face in terms of providing
1388 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
credible, independent intelligence to the Government of the day will also grow. If there
is any doubt about the competence of that, then I think we are in a very sad way.
So 2015 is the centenary year of t he forging of our first nationhood, really, on the
rugged hillsides of Gallipoli and the start of the campaign where New Zealanders first
became part of the world through their participation in World War I. The year is shaping
up to be an extraordinary one . I think that an improving domestic economy and the
opportunities that that will provide in terms of jobs and future opportunities for young
people in particular are important. But the whole rate of technological growth and the
way in which things are cha nging—I saw a thing before I came down here today that
said that the top 10 jobs in industries in Australia did not exist 10 years ago. That is the
rate of change. We are positioned on the cusp of that. Broadly speaking, the measures
that the Government has been following over the last few years position us well to take
advantage of the new opportunities that will arise. There are no blank cheques in
politics and, as I have said, there are issues that I think are important that do need to be
addressed along the way.
Mr Assistant Speaker Mallard, can I begin my contribution this afternoon by
congratulating you on a recent significant event in your life. We all, I am sure, wish you
well from this point. I also want to offer greetings and best wishes to the House as we
start this new year.
More important, I want to support the motion moved by the Prime Minister, the Rt
Hon John Key, and oppose the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition. The
Prime Minister outlined in his very extensive speech the very wide prog ramme that the
Government is currently running. He outlined some of the achievements of the last few
years, but, overall, I think he indicated that this is a Government that is responsive to the
needs of New Zealanders, that does recognise the difficulties  that are in people’s lives,
and that also wants to encourage New Zealanders toward the sort of prosperity that this
country can enjoy on the current policy path that we have.
There were a number of things that have come through in this afternoon’s
contributions and they seem to focus both on national security and on the issues of jobs
and housing. I want to make a couple of comments. Firstly, there were 217,000 new
jobs in the New Zealand economy in the last 5 years under the leadership of the
National Go vernment. That does not happen because a Government has policies; it
happens because people are able to respond to the policies a Government has. It is the
private capital inside our economy that creates the opportunities that provide the jobs.
The Business Growth Agenda, with its 300- plus initiatives, is about opening markets
for New Zealand. It is about getting rid of unnecessary red tape from businesses and
creating an environment where the free flow of capital goes into the productive sector to
provide those jobs—80,000 new jobs last year alone. That is the sort of progress that we
want to see year on year on year. It contributes to the overall3- plus percent economic
growth that we can expect for the near future. It will make a difference to the prosper ity
of New Zealanders. I did not hear one thing from the Leader of the Opposition today
that would convince us that there is anything more that we should be doing. But I can
tell you that if there is more, we will find it and we will do it.
On the issue of housing, which has been brought up by almost every speaker, I think
there are a couple of things that I would take an adverse stance to Mr Dunne on. His
belief is that the Resource Management Act simply needs a little bit of change but no
change to the p urpose because if you change the purpose, you destroy a whole pile of
case law. He actually says that the case law now drives what you can do under the
Resource Management Act, and that is the very problem that we are trying to solve.
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1389
It must be great if you are a developer hearing the likes of the Labour Party, New
Zealand First, the Green Party, and now Mr Dunne saying they do not want to see
changes to the Resource Management Act, because it is that Act that creates the
scarcity—the unnecessary scarcity —of land for development that ensures that you do
have that price moving upward. We have seen that there is now a quantifiable gap in the
amount of housing that is needed in New Zealand to get to a steady state, to get to a
state where places like Auckland will have to put in only about 14,000 to 15,000 houses
a year to keep pace with things. That gap is what forces the price, and that gap is largely
created by scarcity of land and by Resource Management Act rules that ensure that
those who are in a position to put big capital into their developments can sell them at a
premium. We do not mind people making a few quid, but we are not going to have the
sort of soft protection that a law like this provides in the guise of it being
environmentally friendly. It is utter rubbish and Mr Dunne is in the wrong space on this.
I also found it fascinating that when the Leader of the Opposition started talking
about affordable housing today, he started out by telling us about the terrible story of a
young couple who had just bought their first home and had to take on a $700,000
mortgage. Well, let me tell you, I did a bit of quick calculating. What that would mean
is that that young couple had to have an income between them of somewhere in the
vicinity of $207,000 a year to be able to afford the repayments on a 40 percent
mortgage. If the Leader of the Opposition is actually telling us that people on joint
incomes of $200,000 a year are their target, then he has failed before he starts. We have
a programme that will start in April of this year allowing young people to combine their
savings by way of KiwiSaver and their own resources at much, much lower levels to
buy into housing. What he also says is that because he does not want Resource
Management Act change, he accepts t hat there is going to be this massive escalation in
first home prices. That is the sort of thing that you are getting out of the Opposition
members. It is never going to take them anywhere because it will not provide
opportunities for young New Zealanders. It is totally the wrong face.
The other issue that has come up this afternoon, somewhat repeatedly, has been the
issue of the nation’s security. People will have heard the “passioned” way in which Mr
Key spoke about his reaction. I think that typifies the reaction of most New Zealanders
watching on their screens, seeing in their social media, learning about the evils of the
Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) or, as it is better named, Daesh. Giving it the title
of being an Islamic State is unreasonabl e to everyone who proclaims the honest and
peace-loving aspects of the Islamic religion. So let us call them Daesh, these evil people
who have desire to take over a significant part of the world, if not the whole world.
When we look at their tactics, it i s ridiculous for anyone to say that a country like
New Zealand would be immune from that type of activity; we are not. No one can
accuse this Government of rushing to war, as one or two speakers have suggested today.
We have been extremely cautious in the way we have gone about things, and we will
continue to be cautious. There has been no decision made about what sort of
contribution we might make, but I do want to inform the House this afternoon that I
have asked the Chief of Defence Force to begin some p reliminary training of troops
who may be asked to assist in a capacity -building mission in Iraq. That is one of the
things that we are currently considering, but I want to make it very clear that the request
made of the Defence Force today does not pre -empt any decision Cabinet might be
making about a contribution. It is simply recognising that things are moving very, very
fast in this regard and that we do not want to be caught on the back foot.
Since the initial decision we have had some of our military people in the Middle East
go into Iraq to have a look under their own reconnaissance at what the situation is.
Then, of course, we have had an interaction with the Australians, considering what a
1390 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
wider mission might be. But that mission, if it were to be a pproved, is very much to
have a focus on the training of Iraqi troops, on increasing the capacity of the Iraqi
security forces. To those who say: “Well, look, that’s no good because the Americans
spent all that money over those 10 years and it failed.”, al l I will say to them is this: it
failed because there was a corrupt Government there that allowed that military security
force to fall apart. There is a Government there now trying to bring all parties together,
and I want to make it absolutely clear and r epeat the view of the Prime Minister that it
would take an invitation from the legitimate Iraqi Government for us to be involved in
any capacity-building exercise. So, to sum up, no decision has been made. There is a lot
more work to be done, but there is a preparedness should we get caught short, and I
think that is perfectly reasonable.
I want to reserve my final comments for the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who keeps
doing this dance of the seven veils about perhaps going to stand as the candidate in
Northland. Well, I want to say, and if I can quote to you, that he said of a former
member of Parliament who was then a list member of Parliament going to stand in a
seat that the member was a carpetbagger who conveniently forgot his pledge to serve
diligently as a list MP and that he took taxpayers for a ride by not resigning in order to
campaign for the by -election seat. I want to say, then, that if Mr Peters stands by
everything he said, when is he going to resign?
Well, he will not be resigning because he will  not be standing. He did not stand in
Helensville. Everyone remembers in 2010 that he was out there and was going to be in
the 2010 election challenging the Prime Minister. He was the guy who was going to
take him down, but what happened? He limped off int o the corner and nothing
happening there. In 2011 he ended huge amounts of speculation when he kept saying he
was going to stand against Simon Bridges in Tauranga. There was big loud noise and
lots of headlines —Winston was going to do it —but what happened?  Off in the corner
again—off in the corner again. Then, of course, there was the same old act in the last
election. As soon as Colin Craig was in the picture, Winston was up there standing
alongside him on the hustings, saying: “This is the seat I’m going to stand for. I’m
going to take Mr Craig down. I’m going to take the National Party down. I’m the man.”
And what happened? Straight back to the corner. Well, Pita Paraone, let me tell you that
you are likely to be the New Zealand First candidate. Good luck  to you. See you on the
hustings.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I wish to begin by joining those who have
acknowledged Ngati Porou’s loss. There are certainly some leaders in this country who
will not, and cannot, be replaced, and “Uncle Api” was one of those people.
I also want to welcome you back to the Chair, Mr Deputy Speaker. You could be
forgiven, though, for feeling like you never left, especially listening to the Prime
Minister’s statement at the beginning of the sitting of this Parliament. He started with a
motion of confidence, as is the practice in this House —a motion of confidence in his
Government. He claimed that his Government is working for New Zealand.
I decided to listen quite keenly to what evidence the Prime Minister had to back up
the statement that his Government is indeed working for New Zealand. The first thing
that he mentioned in his speech was —amongst the poor -taste jokes—job creation, and
this notion that this has been a Governm ent that has somehow focused on creating
employment. But just because you say it does not make it true. Of course no one is
denying that there have been new jobs created in New Zealand. Of course there have
been. Every time a new start-up employs a new individual—

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Yes, 80,000 new jobs —but how many jobs have been lost?
How many jobs have been lost? How many unemployed individuals are there as a
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1391
result? I think we need to correct your figure, Mr Smith. There are 46,000 more New
Zealanders unemployed today compared with when that Government came into office—
46,000 more New Zealanders unemployed. Surely that is the number that matters. That
is the number that represents individuals w ho find themselves seeking employment,
cannot get into work, and have been in that situation as a result of lax policies around
job creation. In just the last quarter the number of Kiwis out of work grew by 8,000.
The thing that is most devastating about t hose numbers is —as Andrew Little pointed
out in his state of the nation speech at the beginning of the year —it does not have to be
that way. If you make employment, job creation, and work a focus of your Government,
it does not have to be that way.
The last Labour Government, for instance, maintained unemployment levels at 4
percent or lower for 4 straight years from 2004 into 2008. We had the lowest
unemployment in the OECD. Today we are 10 th. [ Interruption] In amongst all of the
other countries, Mr Smith, that have experienced the same global financial crisis, we are
10th. That is not something to be proud of, but we personally believe that we can be the
lowest again if we focus on job creation. It is not just about the jobs we create, though.
It is also about the jobs that we hang on to. There are a number of jobs in sectors like
manufacturing, where we have had extraordinary job losses, and it did not need to be
that way. If we work with business, if we work with unions, if we work with
entrepreneurs, then it is possible to attain the goal that we are aspiring to as a Labour
Party.
We have put a particular focus on small business, and for good reason: 41 percent of
new jobs are coming from that sector. It is an incredibly important sector in the business
community, and yet we have had a tendency to pay mere lip service to the issues that
are quite unique to that sector of the business community. The Inland Revenue
Department is particularly focused, for instance, on consulting with larger corporates
when their needs and their way of doing business are entirely different from those of the
small to medium sized enterprise community. That is just an example of how we could
be making sure that we tailor our response to not only policy but the basic day -to-day
filing of forms. Interaction with the Government could be improved enormously if we
just listened directly to that sector.
There are some new challenges that we need to focus on as well. What are we doing
to support businesses—not start-ups—that have actually been here for 10 years or more
and want to go to the next level but do not have the time or the energy to ensure that
they have the capacity to do that? What are we doing about them? What are we doing
about businesses of the baby boomers, who have not  had the time to even form a
succession plan, and when they leave their business, their business goes? What are we
doing about them? There are so many opportunities that we just need to tap into and that
is what Labour will be focused on over the next few years.
The second piece of evidence I heard from John Key that this Government is
apparently working on for New Zealand was the mystery higher incomes that everyone
is meant to be experiencing. Notice that he always refers to “on average” when he uses
that statistic. My one simple question is: higher incomes for whom? Because if, for
instance, your income is outstripped by the cost of living and your ability to put a roof
over your head, does it count? Well, the average New Zealander certainly does not fee l
better off. That is particularly exacerbated by the housing situation in Auckland in
particular, and there is no denying it.
My challenge to Mr Key, and, actually, to all of the National Government, is to take
five, maybe 10 young people aged between, say, 20 and 35 and ask them how they feel
about housing in this country. Ask them about the prospect that they have of owning
their own home, how daunted they feel about the possibility of their ever entering into
1392 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
the property market, and how that threatens their financial security for the rest of their
lives. This is not something being beaten up by the Opposition. If the members on that
side of the House were talking to those young people, they would know that it is,
genuinely, in their minds, an absolute crisis. How could a real, genuine response from
that Government be to simply sell State houses?
This is something I also do not  understand. State housing is one of the biggest issues
that I have people coming into my office about. It is one of the most significant. There
simply are not enough houses. I would really like to hear —genuinely, hand on heart —
National members tell me tha t the lack of State housing in their areas is not an issue. If
they genuinely believe that it is an issue, how is selling these houses going to improve
the situation? I would wager that there are as many members on that side of the House
who have as many q ualms about this policy as we do. It is not just the tragedy of
housing for those who are most vulnerable, for my entire generation, and for those who
are yet to come into the housing market who are suffering under the lack of action from
this Government.
There were the other bits of evidence that the Prime Minister rattled off in his speech
that were somehow meant to convince us that this Government is working for New
Zealanders. The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) —international issues—was one
of them. I take great offence at the implication from the Prime Minister in his speech
that by challenging his plan, somehow we do not care about human rights. We cannot
shut down debate on the question of whether we send our troops into conflict to face
dire consequences like death on the battlefield just because the Prime Minister thinks
that by raising the debate we do not care about human rights. That is insulting.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Just turn the other way.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: That is insulting. Of course we care. The issue is not whether
or not ISIS is brutal. That is not in question—of course it is brutal. The question is not
whether or not the international community should react —of course we should. The
question is wha t the most effective course of action is. That is the debate that we are
under an obligation to put before that Government, and it is yet to satisfy that question
as to what the most effective course of action is. It is insulting, Mr Smith, that you think
that by challenging the grounds on which you are putting this —the explanation and
evidence under which you propose putting our troops into battle —we somehow do not
care about human rights. That is absolutely insulting.
Finally, the Prime Minister mentione d that under the banner of helping children in
poverty and vulnerable families—something we have been waiting 6 years to hear more
from the Government on —the Government is finally “looking at ways to help families
and children in material hardship”. Materi al hardship is only one of five measures of
poverty. It is one of five. He has clearly used the words “material hardship” on purpose.
If he were genuinely interested in looking at the poverty children are living in, he would
not exclude income poverty. Tha t is where this crucial debate lies. Until we address
that, we will not address the hardship our families are living in.
The Prime Minister may claim that National is working for New Zealanders, but for
which ones? Housebuyers? Those on zero- hour contracts? Children without enough to
get by? Families working hard but going nowhere? Any Government that genuinely
wanted to work on behalf of all New Zealanders should be doing something about them.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, it is a great pleasure
to be back in the House for 2015, and it is certainly a pleasure to welcome you back to
your role in the Chair, a role that you have taken to with some gusto and are performing
very well. Look, I am delighted to be back and looking ahead to another year of the
whole National -led Government delivering genuinely better outcomes for New
Zealanders. You heard it from the Prime Minister today. We were elected with the
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1393
strongest mandate this country has seen under the  MMP system of Government. Every
single one of us is committed to using our time here to make New Zealand a better place
for its inhabitants. We are not here to think about how we can preserve our own political
careers, how we can further our agendas, or how we can last the longest in this place.
Most of us have come from successful careers in the wider world. We have come here
because we are passionate about this country, we are passionate about making a
difference, and we believe that under John Key’s leadership and with the team we have,
we have a team of people who absolutely can do that. That is what gets us up every
morning. That is what we are committed to this year and throughout this term.
This year you are going to see an incredibly busy programme of action from the
National-led Government. You have heard the Prime Minister talk about it this
afternoon. My colleague the Hon Dr Nick Smith will be right at the forefront of that
with some of the most important reforms that are facing New Zealand, I think,
particularly reform of the  Resource Management Act, which anyone who looks at it
sensibly knows is fundamental to getting the outcomes this country needs, both
economically and environmentally. It is not serving anybody well. I wish my colleague
the very best with advancing those reforms that he has worked very hard on. Similarly,
in the freshwater space where excellent progress is being made, in the housing space, in
the creation of more jobs, and in the creation of better healthcare for all of our
community and particularly for those under 13, we will be working to provide better
outcomes for all New Zealanders.
As well as doing that, we understand that it is our job to play our part in the
international community. The security of our people is fundamentally any
Government’s first concern. In the world that we inhabit we all understand that security
is no longer just a domestic issue. Security means taking our part in the international
community, taking it with great caution and care, but knowing that it is not enough to sit
at home and say: “Gosh, isn’t it terrible what’s happening to those people?”. Sometimes
action is required. It is a very difficult decision and one that is taken with extreme care,
but we know that playing our part in the international arena is a core part of what keeps
our country safe.
I want to take the rest of my time this afternoon talking about some of the areas that I
am going to be focusing on in my portfolio. I want to start  with the issue of
connectivity. I am passionate about the fact that New Zealanders’ connectivity to each
other and to the world is an absolute foundation stone of our success. I can tell you that
over the time we have been in Government we have seen a ste p change in New
Zealanders’ ability to connect with each other and connect to the world. Just recently
Statistics New Zealand has announced that we have now seen a 34 percent increase in
the number of Kiwi homes connected to the internet since 2006. We have seen
significant increases in average speeds and we are moving up the OECD rankings. Last
year Akamai noted that New Zealand’s speeds had increased over that year by 37
percent, placing us now well ahead of Australia, which is always comforting. TrueNet
also for the same period noted that our average speeds are up 34 percent. So whatever
measure you want to choose, one thing is being noticed internationally, and that is that
New Zealand is making incredible steps forward in both its connectivity and the s peeds
available to New Zealanders. We are now second in the OECD for the growth of fibre
subscriptions, so in 1 year we have seen 144 percent growth in fibre subscriptions.
This has not happened by accident. It is not just the inevitable march of technology.
It has happened because this Government has committed now $2 billion to the roll -out
of better broadband for our cities, our towns, and our rural communities. We do it
because—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: And what a difference it makes.
1394 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Exactly that. We know that connectivity means that every
town—the smallest village, the smallest rural community —can then trade with the
world and build their own futures. That is what this Government believes in: providing
the tools for r egional, provincial, and rural New Zealand to access the world from
wherever they are. That is why we have committed $2 billion, and that is why you are
seeing from us a big move now to go beyond our first target of 75 percent of New
Zealanders connected w ith fibre to the home to now 80 percent of New Zealanders as
the goal we are working on this term. We are spending $100 million more than we have
already committed to rural broadband infrastructure and another $50 million to ensure
cellphone black spots ar e filled. This is why New Zealand is increasingly seen to be at
the forefront of connectivity. This will be our agenda to continue that rapid pace.
Let me talk now broadly about what is happening in the justice space. Again, we
have a story that I think e very one of us on this side of the House is rightly very proud
of. We are seeing crime at the lowest level for 35 years. I want to acknowledge the
Ministers who have worked before me, yourself included, Mr Deputy Speaker, the Hon
Judith Collins, the Hon Simon Power—all of those Ministers who have worked over the
last 6 years in this space. The record that we now stand on is a very strong one. But, as
ever, there is more we can do. We are not going to sit back and say: “Isn’t that great?
We can now put that one in the ‘done’ box.” There is more work we have to do. This
Government set itself a very bold goal of better public service targets across all of the
areas of service that matter to New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: And we’re delivering.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: We are delivering, but they are hard. We deliberately made
them hard targets because we wanted to stretch the Public Service and ourselves. In the
justice space all of our four targets around total crime, youth crime, reoffendi ng, and
violent offending are on track to meet those targets. But if there is one area where I
think we have to make better progress, it is under that broad umbrella of violent
offending. The thing that makes me sit up and really look at these figures the most is
that half of our violent offending is related to family violence. We have one of the
highest rates of family violence in the OECD. That is not something that I am prepared
to accept and I am sure every member in the House would agree with me that a s a
country we cannot continue to accept this level of family violence. Fifty percent of our
homicides are family violence - related. That means that on average we lose 14 women,
seven men, and eight children every year to family violence. Every 6 minutes there is a
notification to the police for family violence. This is not something that New Zealand
should put in the too-hard basket. It is not something we should simply accept. All of us
have to take steps to change this.
I would love it if there was a s imple initiative—well, it would not be simple —that
the Government could run that would simply fix it. I am certainly open to all
suggestions from around the House and around society as to what the Government can
do. It is not just an issue for the Governme nt; it is an issue for every neighbour, every
friend, every relative, and every colleague when they see someone and think about how
they can reach out.
Some of the things that we are going to be doing in this space are certainly building
on what has been done before. We have seen the roll -out of the victims’ offender levy,
which I remember our opponents across the House said would never work. They
scoffed and said: “You’ll never get it paid.” There has been $16.5 million raised
already—a 75 percent collection rate, which is far and above anything that we had
predicted and certainly yards ahead of what the doomsayers on the other side said would
happen. Those funds are now providing better services for victims so that they can play
their part in the justice system. We are going to go further than that. We have to look at
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1395
more intensive case management for those most at risk. We are going to be appointing a
Chief Victims Adviser and rolling out the safe home programme nationwide. We are
just kicking off a comprehensive review of the Domestic Violence Act and how
protection orders work in this country, because there is room to do that better.
We have to look m ore closely at how the court system provides for the victims of
domestic and sexual violence. In my view there is not a system that will make appearing
in court, telling your story, and having that evidence tested simple or easy, but
absolutely we can do better and I think we must do better. We cannot have a country
where we have senior members of our society telling women: “Don’t come forward
because the process is too horrific.” We will never get on top of the problem if we are
telling victims not to come  forward. We have to encourage them to come forward and
we have to build a system that supports their doing that. That is going to be at the
forefront of my time in the justice sector. I believe that we can do more. I have said
before in this House and I will say it again that my door is open to anyone in this House
who wants to work constructively with me on that.
That is just one of the issues under way in the justice sector. We will be doing a lot
of work this year around continuing the good work to ens ure our courts work faster and
more efficiently, and that cases are progressed quickly. We will be looking at the
ongoing review of our privacy legislation to ensure the right information is being
supplied to the right people at the right time. And, as I h ave been talking about just
recently, we are going to have to take steps to address the issue of deported criminals
coming back when we do not have a good record of that, so we can monitor them. We
have a busy programme of work. It is a Government I remain incredibly proud to be a
part of and I want to wish all members a successful 2015.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I note that this call is taken by the Green Party and will
be a split call, 5 minutes each. I call Denise Roche.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I want to join with previous speakers in the House to
send my condolences to the people of Ngati Porou for the sad passing of Dr Apirana
Mahuika. A great leader has fallen and we acknowledge that.
I have been perusing the statement that the Prime Minister tabled this afternoon in
the House, which outlines the programme of work that National is looking at
introducing this year. I note that in his opening statement the Prime Minister out lines
the four priorities of the Government. One of them is to responsibly manage the
Government’s finances. This comes hot on the heels of the Prime Minister’s comments
today that he has not ruled out putting more taxpayers’ funds into the supposedly free
convention centre that Skycity is building in Auckland. That does not strike me as
responsible fiscal management. For a Government of so- called business people, this
Government has got appalling negotiating skills. It cannot even negotiate a cost -neutral
deal. New Zealanders were supposed to be getting a free convention centre. The
Government’s own papers show that the original deal negotiated goes $67 million in
favour of Skycity for that deal. Right from the start this Government has bent over itself
to give Skycity every opportunity to squeeze more profits out of New Zealand taxpayers
and to pass those profits on to its shareholders. Skycity posted a profit of $69 million
this year and it is coming back and asking the taxpayer for a bailout so that it ca n
increase those profits.
The deal that this Government originally negotiated with Skycity is set to deliver it
$35 million a year so that the $402 million convention centre will be paid off within 10
years. These earnings result from the concessions that  this Government gave to Skycity,
including the changes that this Government brought through legislation through the
House the year before last, and that legislation was passed by only two votes. This
1396 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
Government is saying that it wants to govern for all Ne w Zealanders. That is a woeful
track record so far.
Skycity is obviously the better negotiator. The concessions it got for the convention
centre deal include an extension of its casino licence for another 25 years, effectively
ensuring that Skycity has th e monopoly on gambling at casinos in Auckland, and that
concession alone is worth millions of dollars. The free convention centre is also paid for
with the addition of 230 pokie machines, 12 automated gaming tables, which will
accommodate up to 240 gambler s, and 40 additional card tables. All these gambling
concessions add up, essentially, to a whole new casino added on to the one that Skycity
has already got. The Minister for Economic Development, Steven Joyce, said in 2013
that for little, if any, investment by taxpayers, the convention centre would be built. But
even before this latest approach by Skycity for more money, the taxpayer would still be
paying for this deal. The Government’s own papers show that there will be 6,500
children impacted by problem  gambling as a result of that deal, and the misery that we
will make these children suffer is the price that we will pay.
We have a Prime Minister who is not ruling out bailing out the cost overruns that
Skycity says is the result of its latest design for  its hotel, its casino, and the convention
centre. That overrun is about $140 million—a 25 percent increase— and you cannot
blame Skycity for coming back to the Government to do this because a snake is a snake,
after all. But it is time that we cashed in ou r chips and walked away from this deal. As

items.speaker: Kenny Rogers says
items.text: “You’ve got to know when to fold them.” It is time to walk away.
Thank you.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ngā mihi nui  ki a
koutou. Kia ora. It is great to be back. Happy New Year to all the members. I would
actually like to congratulate the Prime Minister, John Key. I mean, what is it, his
seventh Prime Minister’s statement, and I think this is the first one where he did  not try
to blame Helen Clark for everything going wrong in the country. He had to look in the
mirror a bit himself. But listening to some of the speeches you can see exactly why
young Kiwis are tuning out of our country’s politics. What they heard was neg ative
name-calling, pointless point-scoring, partisan—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: He’s the expert!

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: We know that Nick Smith was one of our country’s youngest
ever members when he came in and he has got to ask the q uestion why Kiwis are not
participating. They tune into this House and they are sick of all this partisan point -
scoring they are seeing. What they want to see is less of the Dr Strangelove, less of the
Dr Dolittle comments, and what they got instead was Dr  Norman, who actually finally
gave them what they want, which is a real debate about the issues, a real discussion, a
real focus on solutions, which is not what we heard from the Government side.
What Dr Norman spoke about was the issues, and he talked about our priorities,
which are climate change and inequality. This is something our Prime Minister could
not mention even once in his speech. We have seen the Pope, the US President, and the
Chinese President all make climate change—the greatest threat of o ur generation—their
priority this year, but our Prime Minister could not mention it even once. It was in his
written speech, but it did not make it into the Prime Minister’s comedy set, but the extra
funding for oil and gas in New Zealand—extra subsidies f rom New Zealand taxpayers
for what is already one of the wealthiest industries in the world—did.
At a time when we have seen the oil price bottom out at around 50 bucks a barrel,
when investment is declining all around the world, at a time when we know that climate
change is one of the most important threats facing us, and even the International Energy
Agency says we cannot afford to burn two- thirds of the oil we have already found, at a
time when you see Stanford University, the Norway sovereign wealth fund, the
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1397
Rockefeller Brothers Fund, Victoria University, Dunedin City Council, and the
Anglican churches all divesting away from fossil fuels, we see our Prime Minister
wanting to invest in more of it from taxpayer subsidies.
We know that climate change an d inequality are environmental, social, moral
questions and challenges, but they are also economic and, as we know, when it comes to
inequality the OECD has estimated that 10 percent of New Zealand’s gross domestic
product has been slashed as a result of our growing inequality. Likewise with climate
change. We have seen from the Stern Review that we could be at risk —10 to 20 percent
of our global GDP. What we heard from the Prime Minister and National, as a party that
cannot get a surplus, is flogging -off o f the assets, and now it is looking at people’s
homes.
Under National, Kiwis work some of the longest hours for some of the lowest pay
and pay some of the highest costs of living in the world. It is a sign that the National
Party does not have a plan for our economy. It is a gambling plan, as we heard from
Denise Roche, when it comes to Skycity, and as we hear with its big picture, its big plan
for the New Zealand economy: hope that someone foreign finds something in the
bottom of the ocean, it is oily, we can export it, and they do not leave too much of a
mess. That is not a plan for our economic future or a richer New Zealand.
A future for New Zealand is a smart Green economy, one built on innovation. The
latest statistics from the Parliamentary Library show that research and development
spending from the Government has actually declined 3 percent. It is great it has got a
target. It has got a target for business to spend 1 percent of GDP on research and
development, but the way the Government is going about it, it could not spend any less,
because we already spend less than half of what average OECD countries do. If we want
to have a richer economy, we need to invest in innovation and research and
development to kickstart a smart Green, innovative economy.
Another area totally ignored by National is the clean energy phenomenal economic
opportunity—a sector that Bloomberg has just said has almost reached a bumper year,
with more than $310 billion in capital investment last year, an  area
PricewaterhouseCoopers says is a $22 billion economic opportunity for New Zealand.
In New Zealand, our solar sector has grown 300 percent in the last 2 years, despite the
uncompetitive barriers in the market that National has put in the way. Every 2½ minutes
another American business or house goes solar.
When it comes to the IT sector, sadly, under National, a quarter of New Zealand
families still do not have internet or computer access. At the current rate National is
addressing it, it is going to take 227 years for all New Zealanders to finally get online.
But at least the Minister Amy Adams is not standing still. I saw she put out a very
important press release today urging Kiwis to change their passwords. So we have got
changing passwords and chan ging the flag but no plan for a richer New Zealand, just a
plan to gamble when it comes to dodgy deals, trying to bet against the house with
Skycity, and hoping someone finds some oil, when the world is moving to a smart
Green clean energy sector.
This is the challenge we issue to the Government. We are going to stand up for a
smart Green economy, one that tackles the challenges of inequality and climate change.
We are looking forward to the next 3 years. We are excited about the opportunity
because, ultimately, our vision is one shared by tens and hundreds of thousands of New
Zealanders who do want a richer New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It is great to be back in
Parliament as part of John Key’s team, which is implementing its ambitious programme
for New Zealand. Today’s speech from the Prime Minister said it all. New Zealand is
going well. We have got a plan to keep New Zealand moving forwa rd, and we are
1398 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
getting on and delivering the things that we got such a strong mandate in September to
deliver on.
A quick rebuttal to a couple of the comments. Disappointment —I live in hope that
one day we will have a Green Party in Parliament that actual ly is concerned about
improving our environment. A change of leadership I note is well overdue, but I just
hear the same old, same old. I also have to note that there is going to be a by -election in
Northland, and I read on the wires that Mr Peters is going to be having a crack and he
has been saying that this is the opportunity for Northland to get help on its way. Well,
let me just put the facts of the record straight, because the way that MMP works is that
if Mr Peters does succeed in Northland—and I have got far more faith in the good sense
of the people of that region than to elect that has -been, but if they do elect him —guess
where help is on its way from. It is from Invercargill, because what would happen
would be that if the people of Northland vote for Winston Peters, they would elect to
Parliament a Ms Ria Bond, the next New Zealand First member on the list, from
Invercargill. I know that there is some unusual Winston- speak, but I do not think the
people of Northland will be voting for a new member of Parliament from Invercargill,
which has a great member of Parliament in Sarah Dowie.
The focus of my contribution on the Prime Minister’s statement is our environment
and housing programme this year. But, first, can I rebut the litany of negativity we have
had from members of the Opposition this afternoon. You see, New Zealand is doing
well, and members opposite hate it. In fact, I cannot recall a time in my 25 years as a
member of this House that New Zealand’s vital economic statistics were in such goo d
shape. Let us have a look. Economic growth—3 percent per year projected by Treasury,
another 3 percent next year, and another 3 percent the year later. The cost of living was
running at 5 percent when we became Government. New Zealanders were going
backwards in their standard of living. Inflation is under 1 percent —the lowest in the 25
years—
Denis O’Rourke: Interest rates are going up.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: —since I have been a member of this House. The member
from New Z ealand First has got the cheek to mention interest rates. Well, as housing
Minister I have got an interest in that. Do you know that interest rates are at the lowest
level they have been for 40 years? In fact, I saw in an ad in the paper that you can get a
first-home mortgage at 5.4 percent. The last time you could do that was in 1967, when I
was in nappies. I look at job growth—80,000 new jobs in the last year. That is
something of which we should be proud. I have a simple message for the whingers
opposite, and that is “Tell me a country right now that is doing better than New
Zealand. Tell me a country right now that is doing better than Godzone, here in New
Zealand.” Kiwis know it —Kiwis know it. I will tell you why Kiwis know it. Do you
know that in the l ast quarter—the last quarter of 2014—for the first time in 25 years,
more New Zealanders left Australia to live here than the other way round. People are
voting with their feet with confidence in the programme of this Government.
Those growth challenges I  spoke of in jobs and in terms of the number of people
living in New Zealand bring with them growing pains, and housing is one of those that I
want to talk about. This Government is on the case with a comprehensive and
considered programme of reforms to in crease both the supply and the affordability of
housing.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Hasn’t got a clue—hasn’t got a clue.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Well, here is a clue for you, Mr Cunliffe . If we look at the
Productivity Commission report, what did it say was the biggest increase in the price of
housing? The price of sections. In fact, it said that the price of a section since 2000 has
gone up from $100,000 a section in Auckland to $300,000. That is an increase of 300
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1399
percent. But if you look in terms of the price of a building, that has actually gone up by
half that. Another way of looking at it is the fact that where a house used to be made up
of 40 percent for the section price, today in Auckland that is 60 percent. And if we look
at the report that has come out from the Motu Economic and Public Policy Research
Trust this year, the report from the Registered Master Builders Federation of New
Zealand—all of them say that the core issue is dealing with the issue of land supply.
So I am aghast when I hear members like the Leader of the Opposition saying
“What’s the RMA got to do with the issue of housing affordability?”. Well, let me tell
him. What is the law that governs the creation of sect ions and land price? It is the
Resource Management Act. And I say to this Parliament that if there is a member in this
House who is seriously concerned about housing affordability, knowing that the biggest
increase has been in section price, you need to look at the law that governs the
development of sections, and that is the Resource Management Act. That is the
Resource Management Act, and when I hear the Leader of the Opposition and other
members in this House steadfastly refusing to consider change to that Act, I say that
they are the enemy of the young family who aspires to own their own home. Let me
give just a simple example: a 29 -hectare block of unimproved land in Auckland—29
hectares—going from a value of $890,000 in 1998 to $115 million since then solely
because of the metropolitan urban limit that has put a rigid barrier around the growth of
Auckland, which has enabled that landowner to make over $100 million at the expense
of young families who want to aspire to own their own homes. And members opposite
refuse to deal with the regulatory issues that are at the heart of that issue.
Su’a William Sio: How many houses?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member opposite has just interrupted. He said “How
many houses?”. Well, l et me tell you about the number of houses. When we came to
Government in November 2008, 1,000 houses were being built per month. Do you
know how many houses last year were built? It was 2,000 houses per month—24,000
houses. Residential building investment in 2014 was $10 billion. That is the most that
this country has ever invested in residential housing both in dollar terms and real terms,
and it shows the progress that we are making as a Government. I say—
Denis O’Rourke: That is not nearly enough.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member says: “It’s not enough. We need to do more.”
We agree, and that is why on 1 April we are introducing the most generous support for
first home owners since the days of the State Advances loans and the days when you
could capitalise your family benefit. That programme worth $430 million, the biggest
new expenditure that this Parliament and this Government have planned, is going to
help 90,000 New Zealanders with a grant for them to be able to pull t ogether a deposit
to own their own home. When members opposite say: “What’s the Government
doing?”, I say that actually investing $430 million and helping 90,000 young, modest -
income families get their first home is the sort of programme that we need to pu ll
forward.
There are changes that we are doing around the Building Act. There are changes that
we are making. Do you know that last year more apprentices in the building industry
were supported by this Government than ever before in the history of New Ze aland? I
originally put in my speech that there were 5,000 extra new apprentices last year. I just
had a phone call message through, saying that they actually had a record month in
December and the number is, in fact, 5,500—another step that we are taking in terms of
growing that industry. So I say, yes, I am looking forward to bringing resource
management reform to this House. I suspect it will be one of the bigger bills that come
before the Parliament this year, and it will be a litmus test as to whether members
opposite are full of noise or whether they are serious about addressing the long -term
1400 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
affordability issues for Kiwi families, and whether this Parliament is prepared to give
Kiwis a fair go in being able to own their own home.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker,
and welcome back. It is lovely to be back again in the House. It is unfortunate, however,
to start the year with a senior member of the G overnment being so confused as to think
that when the Rt Hon Winston Peters wins the seat of Northland—should the board
decide that that is what it will do —somehow the overhang in this Parliament does not
just disappear. Mr Nick Smith seems to have been misinformed by his researchers, and I
suggest he goes back and has a look at the Act, and he would see that it has nothing to
do with Invercargill. It is actually what the people of Northland would get. Should they
see the light and make sure that they elect  the Rt Hon Winston Peters —should he
stand—they would get the whole team of New Zealand First actually up there in
Northland fixing Northland College, for example. Northland College is a school where
this Government tore down half of its buildings and did not bother to go and rebuild
them, so its students have to sit their exams in the hallways. Or there are the other
schools.
One of the other things that the people of Northland will get —and let us talk about
the area of education —is that failing schools l ike Te Kura Hourua ki Whangaruru
would be shut. Those students would be pulled out of Whangaruru and appropriately
resourced in the current alternative school programmes, the teen parent units would be
increased and monitored more effectively, and all thes e other things are what would
happen for Northland, should Northland finally say to National: “We will not give you a
free ride.”
Tell me how many members of Parliament have come out of the north who have
been members of the National Party, and name the things they have done for that area.
Denis O’Rourke: None.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: There you go. And actually, I think what is more important is
that the only person who answered that question is my colleague behind me, because no
member of the National Party could say a single thing that any of its representatives
have done for the north. So all I can say to the north is that if the board of directors of
New Zealand First decides that we will stand a candidate in that electorate and if the Rt
Hon Winston Peters is that candidate, the north will finally —finally—have a person,
have a candidate, and have a representative who absolutely would stand for them, and
finally they would get some voice in this House. That would be all I would sa y about
Mr Smith’s inability to actually understand the Electoral Commission and the rules
around MMP—not that National likes MMP.
Can I just take a moment and acknowledge that this is Safer Internet Day and
acknowledge the work of NetSafe. The Hon Amy Adams there has also tweeted out
about Safer Internet Day. It is an issue, a growing issue with regard to our young people
or even just our communities in general. The Prime Minister made a small statement—a
small acknowledgment of the legislation around cyb er safety and cyber -bullying that
will be coming back into this House. Could I say to the Minister that if she would like to
take a moment to have a good look at new evidence and new information that has come
to light since that bill left the select committee, she might like to consider making a wise
move such as Nikki Kaye did around the Food Bill and send it back to the select
committee. There is some very, very interesting international information that has come
to light since that bill left the select committee and it really should be sent back there for
some more comment. But I will leave that with the Minister. I know she has been
spoken to about it by other parties.
Let us take another single sentence that the Prime Minister made in his speech. He
said: “Good progress is being made on Better Public Services results.” Really? Do we
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1401
think that the reason the Prime Minister made a single cursory mention at all in that
statement about violence against women is that this Government does not actually have
a single target to address what is one of the most major issues affecting 52 percent of
the voting public of New Zealand? This is a major issue because 52 percent of our
population is female. Violence against women, which then leads on to all sorts of
consequences for children, was not even mentioned, or it had a cursory mention. There
were two words, I think.
I want to acknowledge that the Minister of Justice, Amy Adams, actually stood up
and was very passionate about things that she was doing in her ministerial role. But they
are all things that are going to be done after a woman has been beaten, after a woman
has been attacked, after a woman has been raped, and after an incident has happened.
Where, oh where, is the plan from this Government to actually m ove this along —to
change these social circumstances?
We had a Minister sent by this Government. In 2012 the Minister of Women’s
Affairs—the previous Minister, not Louise Upston—went to the United Nations and in
a speech there, when she was reporting back under the Convention on the Elimination
of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, she made a statement that the National
Government was working on a successor to the 2004- 09 action plan on gender equality.
So I wanted to know how this was going. What was in that action plan, Minister, that
you told the United Nations about —stood up at the United Nations and said that your
Government was addressing this issue for women? So I w rote a question for written
answer. I asked the current Minister for Women, Louise Upston, what was the successor
to the 2004- 09 action plan that she said to the United Nations this Government was
working on. The answer was the Better Public Services targe ts, specifically the
following: to reduce the number of people at working age who are on a benefit, to
increase participation in early childhood education, to increase infant immunisation, to
reduce assaults on children, to increase the proportion of 18- year-olds with National
Certificate of Educational Achievement , level 2, and increase the number of 25 to 35-
year-olds with advanced training qualifications. That is the plan.
That is the plan to address the issue of violence against women in this nation—one
that the Government fully admits is an issue, one that Amy Adams just positively,
passionately spoke about. That is the plan: to immunise more 2- year-olds. That is
