unforgivable. What that says is that the Government does not have a plan. The Prime
Minister slides over the top of it when he makes that statement because not a single
thing there is going to help those women who are out there being paid less than their
male colleagues who are doing the same job. I do not know whether this Minister was
deliberately being obtuse or whether this is actually the policy of this Government, but
perhaps some of the other speakers might like to take it up.
We have seen that domestic violence has risen as an overall share of violent
offending over the last few years u nder this Government. The Prime Minister stood up
and suggested that everything is good and well and lovely and that we are on the right
track. I have to say that the Prime Minister’s speech and parts of the speeches that
followed reminded me of speeches b ack in the 1990s. Mr Smith mentioned growing
pains a minute ago and said that of course we are going to have growing pains. What it
reminded me of was when the New Zealand public was told: “No pain, no gain. Hold
on, New Zealand. Keep letting us do this to you. Keep letting us cut your services. Keep
letting us drive you down. Keep letting us sell your assets and make you dependent
upon charity, because at the end of the day it will be good for you.” That is what we
continue to hear.
While we are talking a bout relying on charity, let us not fool ourselves. This
Government is going to sell the housing stock of New Zealand, which belongs to us —to
1402 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
New Zealanders. It is going to sell those houses, it says, so it can provide more
flexibility, and so on and so forth, in the housing market. Let us get real about this.
Right now those houses are assets on the Government’s books. It has to maintain those
assets. It has to make sure it monitors them and looks after them. The moment the
Government sells them, all we ge t is a budgetary item that says the Government will
pay somebody else for the ability to actually rent a house.
What will the Government do next? It will cap that amount of money when the
Salvation Army, or whoever else, has got that asset and needs to maintain it. Then the

items.speaker: Government will say
items.text: “Well, the maintenance is your problem. That’s your problem.
We don’t own it. It’s your asset now, and we’re capping this amount of money.”, and
the Salvation Army will go out of its way to continue to try to provide housing for
people because that is what the Salvation Army does and that is what the other NGOs
do.
That is what this Government works on—emotional blackmail. It is making more
and more people look after their fellow New Zealanders on a charitable basis  because it
refuses to pay for it, at the same time as it opens profit -making schools and hands over
hundreds of thousands of New Zealand dollars to people making a profit out of children
who have to go to school. That is the true state of this nation. Tha t is what should have
been in the Prime Minister’s original speech.
New Zealand First will take this fight to any place in New Zealand that it is required
to take it, but we will fight for it. We will continue to stand up for New Zealanders and
we will continue to stand against the policies of this Government. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I am rising to support the confidence
motion. I rise in support of a confidence motion about a Government that has the
privilege of leading a very confident country. I think that the positive mood of this
country—it is obviously a subjective matter in par t—is very obvious. It is based on a
number of things. Some of them have absolutely nothing to do with whoever is in
charge of the Treasury benches. We have had some great sporting successes that we all
celebrate. The weather has been great—probably too great for some of our farming folk;
let us hope that the rain gives them a little bit of relief. But there is a sense of confidence
around the country.
I think that that is reflected, first of all, at the political level. The people have spoken.
I listened to some of the speeches today wondering what on earth is going through
people’s minds. Is it a “the public have once again made a terrible mistake” scenario?
The reality is this. As the Prime Minister said in his opening statement today, we have
been given a very clear mandate to carry on in a third-term Government, and we are just
brimming with new ideas. We have got some wonderful fresh talent, which has come
into the House at the last election, and I think that those members will serve whoever
forms the l eadership of the National Party in a generation ahead of us. They will be a
tremendous base on which to renovate and keep the country and the party moving
forward. We are in a very confident position.
In terms of results on the street, first of all, we can clearly see those in a number of
areas. I do not have a great deal of professional input into those areas, but I know that
crime rates are at a 35 -year low. People are safer on the streets. Is this good enough?
Absolutely not. What are we going to do? We  are going to carry on and try to drive that
trend line even better. That is the theme of our third- term Government. As you listen to
the speeches that will inevitably be made over the next 2½ years about tired “third-term-
itis”, just look at the facts. As  somebody once said, everybody is entitled to their
opinion, but they are not entitled to their own facts. T his is where we will be coming
from.
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1403
I want to talk now about the economy, because it is absolutely central to what I think
is the confident mood of this country. I think it is  central to why we were re- elected by
the New Zealand people for a third term, and I think it is central to why we feel very
confident about what we are doing. We have a very clear idea about what the next steps
in this process are. Economic fundamentals lie at the heart of this. There was a famous,
very hard-line Treasury secretary in Australia called Dr John Stone, inevitably giving
rise to the phrase “the Stone age”. He said something along these lines: many politicians
decry economic fundamentals and believe  that these are the concerns only of ivory
tower academics, but the history of Western democrac ies is littered with the political
bodies of those who said those things. Ultimately, economic fundamentals will impose
themselves on people.
I am well aware of the old dictum “The public wouldn’t know a deficit if they fell
over it in the street.”, and you could say the same thing of  a number of these issues, like
total factor productivity. Probably not many people sit around at dinner parties worrying
about trends in total factor productivity and whether we are in surplus or not, but finally,
actually, Governments need to be concerned about economic fundamentals because
these will impose themselves on things th at people very muc h understand. They will
impose themselves either positively or very negatively. Right now we are seeing a
drama unfold in Greece around the  issue of “Grexit” , which is all about economic
fundamentals. Successive Governments on the left of centre in Greece spent like
drunken sailors. Admittedly, it was not just their fault. The people who lent them money
were also reckless in lending them more and more money to the point where debt to
GDP ratios exceeded 200 percent. But the reality now is that the poor Gree k people in
the street are suffering from a lack of attention to economic fundamentals, and it is a
long, hard road back up from there.
If Governments do not discharge their  premier responsibility on the economic front
and do not pay attention to the fundamentals —maintaining sound books, keeping
competitiveness in check, making sure there is discipline on public spending, and trying
to protect people who are vulnerable while also maintaining incentives to work—the
people in the street, who, yes, may not know a deficit if they fell over it, will find out
the hard way. What we are seeing now, I think, in New Zealand are very clear signs —
and I do not think they arose just in the last few months; I think we have been seeing
them for at least 12 to 18 months —that the sound attention, led by our Minister of
Finance, Mr English, is starting to produce things that people in the street really can feel
and really can relate to.
On the fundamentals, I think the key issues are that we are moving away from the
projected very large surpluses into what will be, we think—we hope —a paper -thin
surplus. It has been a very tough ask. It has been very difficult to manage the books
without slashing and burning. All the talk about slashing and burning is just fantasy and
political rhetoric. We have done exactly the opposite. We borrowed heavily during the
global financial crisis to protect the poor and vulnerable people of this country, but we
have somehow managed to get through that and still get the books back to a very
sensible position. We are quite happy that Crown debt is projected to be 20 percent by
We have also, thanks to the very able leadership in the Reserve Bank, got monetary
policy into an interesting position. The fact that we have an official cash rate at the
moment of 3.5— I think it is 3.5—is actually a sign of strength. It is way above other
people’s interest rates, but , actually, the countries in serious trouble  are the countries
with either zero or close to zero interest rates or essentially negative intere st rates. They
have run out of any capacity to use monetary policy in a creative way.
1404 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
I recall a very important hedge fund manager saying recently in the Financial Times
that there are certain things we all wish could be un- invented: nuclear weaponry,
chemical weaponry, and boy bands —I leave it to members to speculate on why he
added boy bands into that. He said then, crucially: “I confidently predict we shall add
quantitative easing to that list.” So the United States is now starting to deal with the
realities of essentially zero interest rates, which have massive distortions, and this will
not be easy. Europe is now going to go down that same track. The fact that we have got
a relatively high interest rate—although still the lowest for many years —is actually a
sign of the underlying strength of this economy. It is another reason that will translate
into things that people in the street can understand.
What we now have is —let us start to look at what the people have. First of all, the
people have more jobs, a huge number—I think from memory the figure that the Prime
Minister quoted in his speech was 217,000—and I think 83,000 people have been
employed in the last year. The really intriguing thing about this is, by the way —even
that well-known right-wing commentator Rod Oram said it; I heard it on talkback—that
the important thing to focus on is not the minor flick up from a very low 5.4 percent to
5.7 percent, but the extraordinary growth in the participation rate, which me ans that
finally people who have been a bit marginalised feel confident enough to come back
into the workforce because they know that there are jobs there.
I was very intrigued over the weekend. The United States job market figures are very
interesting in terms of the political debate here in New Zealand because in spite of the
vast difference in size —US GDP is about 100 times larger —there was a tremendous
increase in the number of jobs created in the United States in January, and this is
extremely positive. But, actually, exactly the same thing happened. The unemployment
rate flicked up a tick or two , by, I think, 0.3 percent, but all of the commentators in the
United States said that the really important thing is that the participation rate also
increased. American working-class people who have been marginalised by this crushing
situation in the United States economy have now got enough confidence to come back
and look for work. Yes, it has flicked up the unemployment rate a little bit, but it is a
great sign for the United States that its participation rate went up to 62.8 percent. That
figure is interesting—our figure is 7 percentile points higher than that. We have got an
amazing job record. This Government has got an amazing job record.
You know, although we will hear rhetoric over  the term of this Parliament about
“third-term-itis”, we are dealing with a country that is confident, with a Government
that is confident, and with a very clear vision of what needs to be done. We are going to
carry on, as the Prime Minister has said.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: That was a speech that rivalled the Prime
Minister’s in that it was skeletal, I think, in its lack of substance. It was, at best ,
underwhelming; at worst, barren of any plan or substance apart from a fleeting reference
that life is good in New Zealand because we have had one hell of a good summer. And
that is true—the weather has been great. Mr Groser even managed to take credit for that.
I thought that belonged to the Deity and mother Nature and other powers that be, but Mr
Groser seems to think that the weather is within his gift to give.
Mr Groser talked about the fact that the Government had been accused of “third-
term-itis” an d he asked for some facts to back up that thesis. Can I give him a few:
Richard Worth, Pansy Wong, Judith Collins, and the former member of Parliament Mr
Sabin. I will say no more. They are facts that bear out that the standards that the Prime
Minister wen t to the country with —and it is true, he won a phenomenal election; he
does have a mandate; his Government does have a mandate to govern—and people, it
would seem, did, and do, believe the promises that the Prime Minister and the
Government made. When the Prime Minister talked about higher standards, when the
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1405
Prime Minister talked about lifting Parliament beyond the place it had been for some
time, the community indeed believed him and voted for him. Sadly, in recent days, what
we see playing out within our  judicial system in respect of a former member of
Parliament does not bear that out. It does not bear that promise out; in fact, it is contrary
to the commitment that the Prime Minister made. But I am sure the facts around that
situation and around the var ious Ministers involved within it will come to pass, as they
always do, in the cleansing nature that is the parliamentary Chamber.
Mr Groser also talked about employment and waxed eloquent about how wonderful
things were. He made a point, which I thought was stunning in its arrogance. He said
that people, the communities, do not understand the fundamentals of an economy. That
was his thesis. A number of Ministers have made that comment over a number of years.
I think that comment is made at their peril. Pe ople do indeed understand the
fundamentals of an economy. They understand that, fundamentally, in order to gain
security for your family and in order to gain wealth and have a good and decent life, you
need a thing called a job. That is a fundamental that the communities in New Zealand,
like the 46,000 more people who are unemployed since this Government took office —
there are 46,000 more people unemployed since this Government took office —and the
other thousands of people who are unemployed do understand ve ry clearly that the
fundamental thing you need to survive, let alone prosper, in our little economy is called
a job.
I note that our leader in his state of the nation speech was quite fanatical about the
notion that the Labour Party —its very being—will be devoted to providing low and the
lowest unemployment rate on our globe, and I note that the last Labour Government, of
course, achieved that. We had the lowest unemployment in the OECD from 2004 to
2008. That is a fact. That is not hyperbole; that is a fa ct. And that is something that
Andrew Little has committed himself to return to, not what we have today.
Communities also understand the fundamental proposition that in order to survive
and grow with your family and achieve wealth and have a decent life, even if it may be
a modest life, you need a roof over your head— something called affordable housing.
That is something that this Government has been in denial about since it came into
office, and we now have the grand plan in respect of housing, which has a couple of
elements to it. One is the special housing unit, and Dr Nick Smith got up day after day
last year, talking about the number of consents that had been granted in respect of
housing. That may well be a factual truth, but, of course, a consent, as  Dr Smith would
know, is simply permission to build. It is not the completion of a built dwelling. We
know that, I think, 15 houses —15 houses —have been built as a result of the
Government’s special housing unit. By “built”, I say for those opposite, I mean built
and certified so that people can move into them, you know, and not a piece of paper that
says: “You may build a house, developer.”, and that developer or whoever else it is
might sit on that piece of land for 2 or 3 years. A piece of paper called a consent, I
would argue, would not keep the rain off like an iron roof on a built house would, but
maybe that is a fundamental that the Minister for Building and Housing does not quite
get.
So I would disagree with Mr Groser. People do get it. They underst and that to have a
good life, fundamentally, you need access to a decent health system when you need it.
We know what is happening there, and we know of the stripping of resources that has
occurred over time, thanks to the Government. We all know that beca use people come
into our offices for assistance. It is very rare that people come into your office when you
are an MP to dish out a bouquet of flowers and say that everything is wonderful. It is
more often that people come into your office because they have an issue or because they
have a problem. So, fundamentally, people know that if they are to survive and they are
1406 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
to prosper in, you know, the nation that Mr Key outlined—the prosperous society, or
whatever the slogan was that he used—they need a house. T hey need a job, and a
sustainable job. They need a job that does not allow them just to tread water —because I
have never met people who say that this is as good as it gets; especially parents wanting
better things, as every generation does, for their kids to be better. They need not just any
old job, but a job where they can grow, where they can gain promotion, and where they
can gain a higher income. They want to do better in life. They believed this
Government, as far back as 2008, when Mr Key and his the n shadow Ministers talked
about the prosperous society, ambitious for New Zealand—those sorts of things. That
ambition seems to have crumbled into mediocrity, crumbled into sort of treading water,
and lapsing into going from crisis to crisis, bout of amnesia to bout of amnesia.
The people who are lost in all of that, in the internal machinations of the National
Party as it embarks on “third-term-itis”, off the back of, yes, a large mandate, but “third-
term-itis” has taken effect pretty quick, are the peopl e whom this Government and this
Parliament are charged with serving and paid to serve—our communities, the lost and
lonelies, and those people who struggle each day to survive. They hope that the
promises John Key made over three elections will at some poi nt come true, if ever they
leave their preoccupation with their own foibles, their own discredited Ministers, and
their own MPs and former MPs who do not bring, as we sit here today, a great deal of
credit to this Parliament.
The Government needs to come up with a plan that is outward-looking, not some sort
of battle plan to hold the line, as it has done since the election, which is inward- looking
and myopic. It does centre on jobs. It does centre certainly on housing. Cities and towns
up and down this country —every night you watch the news and there is another series
of stories about younger people, and not so young people actually, who just cannot get
into that property market. What we hear from the other side is that the best shot for
those at the bottom  of the heap is to transfer ownership from the State system to the
community sector or the private sector. Changing ownership from one entity to another,
selling a house from one entity to another, does not build one additional house and it
does not increa se the housing stock one iota. It may do if the guarantee was that the
proceeds from those sales, all 100 percent of them, went back into a regenerated
housing stock. But we know, and at least I suppose the Prime Minister has been honest
about this, that he has said he will in no way guarantee that the proceeds from those
sales will go back into the housing stock.
I suppose that is slightly better than the Bolger Government, pre -1999, which sold
thousands of them and never made any commitment, never said a nything, and frittered
the money away, and not one dime went back into renewing the housing stocks. I
suppose there is a bit of honesty. Now we know that the money is up for grabs. But I
say this. I would like a member to explain to me how transferring the  ownership of a
house from entity A to entity B adds to and increases overall the housing stock one iota.
All it does is relieve the Government of responsibilities, and that seems to be the biggest
policy plank—the relieving of responsibilities that we see  time and again from this
Government.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the next call is a split
call.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker, and welcome to the
new year. It is very good to be back here, refreshed and invigorated after the summer
break. I, like many of us, enjoyed time at the beach, swimming, making sandcastles, and
just mucking around in a boat. Those are some of the great Kiwi pleasures. That is why
it was encouraging when the Prime Minister’s statement said that National proposed to
develop policy to improve the responsible use, management, and conservation of New
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1407
Zealand’s ocean environment. But how can National improve the responsible use of our
oceans when at the same time it is promoting risky deep -sea oil drilling? What the
Prime Minister says and what National actually does are two different things.
New Zealanders love their beaches. They  enjoy them over summer in particular and
they want them open for swimming, for fishing, and for boating, not closed because of
oil spills. That is what National is risking by its subsidies to the oil exploration industry
and by opening up so many of our o cean areas to permits for more deep -sea drilling.
The deeper you go, the riskier it is. So National is prepared to allow drilling even in
areas that are supposed to protect Māui’s  dolphins. We have got only 55 Māui’s
dolphins left, yet National is prepared to allow exploration in an area that is supposed to
protect them. It is paying only lip -service to protecting our oceans. The Prime Minister
also talked about having a policy for a greater range of marine protected areas. At the
moment we have got 45 mari ne reserves. That is less than 0.5 percent of our marine
environment that is protected, and that is tiny given that this National Government has
opened up more than 12 percent of our marine environment to oil and gas exploration.
What National seems to be  proposing now is not legislation to really protect our
biodiversity through no- take marine reserves, which are safe from oil exploration,
which are safe from fishing, but simply recreational parks. We may need some
recreational fishing areas, but we reall y need some no -take marine reserves where our
distinctive biodiversity is genuinely protected. We have not heard anything from the
Prime Minister about that. We need those reserves, not just around the coast but in our
deep oceans beyond the 12 nautical mile limit.
But National’s lip -service to ocean protection is most evident in relation to climate
change and its failure to take real action to reduce our emissions. There was a
significant study on ocean temperatures that was published last week in Nature. It
showed that ocean warming steadily increased between 2000 and 2013. It showed that
the increase in the temperature of the Earth’s oceans was equivalent to putting 2 trillion
100-watt continuously burning lightbulbs into the ocean. What is most w orrying is that
not only is this temperature increase happening on the ocean’s surface but it is
happening up to 2 kilometres deep. The National Institute of Water and Atmospheric
Research has been involved in those studies through it putting out some of t he Argo
floats that help to measure the temperature.
But what the Prime Minister and what the National Government do not seem to be
recognising is that this increase in ocean temperature will affect our weather patterns. It
will contribute to more frequent and intense tropical storms. We are a coastal people.
More than 65 percent of New Zealanders live within 5 kilometres of the coast. More
intense storms, combined with sea -level rise, will expose more areas to coastal hazards
and to coastal erosion. The c ost of this to our country will be immense. The human
misery will be immense. Just last year we had seven severe weather events. They cost
the insurance industry $135 million.
We can take action to arrest our emissions. We can take action to be on the rig ht side
of history in tackling climate change. The Green Party has a platform and a
comprehensive programme of action to arrest our emissions. We will be working this
year to promote those policies, to convince the Government to take its head out of the
sand, to take action to reduce our emissions, and to tackle climate change so that we can
bequeath to our children a stable climate.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: Today the Prime Minister John Key said that
this year the Government will establish a food safety science and research centre at
Massey University. He said that it is to protect consumers, enable innovation, and
minimise costs for business. The Government will also introduce legislation to
strengthen the framework underpinning our food safety system. There are great
1408 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
opportunities in this but I fear —and there is a lot of history behind what has happened
around food safety in this country —that it will not go far enough for New Zealand
consumers. Effectively, this is a response to the melamine scare and the botulism scare
in our dairy industry. It is absolutely important that we have a food safety regime that
does make sure our exports meet the standards that our export markets expect.
But, increasingly, there is a very sad picture of our rural environment. It is a high
input, high pollutant model of farming that leaves farmers exposed on the global
market, especially when the price of milk falls. If there is any hint of a food safety issue,
we stand to fall and fail a lot, lot more. The Government’s endless fixation on growth at
any price, and exporting away our riches, is hurting our people and our planet. The
environment that we travel through when we go through the country is rarely anything
to be particularly proud of, and it has changed. It used to be diverse and it gave a feeling
of safety around the food produced there, and some sort of sustainability, and it is going
rapidly in the other direction. The great experiment —an industrial model of  oil
dependence and chemically based food—is clearly unsustainable.
I use, as an example, Roundup, which used to be advertised with “You can drink the
stuff”—glyphosate being the active ingredient. We do not even seem to test for it in our
waterways. We are using it increasingly, hectare after hectare. Massive areas are being
used for various farm management systems. The reality is that this glyphosate is
damaging the microbiology of our soils and deteriorating the sustainability of that very
soil. It becomes less porous, it cannot handle the rain the same, and it cannot handle the
drought the same.
A story in Stuff today that has just come through from Washington shows a report
saying that people eating organic food are exposed to only half the level of pesticides as
in non- organic food. Other reports show that there are at least four times as many
pesticides in non-organic food. Sometimes people see organics as unaffordable. Do we
really want a tiered society where only the rich who can afford to eat it —or choose to in
that sense—are the only ones who can have a healthy diet? This Government and the
previous Government of National chose not to advance the organic system. It chose not
to help the Organic Advisory Programme, which was so successful in helping people
convert to organics. What does it do? It has done away with environmental monitoring
in many, many cases.
What we could have is some very good progress indicators if we move towards
organics. Glyphosate is showing up in breast milk. But where is the Ministry for
Primary Industries even looking to see how much glyphosate is coming through in
food? We have to remember the herbicide -tolerant swedes in Southland, using a
chemical that is banned in China. How much of that chlorsulfuron went into those
swedes and turnips that the cows ate? In the swedes’ case, some died. In fact, a lot of
cows died. That material, that information in its full form, has not come out yet.
We think the Government should support the organic sector and move towards a
more sustainable society. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Happy New Year. Welcome
back to the House. I am very pleased to stand in support of the Prime Minister’s
statement and support the confidence that this side of the House has in his leadership
and also in where he is taking this country.
I just want to comment on some of the statements that one of my fellow members of
the House, Eugenie Sage, made that will, I think, demonstrate perhaps why New
Zealand, though holding the issues of the environment as a very high value, also trusts
our Government in terms of its development of our resources. She raised the issue of
Māui’s dolphins and the marine reserve off the west coast of the North Island and
decried this Government because of permits that it has granted that touch on some of
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1409
these areas. We know that over the last 40 years of exploration offshore there has been
no detrimental effect on the Māui’s dolphin population. In fact, it is a population that
many people do have concern about, because, as she said, there are only 55 adult
members of that species who are of breeding age.
But as science has shown us, the greatest threat to the Māui’s dolphin is not, in fact,
human intervention and exploration offshore by the oil industry. At Massey University,
where they do biopsies of beach- cast Māui’s dolphins or what they consider to be
Māui’s dolphins, they have discovered that, especially on the west coast of the North
Island, every one that they have found beach cast has been infected with toxoplasmosis,
which is a parasite. Of those that are infected, just under half suffered death because of
that. It is a parasite that affects the Māui’s dolphin and it is something that co mes off, I
guess, the water and the streams that come off the land. It affects them in a very
detrimental way. In fact, what they have also discovered is that the dolphins they have
done biopsies on are actually Hector’s dolphins and not Māui’s dolphins. S o there is
some research, in fact, around this on their mortality. Suffice it to say that it is not
actually petroleum exploration that is the great threat to the species.
Of course, let us keep it to the science, because we also know that Labour, in its
election conservation manifesto, made a determination that it would not allow any
drilling to occur in a marine reserve. We know that that was speaking specifically of the
west coast of the North Island in a particular area where the Pohokura field is. I a m sure
that, by now, Labour would understand that in order to develop that field, which is
producing 40 percent of New Zealand’s domestic gas supply, and in order for that field
to continue, it would have to, at some point in time, go into a second tranche  of
exploration and drilling to get what is called the side pockets of that field to keep
producing. This is absolutely critical to the New Zealand economy. Gas is one of the
best hydrocarbon fuels. It is three times better than coal in terms of its carbon  footprint,
in terms of its reduction of impact. It is considered to be a transition fuel.
When the Māui Pipeline sprang a leak in 2010, over 1 week of repairs while that
pipeline was shut cost the New Zealand economy $200 million, and agriculture $40
million as part of that cost. So we do understand that gas is very important for the New
Zealand economy. It fuels industry as well as fuelling homes. So we understand the
issues around the environment, and we do have policies that protect it, but at the same
time I believe we have a responsible attitude towards using our resources and our
reserves. I think that this is why the general public has confidence in this Government.
We hold those things in balance. We do not say we are going to go and explore the oi l
fields and the gasfields of New Zealand and produce at the expense of the environment.
In fact, you will find that the explorers, as well as the fishermen, are all
environmentalists. They all care for the environment. They are very protective and very
careful, and they have the highest health and safety records, perhaps, of any industry
that operates in New Zealand, because they know about the issues around social licence.
All of this is to say that I believe that this Government under the leadership of John
Key understands the complexities of these issues and handles them for the betterment,
the progress, and the building of the economy of New Zealand in such a way that we do
not compromise on our environment. You would have to say that the Taranaki regi on—
the region that has petroleum exploration in it—is one of the pristine environments as
well. Tourism goes hand in hand. It is a great environment that people come to and
enjoy. So we demonstrate that we do it very, very well.
I just want to say that is  the reason why I believe we have had a Prime Minister, a
leader of our party —in fact, we have had only one leader of our party over the last 8
years, whereas the Opposition has had five over the last 8 years. So I think that sort of
solidarity, that sort of consistency, and that sort of confidence, not only from the public
1410 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
who has voted in National for three consecutive terms now, but a caucus who stands
solidly behind him, demonstrates that we know where we are going, we have a vision,
we have a purpose, we have a plan, and we are making great progress along that.
We have a Cabinet stacked with experience, talent, and energy. We have 14 talented
new MPs, unlike that lot who struggle to find one or two new MPs, but found five new
leaders over that same peri od of time. We have rejuvenation. We have new ideas, fresh
ideas, fresh energy, and great representation in our country. We have had effective
relationships with our confidence and supply partners over the last 6 years —ACT,
United Future, and the Māori Party. Wherever I go people talk very positively about our
relationships, particularly with the Māori Party. I think that what it demonstrates is the
breadth of our ability to relate to New Zealanders. In fact, you go around New Zealand
and people always talk  about the Prime Minister as somebody who is very
approachable. He is the sort of person you could speak to in a pub, yet, at the same time,
he is very comfortable talking to world leaders. So he is approachable. I think this is
where people feel this Gove rnment is successful; we are connected to them. We hear
them and we translate their aspirations into policies.
We have seen some tremendous advantages as we have been in Government. The
economy is growing. We have all heard those figures. Average wages increased 15
percent over 5 years. Look at the last year. Look at inflation and see wage growth in
comparison. It is three times higher than inflation. That is a great indication that this
economy is strong, it is growing, and it is offering a future to New Zealanders. We have
80,000 more people employed than a year ago; 217,000 more people employed than 5
years ago.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: 80,000 employed; 70,000 work visas—how’s that work out?

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: They squawk and bark from the other side of the House, but
I think what we are seeing is that New Zealand is becoming one of the most attractive
places on this planet to live. It is a great place for us to enjoy. But let us be sure that all
of this happens because of a good plan, a strong plan, strong leadership, stable
Government, and a policy set that is consistent with the aspirations of New Zealanders.
We are not lurching one way or the other way; we are making steady progress. I am
very happy to support the Prime Minister’s statement and where we are going as a
country.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a Labour call and a
split call.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Can I extend to you, Mr Assistant Speaker, and
to all other members of Parliament a happy New Year, and also to the officers of
Parliament who look after us. I wish all my parliamentary colleagues varying degrees of
success over the next 12 months.
We have heard a lot about the Prime Minister. That party across the way trades very
much on his brand. There is a lot to be said about a back story. The Prime Minister John
Key’s back story is all about the State house boy who made good—went to university
and went away to the US and made $50 million. It is a great back story. It has done him
well and National has got a third term in Parliament. But there is a problem with that
back story now, because John Key —who was raised in a State house, who had the
benefit of a State house upbringing —wants to sell off 8,000 State houses. So the very
opportunity that the Prime Minister took for himself—the help of the State—he wants to
take away from over 8,000 families around this country. There is a difference of
political ideology here, and right now there is a stark difference. We did not hear a peep
out of this Government about the wholesale sale of State houses before 20 September,
but as soon as we have a state of the nation address this year, John Key says 8,000 Stat e
homes are on the block. Do not forget, this is a man who had an upbringing in a State
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1411
house and the opportunity of a State house and he does not want the most struggling
families in our country to have the same opportunities that he had—of a State house —
because he wants to sell off those State homes. This is a Prime Minister who has
forgotten where he has come from.
I grew up in a State home, too, Prime Minister, but when I get to this place, I am
going to fight for those families who need a State home, not sell them off. I have not
forgotten where I have come from. I have not made $50 million but I will fight for the
State homes that those families, who are in desperate need, need right now —need right
now. I heard Nick Smith, a former housing Minister, say that the problem is the supply
of land. Well, Mr Smith, come to Porirua, where you demolished 16 or 17 houses about
5 years ago and that land still stands empty. Your department has done zilch for the last
5 years to increase—that Minister’s department, that Minister, and this Government
have done nothing over the last 6 years to replace those 17 homes that were take n away
from that community. Where are the replacements? Where are the State homes that
those families were living in? Where are those replacements? This is a Government that
says: “Oh, we can’t get our hands on land.” There have been plans for 22 new units  for
that land. Where is the Government? Is it building them? No. It has not done one single
thing. Then in Hazard Grove and Esk Place —right in the heart of Cannons Creek,
where some of the lowest -paid people in this country live —it plans to demolish more
homes. Is there any plan to replace those homes? Not one. It is going to sell that land. It
will probably go to a developer, who will make a tidy little income out of that.
This is a Government that will sell off State homes and take away opportunity from
those people who need it. It will sell that land off to developers and it does not care. I
am not going to sit here and listen to Nick Smith or the Prime Minister say they a re
going to give opportunities to the most vulnerable Kiwis when they have done nothing
to replace the homes —the 17 homes —that the Government made a decision to
demolish and that it made a decision not to replace. This Government has done nothing
for those  families who need more homes, and then it has its Housing New Zealand
officials say: “Oh, there’s no demand in Porirua East.” Well, come spend a day at my
office, where we get a deluge of people. Two -thirds of the work that comes through my
electorate office is Housing New Zealand work, and this is a Government that has its
officials say there is no demand in Porirua East, just like there will be no demand in
South Auckland.
And you say, Mr Young, that you are connected to the communities. You guys are so
out of touch when it comes to State housing. You can snigger, Mr Young. You can
snigger, but that side of the House does not realise just how deep the hatred of your
State house policy is, because there are a lot of good people who have done good—just
like that Prime Minister there —who do not like what you are doing. They live in their
own homes but they got a start in a State home. They do not like what you are doing
because the opportunity that they got, and that some of the people across that side of the
House got, you are taking away from them and you should be ashamed of that.

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker, I would like
to wish you a wonderful year and I would like to wish all my parliamentary colleagues a
wonderful year for 2015. The state of the nation speeches from the leader of the
National Party and the leader of the Labour Party draw a clear line between the two
parties. Labour stands for jobs whereas Nat ional stands for selling off our State houses.
Labour’s vision is that New Zealand will once again have the lowest unemployment rate
in the developed world. Having a job provides people with a sense of purpose, whether
it is a paid job or an unpaid volunta ry one. When people have jobs, they have more
dignity, they have more self -respect, and they are better able to pay for rent and better
1412 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
able to afford the basic necessities of life. They are better able to give their families the
best chance for a good future.
When the National Government came into office in 2008 the unemployment rate was
4.5 percent. But let us go back a few years to late 2004 and 2005 when the
unemployment rate was 3.8 percent. It went up slightly to 3.9 percent in 2005 and it
went back down to 3.8 percent for the last three quarters of 2005, where it stayed. This
was a time when here in Aotearoa New Zealand we were proud of having the lowest
unemployment rate in the OECD. That was under the Labour Government led by Helen
Clark. Now the very best that this current Government has done in 7 long years is bring
the unemployment rate down to 5.2 percent—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: What?

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: 5.2 percent. And now we are beginning to go in the wrong
direction, with unemployment that has risen from 5.4 percent to 5.7 percent, according
to the household labour force survey from the last quarter in December. In addition to
the rise in the overall unemployment rate, we have gone from having the lowest
unemployment rate in the OECD to being the ninth in the OECD late last year, and now
we have slipped further down to being the 10th in the OECD for the lowest
unemployment rate. This is simply just not good enough. Labour’s goal is to ensure that
New Zealand has the lowest un employment rate amongst OECD countries  once again,
where we used to be just over 10 years ago. It is harder for Kiwis to find a secure, good
job that pays a decent wage nowadays. This shows that the current Government cannot
make the rock star economic recovery work in a way that delivers fairly for all New
Zealanders.
Kiwi families have gone without and done it tough for far too long. The economic
recovery that we constantly hear about from the National Government is a jobless
recovery. Why is it a jobles s recovery? Because it is an economy that is apparently
growing, but at the same time unemployment is also increasing. Currently there are
38,000 more unemployed people than when National got into Government in 2008.
There is something wrong with this pict ure and with how our economy is being
managed. Labour is focused on jobs and we have put creating jobs at the top of our
priorities. The long-term economic plan to create jobs and to assist businesses to grow is
at the top of our agenda, through the Future  of Work Commission. The Future of Work
Commission has five work streams, for technology and security of work.
Labour has always been and will continue to be the party of work and for workers.
Contrary to what the Prime Minister stated earlier on today, the work of the commission
is not to define what a job is —no, not at all. Labour knows what a job is. We are all
about jobs. The more relevant question is when, if at all, this current Government is
actually going to deliver on an unemployment rate that is as low as it used to be when
Labour was last in Government, and why it is taking ever so long to get there. By the
way, Labour got the unemployment rate down to 3.5 percent in 2007. The question is:
can you do it? Is it possible for you to deliver an unemployment rate that is lower than
that? Thank you very much.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : People in future generations will look back and
curse the Key Government —not because of the massive debt that they will inherit, not
because of a lack of genuine economic development, not because of the legacy of a
1960s-style transport system, not because of the failure to diversify the primary sector,
not because of the stratification of Kiwis into a have -not and have society, and not for
the many other negative results of a backward and neglectful neo -liberal Government,
which future generations will be left to cope with. It will be because the worst legacy of
the Key Government will be the impacts of its resour ce management reforms. Those
impacts will have a very long-lasting effect and will be largely irreversible.
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1413
It was a National Government, actually, that finally enacted the Resource
Management Act, although it was the Palmer Labour Government that really can take
credit for it. For the first time it meant that modern, forward -looking legislation put
environmental security first and it made the assessment of environmental impacts on
development proposals effects-based. In so doing it provided a sound basis for planning
in New Zealand. This was especially so for local government, which then produced
district and city plans to ensure that land and other resources were well used, which
avoided significant degradation of that land and those resources and provide d a sound
basis for continued economic development. All of that is now under threat from the
retrograde policies of the current Key Government.
New Zealand First agrees that the Resource Management Act processes need
significant improvement. We agree that there is too much silly red tape. We agree that
there is too much unnecessary delay. We agree that costs are far too high. We agree that
there is too much duplication between territorial and regional councils, and we also
want the Resource Management Act processes to be much easier to use, so that the need
for lawyers can be minimised. We pledge our support for anything that will put forward
those objectives. For example, proposals directed towards reducing and simplifying
planning documents do have merit and so do fixed time limits for the processing of
straightforward non-notified consents. So would approved exemptions for technical or
minor breaches be helpful in the case of urban land use consents.
But—and this is the big but —the Government wants to go much too far by
undermining the effects -based decision -making under the Resource Management Act
and it wants to put economic development equal with environmental security. That, of
course, is actually impossible. One must logically have priority over the other. What it
really means is that the Government is going to have poorly restrained economic
development in priority, in effect, over environmental security. That is actually,
fundamentally, what it is doing. It is bad and it is wrong.
Nick Smith’s rece nt media stunt —in which he stood before a stack of district plans
to announce his attack on the Resource Management Act —convinced very few thinking
people that the proposals will in fact do anything at all to solve the housing crisis, while
at the same time stripping away too many of the Resource Management Act provisions
for environmental security.
In particular, a number of the probable changes will substantially limit the ability of
submitters to put forward evidence as to the environmental impacts of proposals and for
that evidence to be properly considered. Even more troubling are the probable proposals
for greater central government intervention in planning and consent processes. That
really means that the Act will become activity -directed instead of effects-based. So that
is a fundamental and very negative change to the Resource Management Act, which I
hope people out there in the community are really starting to understand.
We are expected to believe, somehow, that these dangerous and fundamental changes
will result in a fast build of the homes the country needs. The Minister for Building and
Housing used the Motu report to try to convince us that there are 40,000 fewer homes
than there would have been had the Resource Management Act already been amended
as proposed, and that the lack of such changes adds $30,000 to a new apartment or
$15,000 to a new home. That document was not a cost -benefit analysis of the Resource
Management Act. In fact, it was nothing more than a review of how developers felt
about what the additional costs were. It is non- scientific and is utterly meaningless, and
yet the Minister used it as his justification for the proposals. In fact, all planning and
regulatory imposts, including the Resource Management Act processes, account  for
only 4 percent of the cost of a new home, according to Local Government New Zealand.
1414 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015
So the Government wants to unnecessarily compromise the fundamental working of
the Resource Management Act without doing anything positive in those methods to
solve the housing crisis. People will not save anything like $30,000 on the cost of a new
apartment, nor $15,000 on the cost of a new home. In fact, Nick Smith has not even
claimed that they would. In fact little or nothing will be saved, and no more land will b e
made available than under the existing provisions of the Act, under which social and
housing needs are already perfectly adequately accommodated.
So what we are seeing on one level is just more incompetent National Government,
willing to compromise the Resource Management Act with no benefit to go with it. On
another level we are seeing an elaborate smokescreen —a hoax—to cover the fact that
housing has become unaffordable to a very large sector of first -home seekers, because
of a failure of Government to actually intervene in the housing market. In actual fact,
this Government did absolutely nothing for 5 years while the housing crisis developed.
It reminds me a little bit of the past Argentinian dictator Juan Perón, whose
Government built elaborate faca des to be filmed and shown to the masses without any
actual substance behind them—a very good analogy, I believe.

items.speaker: Stuart Smith
items.text: A very boring one though.
DENIS O’ROURKE : This is in sharp contrast to what a New Zealand First
Government would do. If anyone wants boring, just look at that member over there. He
is the epitome of it.
New Zealand First would ensure not just sound planning but also that the
Government was involved directly in the housing market. We would have a St ate
agency to buy land and see that it was appropriately developed, and sections would be
sold on concessionary terms. There is a lot more that we would do to make sure that
something genuine was done to assist New Zealanders into homes. There is absolutel y
no excuse for this country to attack the provisions of a well -working piece of
legislation, the Resource Management Act. We should improve its processes, but there
is no need at all to change the fundamental provisions of the Act.
In a nutshell this Government is simply not doing enough. It waited 5 years, as I have
said, before it did anything at all and then it has done too little. Now it wants to put the
Resource Management Act up as a straw man to knock down and to use as a
smokescreen to pretend tha t it is doing something about the housing crisis. But the last
laugh will be on the Government itself as more and more Kiwis see the magnitude of
the Government’s ineptitude over Resource Management Act reform and its utter failure
to deal effectively with  the housing crisis. Shame on Mr Key. Shame on his
Government for even considering that path.

EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL (NO 2)
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I move, That  the Education
Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read a third time . This is an important bill for the
education sector, system, and profession. The bill strengthens the education profession
by establishing a new professional body for teachers. It both clarifies  and strengthens
the regulatory framework and the disciplinary regime for the teaching profession,
modernises governance arrangements for universities and wānanga, establishes a legal
framework for the code of practice for the pastoral care of international students,
10 Feb 2015 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 1415
establishes an independent contract disputes resolution scheme for international students
and their education providers, and strengthens quality assurance arrangements in the
tertiary education sector. The bill also makes an administrative amen dment enabling the
Secretary for Education, after consultation with the Auditor -General, to determine the
form of school boards of trustees’ annual financial statements. Taken together, the
amendments to the Education Act 1989 made by this bill will ensure  that New
Zealand’s education system is equipped to meet the challenges and opportunities of the
modern learning environment.
This bill proposes the establishment of the Education Council of Aotearoa New
Zealand (EDUCANZ), a statutorily independent body f or the teaching profession and
the leadership within it. The bill reflects the recommendations of the 2012 review of the
New Zealand Teachers Council and the 2013 report of the ministerial advisory group. It
represents comprehensive sector -wide engagement on the transformation of the New
Zealand Teachers Council into a body to provide leadership to the profession and
strengthen its status in the 21st century. I wish to thank the very able people who led and
contributed to those reviews and the consultation and advice that laid the groundwork
for this legislation. Amongst the many people involved in this work I wish to thank Dr
Judith Aitken, Robyn Baker, John Morris, and Pauline Winter, who were involved in
the review of the New Zealand Teachers Council. I would like to thank Barbara
Ala’alatoa, Nancy Bell, Irene Cooper, Professor Alister Jones, Lynda Reid, Peter
Simpson, Arihia Stirling, and Patrick W alsh, who formed the ministerial advisory
group, ably charged by Dr Graham Stoop, that recommended the establishment of
EDUCANZ. Their recommendations are given effect in this bill.
As an independent professional body EDUCANZ will use its skill, expertise , and
authority to promote educational leadership, accountability, and consistently high
standards across the education system and drive continuous improvement of quality
assurance processes. EDUCANZ will be governed by a board of nine members. The
majority will come from the education profession, and all will be appointed on the basis
of individual skills and experience. Together they will provide the necessary capability
and balance. The board will not take representative positions on parts of the sector but
will be expected to take a system -wide set of perspectives. There will be an open and
public nominations process to identify appropriately skilled candidates. As is the case
with other statutorily independent professional bodies, the appointments proce ss will
provide for the protection of the public interest—in this case, in education.
The EDUCANZ board will set its strategic direction in consultation with the broad
education sector and can make independent comment on education policy, in keeping
with its independent role. The council will also be able to enter into contracts for the
provision of specific services. The measures set out in the bill present significant new
opportunities for strengthening the profession and support EDUCANZ’s independent
leadership outside the constraints of both Government and industrial organisations.
The bill also creates a regulatory environment that promotes accountability and high
standards, including consistently high standards of entry into the profession and
ongoing competence of teachers and education leaders. The bill clearly separates
registration, which recognises that a graduate is qualified to become a member of the
profession, from the issuing of practising certificates, which recognise the competencies
and experience required to work successfully as a teacher. The bill provides a new audit
and moderation function designed to ensure that appraisals for the issue and renewal of
practising certificates reach a consistent standard. The audit and moderation functi on is
a response to both persistent reports of inconsistency and a lack of rigour in assessments
and ensures constant raising of the quality of teaching and leadership. The council’s
ability to set its own standards for the profession will further contribute to this.
1416 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 10 Feb 2015
The new professional body is a cornerstone of our Government’s programme to raise
the status of the profession and publicly recognise the value it contributes to New
Zealand. This is the culmination of 3 years of widespread consultation, discussion,
deliberation, and consolidated review. We know that we must attract the best and the
brightest to the profession, raise the profile of teaching and its contribution to our
nation, continuously improve the quality of teaching practice, and invest in capable and
inspirational leadership. We must do this for our children and young people at all points
in their learning pathway, whether at early childhood institutions or in primary or
secondary schools.
The council will strengthen the disciplinary frame work by having open proceedings
unless there is good reason to withhold information, enabling the investigation of
matters on its own motion, referring all matters of serious misconduct to the disciplinary
tribunal, and developing a code of conduct. The bi ll bolsters and simplifies the
disciplinary regime for teachers to ensure high standards of conduct and a timely,
effective, and fair response to possible misconduct. The new disciplinary procedures
will give parents even more confidence that the professional quality and personal
attributes of the education workforce are of the required standard when dealing with
their children. A national professional code of conduct will clarify the standards that are
expected of teachers and the consequences of not meeti ng those standards. This differs
from a code of ethics, which establishes the values and principles of the profession. A
code of conduct was one of the recommendations of the ministerial inquiry into the
employment of a sex offender in the education sector.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The bill has generated a lot of public interest, reflected in
the number of submissions received by the Education and Science Committee. The
committee’s careful consideratio n resulted in a small number of important changes to
the bill, helping to further clarify the intent of the bill and the functions of EDUCANZ.
Again, I wish to thank the members of the committee, both past and present, for their
thorough consideration of all aspects of the bill and their work throughout the process.
To support the change to EDUCANZ from the New Zealand Teachers Council, there
has been a very skilled transition board ensuring a well -planned and seamless transition
to the new arrangements. T he transition board has played a key role in shaping the
direction and vision of the new body with the profession. Much of this work has been
undertaken over the last year and is now ready. The board of EDUCANZ, once
appointed, will be able to consider thi s as part of its initial work. I want to thank that
transition board, in particular Nancy Bell, Professor Graham Hingangaroa Smith, Hon
Steve Maharey, Paul Matthews, John Morris, Richard Newton, Hoana Pearson, Dr
Margaret Southwick, Arihia Stirling, Linda Tame, and Allan Vester, who have provided
great leadership throughout the EDUCANZ transition board.
I would also like to again express my deep appreciation to the board and staff of the
New Zealand Teachers Council, in particular to Alison McAlpine as chai r and to Dr
Peter Lind, long- time director, and latterly to Rob McIntosh in his recent acting
capacity. I also want to acknowledge the seamless transition and the professionalism of
the staff of the council, which has engendered this transition. The Teache rs Council has
developed a broad body of work in over a decade of operation that sets a strong
platform for the new body.
In conclusion, the teaching profession makes a powerful and critical contribution to
lifting student achievement. The quality of teaching and the education leadership have a
direct impact on educational success. Supporting a transformed professional body is one
of a number of reforms by this Government to grow the quality of teaching, leading, and
10 Feb 2015 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 1417
learning, and is the cornerstone of our  quality teaching agenda. I commend the
Education Amendment Bill (No 2) to the House.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: The Education Amendment Bill (No 2)
represents a hugely wasted opportunity to make some changes that would genuinely
increase the quality of teaching in New Zealand and genuinely lead to better outcomes
for New Zealand students. The review of the New Zealand Teachers Council was
welcomed by the whole profession. There was nobody in the teaching profession who
thought that things were going swimmingly well and that there was not room for
improvement. Everybody whom I have spoken to in the teaching profession believes
that there is a significant role for a regulatory body like the Teachers Council to set the
standards of entry into the teaching profession, to review and manage the registration
and renewal of practising certificates, and to manage the competency and disciplinary
functions that the council should have. Everybody ac cepts that there is a role for that
body, and the teaching profession want to ensure that it is a quality body that will
genuinely be owned and driven by the profession.
So right from the outset this bill is flawed and the measures in this bill are flawed
because it simply removes the autonomy of that whole teaching profession and gives
away complete control of the regulation of the profession to the Government. All of the
appointees on the Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand (EDUCANZ) will be
selected by the Minister of Education. What other profession that we genuinely believe
is a profession and that we genuinely respect the autonomy of would we do that to? We
do not do it to lawyers, doctors, or engineers, and we do not even do it to real estate
agents. Yet the Government seems to think that it can take complete control of the
profession. I can see the knowing smile from the Deputy Speaker, but it is absolutely
important that we ensure that if this is going to be a professional body for teachers,
teachers feel that they have some ownership over it, and they simply do not.
The Minister of Education mentioned in her opening remarks in this debate that there
was widespread consultation and there were a huge number of submissions to the
Education and Science Committee. That is true. There was widespread consultation and
there was a huge volume of submissions to the select committee. Those submissions
were listened to but they were not heard. The Government members sat there on their
email checking their  messages. They did not listen. The overwhelming feedback from
the hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of people who came along and gave up their
time to have their say on this bill was that they were opposed to it and that they did not
support the provisions of the bill. They made some very constructive suggestions for
improvement, because, like I said, there is not a teacher in the country who does not
want the education system to be better. That is why they go to work every single day.
They want better outcomes for Kiwi kids and they have been completely ignored by this
Government and the changes that are being made in this legislation. So although there
was widespread consultation, it was listened to but it was not heard.
The Government is going to handpick all of the members of this council. I went and
had a look at what other jurisdictions do. In Australia they have elected representatives.
In Scotland, in England, and in all of those other countries where we look to compare
our education system, they a ll have some form of elected representation on the
professional body for teachers —not here; not in New Zealand under a National
Government.
This bill creates a huge duplication of roles and confuses responsibilities rather than
clarifying them. For example, the bill gives the Education Council of Aotearoa New
Zealand the responsibility for sharing best practice. Is that not the role of the Ministry of
Education, the Education Review Office, the New Zealand Qualifications Authority, the
New Zealand Council for Educational Research, and so many other Government
1418 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 10 Feb 2015
agencies? Now it is being given to another agency, and it is simply dissecting that very
important task down even further and confusing more roles.
And, of course it adds to the burden of costs on individual teachers themselves,
because who pays for this? It is not the taxpayer. It is not the Government. It is actually
individual teachers. Their teaching registration fees are going to go up. Most teachers
that I have spoken to would say: “Well, what  are we going to get from this increase in
the cost of our teacher registration?”. A lot of it is simply going to go into bureaucracy.
Another example is that the bill requires 10 percent of all practising certificate renewals
in any given year to be audit ed. That audit will be a paper -based process undertaken in
Wellington. It will not result in one additional appraisal of a teacher in their
classroom—not one. It will not result in one additional person sitting in somebody’s
classroom, monitoring their tea ching, and giving them constructive feedback on how
they can be better teachers. This is going to increase bureaucracy. It is going to increase
bureaucracy, which individual teachers will pay for. It is not going to increase the
quality of teaching and learning that take place in our classrooms.
What we need to do is take best practice and make it common practice without
making it standard practice. When we make it standard practice it becomes form -filling
compliance, a bureaucratic exercise, and it completely defeats the purpose, and that is
what this bill does. Everyone will have seen news stories about people who simply
should not be in classrooms because somehow they have fallen through the cracks and
something bad has happened. Let us be clear about this: the provisions of this bill would
not have changed the outcome in any one of those cases. Not one of those people who
should not have been teaching would be prevented from getting into the classroom by
the provisions of this bill. It would not have made one bit of difference. We all agree
that we do not want people who should not be in classrooms to be in classrooms, so
how can we effectively do that?
It actually starts with quality professional development from the top of the system to
the bottom. School boards of trustees need quality professional development when it
comes to the recruitment and appraisal of school principals. School principals need
quality professional development when it comes to the recruitment, appraisal, and
professional development for their teaching staff. And yes, principals need support on
how to deal with teachers who are not performing, because at the end of the day who is
responsible for removing teachers from classrooms who should not be there? In most
cases, in almost every instance, the first port of call for that is the school’s principal.
And if the school’s principal is not being supported in that role, then we are going to
end up with teachers in classrooms who should not be there.
This bill does nothing —absolutely nothing —to deal with that. It does nothing to
provide the additional support to where it will actually make a difference. These are not
functions that should be undertaken by regulators; these are functions that should be
undertaken in schools by getting the right support in the right place. This bill simply is
not going to deliver on any of that. There is a disconnection, for example, between the
Education Review Office, which will go in and audit whether a school is doing what it
should do in terms of its teacher appraisal processes, and where the support comes from.
So if a school is found to have ineffective leadership, there has not been early enough
intervention in there. If it is found that a school does not have the right systems in place
for the deve lopment of its staff, the follow -up is so critical, and yet there is a real
disconnect. Those are the things that we should be debating. Those are the things that
the Government should be working on fixing. This bill does not address any of them.
The Educ ation Council of Aotearoa New Zealand is being set up to fail from the
beginning. It is being set up to fail because it does not have the support of the profession
because the profession does not have any say on who is going to be on its governing
10 Feb 2015 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 1419
body. It  is set up to fail because it is being given a massive increase in its remit
compared with what the Teachers Council had, and yet, as we know from past
experience, the Teachers Council had not fully got on top of the remit that it already
had. There was ro om for improvement there, and it was making incredible strides. It
was making big improvements, but to throw more responsibilities on to it before it has
really nailed down what it was already doing is simply irresponsible, and yet that is
what this bill and this Government are doing at the moment.
And is there not an enormous double standard at play here where the Government
talks about wanting to increase the quality of teaching and increase the status of the
teaching profession and yet it says that char ter schools do not have to employ registered
and qualified teachers? And then it talks about EDUCANZ having to have openness as
its default setting, and yet the charter schools have no such provisions. They are not
subject to the Official Information Act. And this Government still will not release their
quarterly reports from last year, so while schools are enrolling new kids for this year,
the Government still will not tell anybody how those schools actually performed last
year.
This is bad legislation. It is bad for the teaching profession. It is not going to result in
better education for New Zealand kids. That is what the Government should be focused
on. This is going to increase bureaucracy and increase red tape, and it is not going to
result in the removal of one ineffective teacher from any school in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: I rise to speak on the third reading of the Education
Amendment Bill (No 2). Before I come to the content of t he bill, I would like to
emphasise that the National Government pays special attention to education. We have
made a consistent effort to ensure a good education for all, because we share the Kiwi
concept of giving everyone a fair go. I would like to note t hat of 32 developed countries
surveyed in the OECD’s 2013 Better Life index, New Zealand devoted the highest
percentage of public expenditure to education. According to the OECD, New Zealand is
a top-performing country in terms of the quality of its educational system. We are very
proud of our world-class education system, but we can make it even better and we must
make it better because a good education is an essential requirement for a skill ed,
creative, and productive workforce, and this is exactly what this bill is trying to achieve.
The purpose of this bill is to help the education sector meet the challenges and
opportunities of modern learning and promote high standards of safety and
accountability. The bill will strengthen the regulatory framework for teachers with the
establishment of the Education Council of Aotearoa New Zealand , or EDUCANZ; it
will improve the discipline and reporting requirements that protect children; and it will
continue to improve the accountability of the education profession. It will also
strengthen and streamline the quality assurance framework for the tertiary education
sector.
In addition, the bill makes a good effort to protect our international students. It
establishes a new legal framework for a revised code of practice for the pastoral care of
international students. It also establishes an independent contract disputes resolution
scheme for international students and their education providers. I used to be  an
international student, and I fully understand the importance of pastoral care for
international students. International education is a significant service export and a key
contributor to the Government’s Business Growth Agenda. International education
contributes around $2.6 billion to the New Zealand economy. International education is
also important to our cultural and social links with the world. So I commend the bill to
the House.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: I would like to address three
particular issues related to this bill. First of all, the Labour Party does not support it.
1420 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 10 Feb 2015
Secondly, the first issue I would like to address is the make-up of the Education Council
of Aotearoa New Zealand (EDUCANZ) . Chris Hipkins has already alluded to the fact
that the Minister of Education is going to be the person who appoints the members of
the council. As Chris Hipkins said, there are no other careers or places of work where
the people who work in the sector are not elected to represent their sector. It just goes to
show that the voice of teachers is not being listened to. As a former teacher and as a
former principal, I would like to think that the people who were representing me on a ny
council were people whom the sector had put there —at least the majority of them. I see
in the first draft of the bill that there was going to be a maximum of five teachers put on
to the council; however, there was no minimum. So what we are saying is that there
could have been a case where absolutely no teachers were part of that council. I know
that teachers would find that abhorrent.
The second point I would like to make is around the appraisal audits. I see that 10
percent of appraisals for re- registration are going to be audited. I think that what this
does is it undermines or underestimates the complexity of teaching—the complexity and
the dynamic nature of being a teacher. EDUCANZ is going to be responsible for
auditing 10 percent of appraisals. What I would like to know, then, is what the criteria
are that those appraisals are going to be subject to. We have got 2,000 or thereabouts
schools in New Zealand, and every one of those schools does its appraisals according to
its own needs. So there is not a standard format for appraisal, and yet the council is
going to come along and audit them and say to this school over here “Well, your
appraisal system is good.” and to this school over here “Your appraisal system isn’t
good.” But based on whose criteri a? Is it based on what suits the council? Nobody
knows, so we need to actually have some criteria, but that is problematic in itself
because then if we have criteria for appraisal, we are absolutely going to narrow down
appraisal and the curriculum and education to what the council thinks is important for
education. That is unacceptable because education and teaching are such dynamic work.
When we look at the breakdown of the curriculum —at least , when I was still
teaching, some 7 years ago, there were seven curriculum areas. Each of those
curriculum areas was broken down into strands. Each of those curriculum areas was
broken down into levels. There are so many aspects of the curriculum that a teacher
could be appraised on. So what is important to EDUCANZ? Is it what is important to
the communities of those schools? I am not sure, because we do not know what the
criteria are. But if we do have criteria, then we narrow down the way teachers are going
to teach and be appraised, and that is not good for education.
If we focus the appraisals solely on the curriculum, then that absolutely ignores the
rest of the work that teachers do. For example, are teachers going to be appraised on the
extracurricular work they do—the sports teams they coach, the music groups they
coach, running a school fair, having a school drama or play, all the duties they do, and
the camps they run? Are teachers going to be given credit for the broad nature of the
work they do, or are their appraisals going to be audited, basically, on a very narrow set
of criteria? It is really important that teachers are recognised and valued for the dynamic
nature of the work they do. It is such a relentless job, and they are not getting credit for
what they do in the schools on a daily basis for all the children in our communities.
