The last Labour Government, for instance, maintained unemployment levels at 4 
percent or lower for 4 straight years from 2004 into 2008. We had the lowest 
unemployment in the OECD. Today we are 10 th. [ Interruption] In amongst all of the 
other countries, Mr Smith, that have experienced the same global financial crisis, we are 
10th. That is not something to be proud of, but we personally believe that we can be the 
lowest again if we focus on job creation. It is not just about the jobs we create, though. 
It is also about the jobs that we hang on to. There are a number of jobs in sectors like 
manufacturing, where we have had extraordinary job losses, and it did not need to be 
that way. If we work with business, if we work with unions, if we work with 
entrepreneurs, then it is possible to attain the goal that we are aspiring to as a Labour 
Party.  
We have put a particular focus on small business, and for good reason: 41 percent of 
new jobs are coming from that sector. It is an incredibly important sector in the business 
community, and yet we have had a tendency to pay mere lip service to the issues that 
are quite unique to that sector of the business community. The Inland Revenue 
Department is particularly focused, for instance, on consulting with larger corporates 
when their needs and their way of doing business are entirely different from those of the 
small to medium sized enterprise community. That is just an example of how we could 
be making sure that we tailor our response to not only policy but the basic day -to-day 
filing of forms. Interaction with the Government could be improved enormously if we 
just listened directly to that sector.  
There are some new challenges that we need to focus on as well. What are we doing 
to support businesses—not start-ups—that have actually been here for 10 years or more 
and want to go to the next level but do not have the time or the energy to ensure that 
they have the capacity to do that? What are we doing about them? What are we doing 
about businesses of the baby boomers, who have not  had the time to even form a 
succession plan, and when they leave their business, their business goes? What are we 
doing about them? There are so many opportunities that we just need to tap into and that 
is what Labour will be focused on over the next few years.  
The second piece of evidence I heard from John Key that this Government is 
apparently working on for New Zealand was the mystery higher incomes that everyone 
is meant to be experiencing. Notice that he always refers to “on average” when he uses 
that statistic. My one simple question is: higher incomes for whom? Because if, for 
instance, your income is outstripped by the cost of living and your ability to put a roof 
over your head, does it count? Well, the average New Zealander certainly does not fee l 
better off. That is particularly exacerbated by the housing situation in Auckland in 
particular, and there is no denying it.  
My challenge to Mr Key, and, actually, to all of the National Government, is to take 
five, maybe 10 young people aged between, say, 20 and 35 and ask them how they feel 
about housing in this country. Ask them about the prospect that they have of owning 
their own home, how daunted they feel about the possibility of their ever entering into 
1392 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015 
 
the property market, and how that threatens their financial security for the rest of their 
lives. This is not something being beaten up by the Opposition. If the members on that 
side of the House were talking to those young people, they would know that it is, 
genuinely, in their minds, an absolute crisis. How could a real, genuine response from 
that Government be to simply sell State houses?  
This is something I also do not  understand. State housing is one of the biggest issues 
that I have people coming into my office about. It is one of the most significant. There 
simply are not enough houses. I would really like to hear —genuinely, hand on heart —
National members tell me tha t the lack of State housing in their areas is not an issue. If 
they genuinely believe that it is an issue, how is selling these houses going to improve 
the situation? I would wager that there are as many members on that side of the House 
who have as many q ualms about this policy as we do. It is not just the tragedy of

There were the other bits of evidence that the Prime Minister rattled off in his speech 
that were somehow meant to convince us that this Government is working for New 
Zealanders. The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) —international issues—was one 
of them. I take great offence at the implication from the Prime Minister in his speech 
that by challenging his plan, somehow we do not care about human rights. We cannot 
shut down debate on the question of whether we send our troops into conflict to face 
dire consequences like death on the battlefield just because the Prime Minister thinks 
that by raising the debate we do not care about human rights. That is insulting.  
Hon Dr Nick Smith: Just turn the other way.  
JACINDA ARDERN: That is insulting. Of course we care. The issue is not whether 
or not ISIS is brutal. That is not in question—of course it is brutal. The question is not 
whether or not the international community should react —of course we should. The 
question is wha t the most effective course of action is. That is the debate that we are 
under an obligation to put before that Government, and it is yet to satisfy that question 
as to what the most effective course of action is. It is insulting, Mr Smith, that you think 
that by challenging the grounds on which you are putting this —the explanation and 
evidence under which you propose putting our troops into battle —we somehow do not 
care about human rights. That is absolutely insulting.  
Finally, the Prime Minister mentione d that under the banner of helping children in 
poverty and vulnerable families—something we have been waiting 6 years to hear more 
from the Government on —the Government is finally “looking at ways to help families 
and children in material hardship”. Materi al hardship is only one of five measures of 
poverty. It is one of five. He has clearly used the words “material hardship” on purpose. 
If he were genuinely interested in looking at the poverty children are living in, he would 
not exclude income poverty. Tha t is where this crucial debate lies. Until we address 
that, we will not address the hardship our families are living in.  
The Prime Minister may claim that National is working for New Zealanders, but for 
which ones? Housebuyers? Those on zero- hour contracts? Children without enough to 
get by? Families working hard but going nowhere? Any Government that genuinely 
wanted to work on behalf of all New Zealanders should be doing something about them.  
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister of Justice): Mr Deputy Speaker, it is a great pleasure 
to be back in the House for 2015, and it is certainly a pleasure to welcome you back to 
your role in the Chair, a role that you have taken to with some gusto and are performing 
very well. Look, I am delighted to be back and looking ahead to another year of the 
whole National -led Government delivering genuinely better outcomes for New 
Zealanders. You heard it from the Prime Minister today. We were elected with the 
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1393 
 
strongest mandate this country has seen under the  MMP system of Government. Every 
single one of us is committed to using our time here to make New Zealand a better place 
for its inhabitants. We are not here to think about how we can preserve our own political 
careers, how we can further our agendas, or how we can last the longest in this place. 
Most of us have come from successful careers in the wider world. We have come here 
because we are passionate about this country, we are passionate about making a 
difference, and we believe that under John Key’s leadership and with the team we have, 
we have a team of people who absolutely can do that. That is what gets us up every 
morning. That is what we are committed to this year and throughout this term.  
This year you are going to see an incredibly busy programme of action from the 
National-led Government. You have heard the Prime Minister talk about it this 
afternoon. My colleague the Hon Dr Nick Smith will be right at the forefront of that 
with some of the most important reforms that are facing New Zealand, I think, 
particularly reform of the  Resource Management Act, which anyone who looks at it 
sensibly knows is fundamental to getting the outcomes this country needs, both 
economically and environmentally. It is not serving anybody well. I wish my colleague 
the very best with advancing those reforms that he has worked very hard on. Similarly, 
in the freshwater space where excellent progress is being made, in the housing space, in 
the creation of more jobs, and in the creation of better healthcare for all of our 
community and particularly for those under 13, we will be working to provide better 
outcomes for all New Zealanders.  
As well as doing that, we understand that it is our job to play our part in the 
international community. The security of our people is fundamentally any 
Government’s first concern. In the world that we inhabit we all understand that security

at home and say: “Gosh, isn’t it terrible what’s happening to those people?”. Sometimes 
action is required. It is a very difficult decision and one that is taken with extreme care, 
but we know that playing our part in the international arena is a core part of what keeps 
our country safe.  
I want to take the rest of my time this afternoon talking about some of the areas that I 
am going to be focusing on in my portfolio. I want to start  with the issue of 
connectivity. I am passionate about the fact that New Zealanders’ connectivity to each 
other and to the world is an absolute foundation stone of our success. I can tell you that 
over the time we have been in Government we have seen a ste p change in New 
Zealanders’ ability to connect with each other and connect to the world. Just recently  
Statistics New Zealand has announced that we have now seen a 34 percent increase in 
the number of Kiwi homes connected to the internet since 2006. We have seen 
significant increases in average speeds and we are moving up the OECD rankings. Last 
year Akamai noted that New Zealand’s speeds had increased over that year by 37 
percent, placing us now well ahead of Australia, which is always comforting. TrueNet 
also for the same period noted that our average speeds are up 34 percent. So whatever 
measure you want to choose, one thing is being noticed internationally, and that is that 
New Zealand is making incredible steps forward in both its connectivity and the s peeds 
available to New Zealanders. We are now second in the OECD for the growth of fibre 
subscriptions, so in 1 year we have seen 144 percent growth in fibre subscriptions.  
This has not happened by accident. It is not just the inevitable march of technology. 
It has happened because this Government has committed now $2 billion to the roll -out 
of better broadband for our cities, our towns, and our rural communities. We do it 
because— 
Tim Macindoe: And what a difference it makes. 
1394 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015 
 
Hon AMY ADAMS : Exactly that. We know that connectivity means that every 
town—the smallest village, the smallest rural community —can then trade with the 
world and build their own futures. That is what this Government believes in: providing 
the tools for r egional, provincial, and rural New Zealand to access the world from 
wherever they are. That is why we have committed $2 billion, and that is why you are 
seeing from us a big move now to go beyond our first target of 75 percent of New

cellphone black spots ar e filled. This is why New Zealand is increasingly seen to be at 
the forefront of connectivity. This will be our agenda to continue that rapid pace.  
Let me talk now broadly about what is happening in the justice space. Again, we 
have a story that I think e very one of us on this side of the House is rightly very proud 
of. We are seeing crime at the lowest level for 35 years. I want to acknowledge the 
Ministers who have worked before me, yourself included, Mr Deputy Speaker, the Hon 
Judith Collins, the Hon Simon Power—all of those Ministers who have worked over the 
last 6 years in this space. The record that we now stand on is a very strong one. But, as 
ever, there is more we can do. We are not going to sit back and say: “Isn’t that great? 
We can now put that one in the ‘done’ box.” There is more work we have to do. This 
Government set itself a very bold goal of better public service targets across all of the 
areas of service that matter to New Zealanders.  
Tim Macindoe: And we’re delivering.  
Hon AMY ADAMS : We are delivering, but they are hard. We deliberately made 
them hard targets because we wanted to stretch the Public Service and ourselves. In the 
justice space all of our four targets around total crime, youth crime, reoffendi ng, and 
violent offending are on track to meet those targets. But if there is one area where I 
think we have to make better progress, it is under that broad umbrella of violent 
offending. The thing that makes me sit up and really look at these figures the most is 
that half of our violent offending is related to family violence. We have one of the 
highest rates of family violence in the OECD. That is not something that I am prepared 
to accept and I am sure every member in the House would agree with me that a s a 
country we cannot continue to accept this level of family violence. Fifty percent of our 
homicides are family violence - related. That means that on average we lose 14 women, 
seven men, and eight children every year to family violence. Every 6 minutes there is a 
notification to the police for family violence. This is not something that New Zealand 
should put in the too-hard basket. It is not something we should simply accept. All of us 
have to take steps to change this.  
I would love it if there was a s imple initiative—well, it would not be simple —that 
the Government could run that would simply fix it. I am certainly open to all 
suggestions from around the House and around society as to what the Government can 
do. It is not just an issue for the Governme nt; it is an issue for every neighbour, every 
friend, every relative, and every colleague when they see someone and think about how 
they can reach out.  
Some of the things that we are going to be doing in this space are certainly building 
on what has been done before. We have seen the roll -out of the victims’ offender levy, 
which I remember our opponents across the House said would never work. They 
scoffed and said: “You’ll never get it paid.” There has been $16.5 million raised 
already—a 75 percent collection rate, which is far and above anything that we had 
predicted and certainly yards ahead of what the doomsayers on the other side said would 
happen. Those funds are now providing better services for victims so that they can play 
their part in the justice system. We are going to go further than that. We have to look at 
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1395 
 
more intensive case management for those most at risk. We are going to be appointing a 
Chief Victims Adviser and rolling out the safe home programme nationwide. We are 
just kicking off a comprehensive review of the Domestic Violence Act and how 
protection orders work in this country, because there is room to do that better.  
We have to look m ore closely at how the court system provides for the victims of 
domestic and sexual violence. In my view there is not a system that will make appearing

who wants to work constructively with me on that.  
That is just one of the issues under way in the justice sector. We will be doing a lot 
of work this year around continuing the good work to ens ure our courts work faster and 
more efficiently, and that cases are progressed quickly. We will be looking at the 
ongoing review of our privacy legislation to ensure the right information is being 
supplied to the right people at the right time. And, as I h ave been talking about just 
recently, we are going to have to take steps to address the issue of deported criminals 
coming back when we do not have a good record of that, so we can monitor them. We 
have a busy programme of work. It is a Government I remain incredibly proud to be a 
part of and I want to wish all members a successful 2015.

Government is saying that it wants to govern for all Ne w Zealanders. That is a woeful

GARETH HUGHES: We know that Nick Smith was one of our country’s youngest

I want to talk now about the economy, because it is absolutely central to what I think 
is the confident mood of this country. I think it is  central to why we were re- elected by 
the New Zealand people for a third term, and I think it is central to why we feel very 
confident about what we are doing. We have a very clear idea about what the next steps 
in this process are. Economic fundamentals lie at the heart of this. There was a famous, 
very hard-line Treasury secretary in Australia called Dr John Stone, inevitably giving 
rise to the phrase “the Stone age”. He said something along these lines: many politicians 
decry economic fundamentals and believe  that these are the concerns only of ivory 
tower academics, but the history of Western democrac ies is littered with the political 
bodies of those who said those things. Ultimately, economic fundamentals will impose 
themselves on people.  
I am well aware of the old dictum “The public wouldn’t know a deficit if they fell 
over it in the street.”, and you could say the same thing of  a number of these issues, like 
total factor productivity. Probably not many people sit around at dinner parties worrying 
about trends in total factor productivity and whether we are in surplus or not, but finally, 
actually, Governments need to be concerned about economic fundamentals because 
these will impose themselves on things th at people very muc h understand. They will 
impose themselves either positively or very negatively. Right now we are seeing a 
drama unfold in Greece around the  issue of “Grexit” , which is all about economic 
fundamentals. Successive Governments on the left of centre in Greece spent like 
drunken sailors. Admittedly, it was not just their fault. The people who lent them money 
were also reckless in lending them more and more money to the point where debt to 
GDP ratios exceeded 200 percent. But the reality now is that the poor Gree k people in 
the street are suffering from a lack of attention to economic fundamentals, and it is a 
long, hard road back up from there.  
If Governments do not discharge their  premier responsibility on the economic front 
and do not pay attention to the fundamentals —maintaining sound books, keeping 
competitiveness in check, making sure there is discipline on public spending, and trying 
to protect people who are vulnerable while also maintaining incentives to work—the 
people in the street, who, yes, may not know a deficit if they fell over it, will find out 
the hard way. What we are seeing now, I think, in New Zealand are very clear signs —
and I do not think they arose just in the last few months; I think we have been seeing 
them for at least 12 to 18 months —that the sound attention, led by our Minister of 
Finance, Mr English, is starting to produce things that people in the street really can feel 
and really can relate to.  
On the fundamentals, I think the key issues are that we are moving away from the 
projected very large surpluses into what will be, we think—we hope —a paper -thin 
surplus. It has been a very tough ask. It has been very difficult to manage the books 
without slashing and burning. All the talk about slashing and burning is just fantasy and 
political rhetoric. We have done exactly the opposite. We borrowed heavily during the 
global financial crisis to protect the poor and vulnerable people of this country, but we 
have somehow managed to get through that and still get the books back to a very 
sensible position. We are quite happy that Crown debt is projected to be 20 percent by 
2020.  
We have also, thanks to the very able leadership in the Reserve Bank, got monetary 
policy into an interesting position. The fact that we have an official cash rate at the 
moment of 3.5— I think it is 3.5—is actually a sign of strength. It is way above other 
people’s interest rates, but , actually, the countries in serious trouble  are the countries 
with either zero or close to zero interest rates or essentially negative intere st rates. They 
have run out of any capacity to use monetary policy in a creative way.

underwhelming; at worst, barren of any plan or substance apart from a fleeting reference 
that life is good in New Zealand because we have had one hell of a good summer. And 
that is true—the weather has been great. Mr Groser even managed to take credit for that. 
I thought that belonged to the Deity and mother Nature and other powers that be, but Mr 
Groser seems to think that the weather is within his gift to give.  
Mr Groser talked about the fact that the Government had been accused of “third-
term-itis” an d he asked for some facts to back up that thesis. Can I give him a few: 
Richard Worth, Pansy Wong, Judith Collins, and the former member of Parliament Mr 
Sabin. I will say no more. They are facts that bear out that the standards that the Prime 
Minister wen t to the country with —and it is true, he won a phenomenal election; he 
does have a mandate; his Government does have a mandate to govern—and people, it 
would seem, did, and do, believe the promises that the Prime Minister and the 
Government made. When the Prime Minister talked about higher standards, when the 
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1405 
 
Prime Minister talked about lifting Parliament beyond the place it had been for some 
time, the community indeed believed him and voted for him. Sadly, in recent days, what 
we see playing out within our  judicial system in respect of a former member of 
Parliament does not bear that out. It does not bear that promise out; in fact, it is contrary 
to the commitment that the Prime Minister made. But I am sure the facts around that 
situation and around the var ious Ministers involved within it will come to pass, as they 
always do, in the cleansing nature that is the parliamentary Chamber.  
Mr Groser also talked about employment and waxed eloquent about how wonderful 
things were. He made a point, which I thought was stunning in its arrogance. He said 
that people, the communities, do not understand the fundamentals of an economy. That 
was his thesis. A number of Ministers have made that comment over a number of years. 
I think that comment is made at their peril. Pe ople do indeed understand the 
fundamentals of an economy. They understand that, fundamentally, in order to gain 
security for your family and in order to gain wealth and have a good and decent life, you 
need a thing called a job. That is a fundamental that the communities in New Zealand, 
like the 46,000 more people who are unemployed since this Government took office —
there are 46,000 more people unemployed since this Government took office —and the 
other thousands of people who are unemployed do understand ve ry clearly that the 
fundamental thing you need to survive, let alone prosper, in our little economy is called 
a job.  
I note that our leader in his state of the nation speech was quite fanatical about the 
notion that the Labour Party —its very being—will be devoted to providing low and the 
lowest unemployment rate on our globe, and I note that the last Labour Government, of 
course, achieved that. We had the lowest unemployment in the OECD from 2004 to 
2008. That is a fact. That is not hyperbole; that is a fa ct. And that is something that 
Andrew Little has committed himself to return to, not what we have today.  
Communities also understand the fundamental proposition that in order to survive 
and grow with your family and achieve wealth and have a decent life, even if it may be 
a modest life, you need a roof over your head— something called affordable housing. 
That is something that this Government has been in denial about since it came into 
office, and we now have the grand plan in respect of housing, which has a couple of 
elements to it. One is the special housing unit, and Dr Nick Smith got up day after day 
last year, talking about the number of consents that had been granted in respect of 
housing. That may well be a factual truth, but, of course, a consent, as  Dr Smith would 
know, is simply permission to build. It is not the completion of a built dwelling. We 
know that, I think, 15 houses —15 houses —have been built as a result of the 
Government’s special housing unit. By “built”, I say for those opposite, I mean built 
and certified so that people can move into them, you know, and not a piece of paper that 
says: “You may build a house, developer.”, and that developer or whoever else it is 
might sit on that piece of land for 2 or 3 years. A piece of paper called a consent, I 
would argue, would not keep the rain off like an iron roof on a built house would, but 
maybe that is a fundamental that the Minister for Building and Housing does not quite 
get.  
So I would disagree with Mr Groser. People do get it. They underst and that to have a 
good life, fundamentally, you need access to a decent health system when you need it. 
We know what is happening there, and we know of the stripping of resources that has 
occurred over time, thanks to the Government. We all know that beca use people come 
into our offices for assistance. It is very rare that people come into your office when you 
are an MP to dish out a bouquet of flowers and say that everything is wonderful. It is 
more often that people come into your office because they have an issue or because they 
have a problem. So, fundamentally, people know that if they are to survive and they are 
1406 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015 
 
to prosper in, you know, the nation that Mr Key outlined—the prosperous society, or 
whatever the slogan was that he used—they need a house. T hey need a job, and a 
sustainable job. They need a job that does not allow them just to tread water —because I 
have never met people who say that this is as good as it gets; especially parents wanting 
better things, as every generation does, for their kids to be better. They need not just any 
old job, but a job where they can grow, where they can gain promotion, and where they 
can gain a higher income. They want to do better in life. They believed this 
Government, as far back as 2008, when Mr Key and his the n shadow Ministers talked 
about the prosperous society, ambitious for New Zealand—those sorts of things. That 
ambition seems to have crumbled into mediocrity, crumbled into sort of treading water, 
and lapsing into going from crisis to crisis, bout of amnesia to bout of amnesia.  
The people who are lost in all of that, in the internal machinations of the National 
Party as it embarks on “third-term-itis”, off the back of, yes, a large mandate, but “third-
term-itis” has taken effect pretty quick, are the peopl e whom this Government and this 
Parliament are charged with serving and paid to serve—our communities, the lost and 
lonelies, and those people who struggle each day to survive. They hope that the 
promises John Key made over three elections will at some poi nt come true, if ever they 
leave their preoccupation with their own foibles, their own discredited Ministers, and 
their own MPs and former MPs who do not bring, as we sit here today, a great deal of 
credit to this Parliament.  
The Government needs to come up with a plan that is outward-looking, not some sort 
of battle plan to hold the line, as it has done since the election, which is inward- looking 
and myopic. It does centre on jobs. It does centre certainly on housing. Cities and towns 
up and down this country —every night you watch the news and there is another series 
of stories about younger people, and not so young people actually, who just cannot get 
into that property market. What we hear from the other side is that the best shot for 
those at the bottom  of the heap is to transfer ownership from the State system to the 
community sector or the private sector. Changing ownership from one entity to another, 
selling a house from one entity to another, does not build one additional house and it 
does not increa se the housing stock one iota. It may do if the guarantee was that the 
proceeds from those sales, all 100 percent of them, went back into a regenerated 
housing stock. But we know, and at least I suppose the Prime Minister has been honest 
about this, that he has said he will in no way guarantee that the proceeds from those 
sales will go back into the housing stock.  
I suppose that is slightly better than the Bolger Government, pre -1999, which sold 
thousands of them and never made any commitment, never said a nything, and frittered 
the money away, and not one dime went back into renewing the housing stocks. I 
suppose there is a bit of honesty. Now we know that the money is up for grabs. But I 
say this. I would like a member to explain to me how transferring the  ownership of a 
house from entity A to entity B adds to and increases overall the housing stock one iota. 
All it does is relieve the Government of responsibilities, and that seems to be the biggest 
policy plank—the relieving of responsibilities that we see  time and again from this 
Government.

EUGENIE SAGE (Green) : Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker, and welcome to the 
new year. It is very good to be back here, refreshed and invigorated after the summer 
break. I, like many of us, enjoyed time at the beach, swimming, making sandcastles, and 
just mucking around in a boat. Those are some of the great Kiwi pleasures. That is why 
it was encouraging when the Prime Minister’s statement said that National proposed to 
develop policy to improve the responsible use, management, and conservation of New 
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1407 
 
Zealand’s ocean environment. But how can National improve the responsible use of our 
oceans when at the same time it is promoting risky deep -sea oil drilling? What the 
Prime Minister says and what National actually does are two different things.  
New Zealanders love their beaches. They  enjoy them over summer in particular and 
they want them open for swimming, for fishing, and for boating, not closed because of 
oil spills. That is what National is risking by its subsidies to the oil exploration industry 
and by opening up so many of our o cean areas to permits for more deep -sea drilling. 
The deeper you go, the riskier it is. So National is prepared to allow drilling even in 
areas that are supposed to protect Māui’s  dolphins. We have got only 55 Māui’s 
dolphins left, yet National is prepared to allow exploration in an area that is supposed to 
protect them. It is paying only lip -service to protecting our oceans. The Prime Minister 
also talked about having a policy for a greater range of marine protected areas. At the 
moment we have got 45 mari ne reserves. That is less than 0.5 percent of our marine 
environment that is protected, and that is tiny given that this National Government has 
opened up more than 12 percent of our marine environment to oil and gas exploration.  
What National seems to be  proposing now is not legislation to really protect our 
biodiversity through no- take marine reserves, which are safe from oil exploration, 
which are safe from fishing, but simply recreational parks. We may need some 
recreational fishing areas, but we reall y need some no -take marine reserves where our 
distinctive biodiversity is genuinely protected. We have not heard anything from the 
Prime Minister about that. We need those reserves, not just around the coast but in our 
deep oceans beyond the 12 nautical mile limit.  
But National’s lip -service to ocean protection is most evident in relation to climate 
change and its failure to take real action to reduce our emissions. There was a 
significant study on ocean temperatures that was published last week in Nature. It 
showed that ocean warming steadily increased between 2000 and 2013. It showed that 
the increase in the temperature of the Earth’s oceans was equivalent to putting 2 trillion 
100-watt continuously burning lightbulbs into the ocean. What is most w orrying is that 
not only is this temperature increase happening on the ocean’s surface but it is 
happening up to 2 kilometres deep. The National Institute of Water and Atmospheric 
Research has been involved in those studies through it putting out some of t he Argo 
floats that help to measure the temperature.  
But what the Prime Minister and what the National Government do not seem to be 
recognising is that this increase in ocean temperature will affect our weather patterns. It 
will contribute to more frequent and intense tropical storms. We are a coastal people. 
More than 65 percent of New Zealanders live within 5 kilometres of the coast. More 
intense storms, combined with sea -level rise, will expose more areas to coastal hazards 
and to coastal erosion. The c ost of this to our country will be immense. The human 
misery will be immense. Just last year we had seven severe weather events. They cost 
the insurance industry $135 million.  
We can take action to arrest our emissions. We can take action to be on the rig ht side 
of history in tackling climate change. The Green Party has a platform and a 
comprehensive programme of action to arrest our emissions. We will be working this 
year to promote those policies, to convince the Government to take its head out of the 
sand, to take action to reduce our emissions, and to tackle climate change so that we can 
bequeath to our children a stable climate. 
STEFFAN BROWNING (Green) : Today the Prime Minister John Key said that 
this year the Government will establish a food safety science and research centre at 
Massey University. He said that it is to protect consumers, enable innovation, and 
minimise costs for business. The Government will also introduce legislation to 
strengthen the framework underpinning our food safety system. There are great 
1408 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015 
 
opportunities in this but I fear —and there is a lot of history behind what has happened 
around food safety in this country —that it will not go far enough for New Zealand 
consumers. Effectively, this is a response to the melamine scare and the botulism scare 
in our dairy industry. It is absolutely important that we have a food safety regime that 
does make sure our exports meet the standards that our export markets expect.  
But, increasingly, there is a very sad picture of our rural environment. It is a high 
input, high pollutant model of farming that leaves farmers exposed on the global 
market, especially when the price of milk falls. If there is any hint of a food safety issue, 
we stand to fall and fail a lot, lot more. The Government’s endless fixation on growth at 
any price, and exporting away our riches, is hurting our people and our planet. The 
environment that we travel through when we go through the country is rarely anything 
to be particularly proud of, and it has changed. It used to be diverse and it gave a feeling 
of safety around the food produced there, and some sort of sustainability, and it is going 
rapidly in the other direction. The great experiment —an industrial model of  oil 
dependence and chemically based food—is clearly unsustainable.  
I use, as an example, Roundup, which used to be advertised with “You can drink the 
stuff”—glyphosate being the active ingredient. We do not even seem to test for it in our 
waterways. We are using it increasingly, hectare after hectare. Massive areas are being 
used for various farm management systems. The reality is that this glyphosate is 
damaging the microbiology of our soils and deteriorating the sustainability of that very 
soil. It becomes less porous, it cannot handle the rain the same, and it cannot handle the 
drought the same.  
A story in Stuff today that has just come through from Washington shows a report 
saying that people eating organic food are exposed to only half the level of pesticides as 
in non- organic food. Other reports show that there are at least four times as many 
pesticides in non-organic food. Sometimes people see organics as unaffordable. Do we 
really want a tiered society where only the rich who can afford to eat it —or choose to in 
that sense—are the only ones who can have a healthy diet? This Government and the 
previous Government of National chose not to advance the organic system. It chose not 
to help the Organic Advisory Programme, which was so successful in helping people 
convert to organics. What does it do? It has done away with environmental monitoring 
in many, many cases.  
What we could have is some very good progress indicators if we move towards 
organics. Glyphosate is showing up in breast milk. But where is the Ministry for 
Primary Industries even looking to see how much glyphosate is coming through in 
food? We have to remember the herbicide -tolerant swedes in Southland, using a 
chemical that is banned in China. How much of that chlorsulfuron went into those 
swedes and turnips that the cows ate? In the swedes’ case, some died. In fact, a lot of 
cows died. That material, that information in its full form, has not come out yet.  
We think the Government should support the organic sector and move towards a 
more sustainable society. Thank you. 
JONATHAN YOUNG (National —New Plymouth) : Happy New Year. Welcome 
back to the House. I am very pleased to stand in support of the Prime Minister’s 
statement and support the confidence that this side of the House has in his leadership 
and also in where he is taking this country.  
I just want to comment on some of the statements that one of my fellow members of 
the House, Eugenie Sage, made that will, I think, demonstrate perhaps why New 
Zealand, though holding the issues of the environment as a very high value, also trusts 
our Government in terms of its development of our resources. She raised the issue of 
Māui’s dolphins and the marine reserve off the west coast of the North Island and 
decried this Government because of permits that it has granted that touch on some of 
10 Feb 2015 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 1409 
 
these areas. We know that over the last 40 years of exploration offshore there has been 
no detrimental effect on the Māui’s dolphin population. In fact, it is a population that 
many people do have concern about, because, as she said, there are only 55 adult 
members of that species who are of breeding age.  
But as science has shown us, the greatest threat to the Māui’s dolphin is not, in fact, 
human intervention and exploration offshore by the oil industry. At Massey University, 
where they do biopsies of beach- cast Māui’s dolphins or what they consider to be 
Māui’s dolphins, they have discovered that, especially on the west coast of the North 
Island, every one that they have found beach cast has been infected with toxoplasmosis, 
which is a parasite. Of those that are infected, just under half suffered death because of 
that. It is a parasite that affects the Māui’s dolphin and it is something that co mes off, I 
guess, the water and the streams that come off the land. It affects them in a very 
detrimental way. In fact, what they have also discovered is that the dolphins they have 
done biopsies on are actually Hector’s dolphins and not Māui’s dolphins. S o there is 
some research, in fact, around this on their mortality. Suffice it to say that it is not 
actually petroleum exploration that is the great threat to the species.  
Of course, let us keep it to the science, because we also know that Labour, in its 
election conservation manifesto, made a determination that it would not allow any 
drilling to occur in a marine reserve. We know that that was speaking specifically of the 
west coast of the North Island in a particular area where the Pohokura field is. I a m sure 
that, by now, Labour would understand that in order to develop that field, which is 
producing 40 percent of New Zealand’s domestic gas supply, and in order for that field 
to continue, it would have to, at some point in time, go into a second tranche  of 
exploration and drilling to get what is called the side pockets of that field to keep 
producing. This is absolutely critical to the New Zealand economy. Gas is one of the 
best hydrocarbon fuels. It is three times better than coal in terms of its carbon  footprint, 
in terms of its reduction of impact. It is considered to be a transition fuel.  
When the Māui Pipeline sprang a leak in 2010, over 1 week of repairs while that 
pipeline was shut cost the New Zealand economy $200 million, and agriculture $40 
million as part of that cost. So we do understand that gas is very important for the New 
Zealand economy. It fuels industry as well as fuelling homes. So we understand the 
issues around the environment, and we do have policies that protect it, but at the same  
time I believe we have a responsible attitude towards using our resources and our 
reserves. I think that this is why the general public has confidence in this Government. 
We hold those things in balance. We do not say we are going to go and explore the oi l 
fields and the gasfields of New Zealand and produce at the expense of the environment. 
In fact, you will find that the explorers, as well as the fishermen, are all 
environmentalists. They all care for the environment. They are very protective and very 
careful, and they have the highest health and safety records, perhaps, of any industry 
that operates in New Zealand, because they know about the issues around social licence.  
All of this is to say that I believe that this Government under the leadership of John 
Key understands the complexities of these issues and handles them for the betterment, 
the progress, and the building of the economy of New Zealand in such a way that we do 
not compromise on our environment. You would have to say that the Taranaki regi on—
the region that has petroleum exploration in it—is one of the pristine environments as 
well. Tourism goes hand in hand. It is a great environment that people come to and 
enjoy. So we demonstrate that we do it very, very well.  
I just want to say that is  the reason why I believe we have had a Prime Minister, a 
leader of our party —in fact, we have had only one leader of our party over the last 8 
years, whereas the Opposition has had five over the last 8 years. So I think that sort of 
solidarity, that sort of consistency, and that sort of confidence, not only from the public 
1410 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 10 Feb 2015 
 
who has voted in National for three consecutive terms now, but a caucus who stands 
solidly behind him, demonstrates that we know where we are going, we have a vision, 
we have a purpose, we have a plan, and we are making great progress along that. 
We have a Cabinet stacked with experience, talent, and energy. We have 14 talented

We have seen some tremendous advantages as we have been in Government. The

years ago.  
Tracey Martin: 80,000 employed; 70,000 work visas—how’s that work out? 
JONATHAN YOUNG: They squawk and bark from the other side of the House, but

to all other members of Parliament a happy New Year, and also to the officers of 
Parliament who look after us. I wish all my parliamentary colleagues varying degrees of

to wish you a wonderful year and I would like to wish all my parliamentary colleagues a 
wonderful year for 2015. The state of the nation speeches from the leader of the 
National Party and the leader of the Labour Party draw a clear line between the two

Labour’s vision is that New Zealand will once again have the lowest unemployment rate 
in the developed world. Having a job provides people with a sense of purpose, whether 
it is a paid job or an unpaid volunta ry one. When people have jobs, they have more 
dignity, they have more self -respect, and they are better able to pay for rent and better

able to afford the basic necessities of life. They are better able to give their families the

EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL (NO 2) 
Third Reading 
Hon HEKIA PARATA (Minister of Education) : I move, That  the Education 
Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read a third time . This is an important bill for the 
education sector, system, and profession. The bill strengthens the education profession 
by establishing a new professional body for teachers. It both clarifies  and strengthens 
the regulatory framework and the disciplinary regime for the teaching profession, 
modernises governance arrangements for universities and wānanga, establishes a legal 
framework for the code of practice for the pastoral care of international students, 
10 Feb 2015 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 1415 
 
establishes an independent contract disputes resolution scheme for international students 
and their education providers, and strengthens quality assurance arrangements in the 
tertiary education sector. The bill also makes an administrative amen dment enabling the 
Secretary for Education, after consultation with the Auditor -General, to determine the 
form of school boards of trustees’ annual financial statements. Taken together, the 
amendments to the Education Act 1989 made by this bill will ensure  that New 
Zealand’s education system is equipped to meet the challenges and opportunities of the 
modern learning environment.  
This bill proposes the establishment of the Education Council of Aotearoa New 
Zealand (EDUCANZ), a statutorily independent body f or the teaching profession and 
the leadership within it. The bill reflects the recommendations of the 2012 review of the 
New Zealand Teachers Council and the 2013 report of the ministerial advisory group. It 
represents comprehensive sector -wide engagement on the transformation of the New 
Zealand Teachers Council into a body to provide leadership to the profession and 
strengthen its status in the 21st century. I wish to thank the very able people who led and 
contributed to those reviews and the consultation and advice that laid the groundwork 
for this legislation. Amongst the many people involved in this work I wish to thank Dr 
Judith Aitken, Robyn Baker, John Morris, and Pauline Winter, who were involved in 
the review of the New Zealand Teachers Council. I would like to thank Barbara 
Ala’alatoa, Nancy Bell, Irene Cooper, Professor Alister Jones, Lynda Reid, Peter 
Simpson, Arihia Stirling, and Patrick W alsh, who formed the ministerial advisory 
group, ably charged by Dr Graham Stoop, that recommended the establishment of 
EDUCANZ. Their recommendations are given effect in this bill.  
As an independent professional body EDUCANZ will use its skill, expertise , and 
authority to promote educational leadership, accountability, and consistently high 
standards across the education system and drive continuous improvement of quality 
assurance processes. EDUCANZ will be governed by a board of nine members. The 
majority will come from the education profession, and all will be appointed on the basis 
of individual skills and experience. Together they will provide the necessary capability 
and balance. The board will not take representative positions on parts of the sector but 
will be expected to take a system -wide set of perspectives. There will be an open and 
public nominations process to identify appropriately skilled candidates. As is the case 
with other statutorily independent professional bodies, the appointments proce ss will 
provide for the protection of the public interest—in this case, in education.  
The EDUCANZ board will set its strategic direction in consultation with the broad 
education sector and can make independent comment on education policy, in keeping 
with its independent role. The council will also be able to enter into contracts for the 
provision of specific services. The measures set out in the bill present significant new 
opportunities for strengthening the profession and support EDUCANZ’s independent 
leadership outside the constraints of both Government and industrial organisations.  
The bill also creates a regulatory environment that promotes accountability and high 
standards, including consistently high standards of entry into the profession and 
ongoing competence of teachers and education leaders. The bill clearly separates 
registration, which recognises that a graduate is qualified to become a member of the 
profession, from the issuing of practising certificates, which recognise the competencies 
and experience required to work successfully as a teacher. The bill provides a new audit 
and moderation function designed to ensure that appraisals for the issue and renewal of 
practising certificates reach a consistent standard. The audit and moderation functi on is 
a response to both persistent reports of inconsistency and a lack of rigour in assessments 
and ensures constant raising of the quality of teaching and leadership. The council’s 
ability to set its own standards for the profession will further contribute to this.  
1416 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 10 Feb 2015 
 
The new professional body is a cornerstone of our Government’s programme to raise 
the status of the profession and publicly recognise the value it contributes to New 
Zealand. This is the culmination of 3 years of widespread consultation, discussion, 
deliberation, and consolidated review. We know that we must attract the best and the 
brightest to the profession, raise the profile of teaching and its contribution to our 
nation, continuously improve the quality of teaching practice, and invest in capable and 
inspirational leadership. We must do this for our children and young people at all points 
in their learning pathway, whether at early childhood institutions or in primary or 
secondary schools.  
The council will strengthen the disciplinary frame work by having open proceedings 
unless there is good reason to withhold information, enabling the investigation of 
matters on its own motion, referring all matters of serious misconduct to the disciplinary 
tribunal, and developing a code of conduct. The bi ll bolsters and simplifies the 
disciplinary regime for teachers to ensure high standards of conduct and a timely, 
effective, and fair response to possible misconduct. The new disciplinary procedures 
will give parents even more confidence that the professional quality and personal 
attributes of the education workforce are of the required standard when dealing with 
their children. A national professional code of conduct will clarify the standards that are 
expected of teachers and the consequences of not meeti ng those standards. This differs 
from a code of ethics, which establishes the values and principles of the profession. A 
code of conduct was one of the recommendations of the ministerial inquiry into the 
employment of a sex offender in the education sector.

Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and 
Employment): This is another imp ortant bill that will improve our education system. I 
would like to thank members for the work they have done on the bill. Their suggestions 
and amendments have improved it. I have listened carefully to the two previous Labour 
Party speakers. I have to say that we respectfully disagree with their connotations on the 
bill, and I suspect that will be true for subsequent speakers as well, although we shall 
wait and see.  
I want to focus on the areas of the bill that are related to my role as the Minister for 
Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment. The changes proposed are the latest in a 
series of reforms made by this Government to improve the performance and quality of 
1422 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 10 Feb 2015 
 
tertiary education in this country. We have reduced the spending in low -value areas, 
such as student loans for people who consistently fail their courses, and we have 
improved the way the system targets need. We have set performance incentives on 
providers and students and have improved information for students about the 
performance providers and the outcomes of their study, and our approach is paying off. 
The tertiary system delivered a record number of qualifications in 2013. Also in that 
year 26,200 Bachelor’s degrees were completed by domestic students, up by just over 
4,500 since 2010. Rig ht through the 2000s the number of degree graduates flat -lined, 
despite big increases in tertiary funding by the previous Government, so these results 
are great to see.  
We are also in the process of improving outcomes for Māori and Pasifika students. 
The number of Māori students enrolled in qualifications at Bachelor’s level or higher 
increased from 17,500 in 2007 to 22,100 in 2013, and the number of Pasifika students 
enrolled in qualifications at Bachelor’s level or higher has increased from 8,570 in 2007  
to 12,602 in 2013. There is more work to do, but the direction is positive.  
The changes to university and wānanga governance proposed in this bill build on 
these gains. There are four major changes from the current model. Firstly, councils will 
decrease in size, from 12 to 20 members to 8 to 12 members. Universities and wānanga  
will choose their council size from within those limits. Secondly, council membership 
requirements will be made more flexible by the removal of specific representative 
requirements. Thirdly, the Minister and councils will be required to appoint members 
with relevant knowledge, skills, or experience. And, fourthly, the duties and 
accountabilities of individual council members will be clarified, including the 
circumstances in which a member may be dismissed. All university and wānanga 
councils will be required to have at least one Māori member to assist the Government’s 
goal of raising achievement for Māori, and I would note that that would not involve 
significant change to current arrangements.  
These changes will support councils to respond effectively to a rapidly changing 
employment market, to adapt to new challenges from changing technology and 
teaching, and to operate more strategically and effectively in an increasingly 
competitive international university environment. The changes will help address the 
difficulties large councils can have with timely decision -making and communication. 
They will bring university and wānanga councils more in line with the governance 
bodies of other organisations of all types.  
The changes are particularly important for wānanga. The current governance settings 
were not written with them in mind. The changes will allow increased flexibility for 
wānanga to reflect their unique stakeholders, particularly iwi, on their councils. 
Some members of this House have expressed concern that these changes would 
compromise institutional autonomy or academic freedom. That is simply not the case, 
as a reading of the Act will tell you, as these are guaranteed— 
Dr Megan Woods: So all the vice -chancellors are wrong —the vice-chancellors of 
all 11 universities are wrong. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : —just for the member’s benefit —by section 161 of the 
Education Act 1989, and, again for member’s benefit, that section is not changing.  
Some members have claimed that council members will owe their duties only to the 
Minister, or that the Minister will be able to remove council members if he or she 
disagrees with a council member’s decision. That is also incorrect. Members will owe 
their duties to the council and the Minister, and the Minister could remove a council 
member only on the recommendation of the council and with just cause.  
Some members have also expressed concern about staff and student representation 
on councils. These changes will mean it is for institutions to decide whether they want 
10 Feb 2015 Education Amendment Bill (No 2) 1423 
 
staff and student representatives on their councils, and given the feedback from 
institutions about the contributions of these stakeholders, I would expect that many 
institutions will choose to retain that representation.  
Universities and wānanga will not be expected to transition to the new councils 
immediately. They will have until 30 June next year, which will give them plenty of 
time to draft new constitutions and statutes in consultation with their stakeholders, and, 
if required, to hold elections for new members. However, those institutions that wish to 
transition to new councils immediately will be able to do so.  
The bill will also improve the tertiary education system’s responsiveness to the needs 
of international students. International education is very important to New Zealand. It 
contributes, the latest figures say, $2.85 billion a year to our economy and over 30,000 
additional jobs for New Zealanders. The leadership statement for international 
education has set the goal of doubling the total value of New Zealand’s international 
education sector from where it was a few years ago to $5 billion by 2025.  
International education also showcases New Zealand to the world and improves our 
connectedness as a country. It provides us with lifelong ambassadors. Graduates return 
to their home countries and share  their experiences with their friends, families, and 
colleagues. International education also enhances teaching and research, as students 
share their knowledge with New Zealand teachers and researchers.  
Of course, if New Zealand is to sustain and grow the  international sector, 
international students and their families must have confidence that they will be well 
cared for and have a great experience in this country. This bill strengthens the legal 
framework governing the care and support of international st udents and improves the 
responsiveness of the education system to the needs of those students. This bill creates a 
strengthened legal framework for a revised code of practice for the pastoral care of 
international students. The bill targets intervention to  providers who are not complying 
with their obligations under the code. It requires that all reasonable steps are taken to 
protect international students in a timely manner and to ensure that they have a positive 
experience in this country.  
The bill also establishes a dedicated independent contract disputes resolution scheme 
for international students and improves the student fee protection regime, which covers 
both domestic and international students. The bill also strengthens quality assurance to 
promote accountability and high standards. To protect the quality of tertiary education, 
the bill strengthens enforcement and offence provisions.  
This bill builds on the strong foundations of the tertiary education system and the 
Government’s commitment to continually improving that system. It makes important 
changes to the governance of our universities and wānanga so that they can respond 
more quickly and strategically to the challenges of modern- day tertiary education. The 
bill will create a more robust regula tory framework for our international education 
sector, and it will improve the quality assurance of our tertiary providers. I commend 
this bill to the House.

protect their rights. So not only has the Government taken away these protections from 
migrants but it has also taken them away from all New Zealanders. That is the first 
thing. 
The second thing is that if you want to stop exploitation, you need to detect it. How 
do you detect it? Well, the International Labour Organization says that having a labour 
inspectorate is the way to do it and that in an advanced country like New Zealand there 
should be one labour inspector per 10,000 workers —one per 10,000 workers. Do you 
know what the actual ratio of the labour inspectorate to workers is in New Zealand, Mr 
Hudson? Do you know? It is not 1:10,000; it is 1:56,000. We do not come anywhere 
near the international standards for protecting our workforce against exploitation. Even 
with the Aussies it is 1:19,000. The Aussies are three times better off than we are. So if 
the Government really wants to stop exploitation by the unscrupulous employer —not 
the majority of employers but the unscrupulous employer —then surely it would 
strengthen the labour inspectorate. There is nothing in this bill —nothing in the declared 
intentions of the Government—to address that problem. 
The third area is the one that I talked about before. If you genuinely want to give 
migrant workers the chance to come forward, make it easy for them. Do not make them 
go to the agency that is there to enforce  visa conditions; let them go to the labour 
inspectorate.  
There is something else that could be done. Some years ago I was involved with a 
piece of legislation called the Protected Disclosures Act. It was quite good for its time. 
Now it needs modernising, updating, and strengthening. It needs to apply as strongly in 
the private sector as it does in the public sector. There is nothing here for that. When I 
go through the litany of cases about people being exploited, I see what we fought 
against, or our forebears fought against, in the late 19 th century and early 20th century. I 
see people who pay their employers for the privilege of working, because having a job 
is a condition of their visa to be in New Zealand. I see cases of people being paid $2 an 
hour or  $5 an hour. I am not making this up. These are case studies that have been 
10 Feb 2015 Immigration Amendment Bill (No 2) 1447 
 
published. That exploitation is getting worse as our migrant population increases and as 
our student population with work visas increases. It is a disgrace in New Zealand to see 
that sort of exploitation. What we need is a real effort, not the window dressing that this 
bill represents. 
BRETT HUDSON (National): Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker— 
Hon Member: Oh, it speaks. 
BRETT HUDSON: It does, indeed. I would just like to just wish you, Mr Assistant 
Speaker, and my parliamentary colleagues around the House a happy New Year. It is 
great to be back and to speak on this Immigration Amendment Bill (No 2). If y ou are 
looking to change behaviours in a workplace or in an environment, you do not do it by 
trying to create more regulators and more workforce to look at what has gone wrong. 
You change people’s behaviours. This is a key part of this bill. 
So what do we do? When you are talking about a power imbalance, what do you do? 
You punish the perpetrators, not the victims. So what does this bill do? It says that, 
unfortunately, so many of the people who exploit migrant workers are migrants 
themselves. So what power  does this bill give? It gives the power to deport those 
exploiters of migrant workers, if the exploiters have been resident for fewer than 10 
years. So what do you have? You have the exploited worker, who is suddenly in a 
position of greater power. If the y complain, they are not the ones who will be leaving 
New Zealand. It is their employer who is going to be thrown out. If you are trying to 
change behaviour, you address the source of the problem; you do not address the victim. 
That is what this bill is doing. I commend it to the House. Thank you.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (NO 3) 
Second Reading 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Minister for Social Development) : I move, That the Social 
Security Amendment Bill (No 3) be now read a second time . This bill amends the Social 
Security Act 1964  so that the benefit system treats people in similar circumstances 
consistently, because if it is not consistent, it is not fair. We need these changes because 
at the moment the Act allows some people receivin g weekly compensation to be treated 
differently depending on who pays that compensation, and it also allows some students 
to access a higher rate of accommodation assistance than others. 
1448 Social Security Amendment Bill (No 3) 10 Feb 2015 
 
I thank the Social Services Committee for its thorough and careful at tention to this 
bill. Two submissions were made to the committee; however, both urged the 
Government to increase the amount of accommodation assistance available to students, 
and the committee rightly ruled that as being outside the scope of this bill. 
One submission expressed concern about the possibility of students who are part-way 
through their studies having their accommodation assistance reduced immediately as a 
result of this bill being passed. Any adjustment for students affected by changes in the 
bill will be made when their assistance is next reviewed; it will not be triggered 
immediately by the change in the law. So for students whose circumstances do not 
change, the adjustment will most likely be made when they make their next application 
covering a further period of study. 
The changes set out in this bill do affect some students —they are students who have 
spotted a loophole in the Social Security Act. Using this loophole, they apply for the 
accommodation supplement rather than applying for the as sistance they should receive 
under the student allowance scheme. The design of assistance for students —student 
allowance, student loans, and the accommodation benefit —recognises that the students’ 
future earnings prospects are improved by their investment in study, and it is only right 
for them and their families to meet some of the costs involved. The accommodation 
supplement is designed for a more diverse group of people, including full -time workers, 
beneficiaries, and superannuitants, and we cannot assum e that all of the people who get 
it are doing something that will improve their future earnings prospects. The design of 
the accommodation supplement simply takes into account their current situation, their 
income and assets, accommodation costs, the residential location, and the family’s 
accommodation needs. 
Students should receive the assistance designed for them. Students who are eligible 
for student allowances should not be able to take advantage of the system and request an 
accommodation supplement. So the current wording in the Social Security Act is not 
clear enough, and it leaves open the loophole that allows people to claim the 
accommodation supplement if they give up the student allowance and accommodation 
benefit, or simply do not apply for a student allowance. This bill closes that loophole. It 
provides clear wording to exclude students who have access to the student allowance 
scheme from being granted the accommodation supplement. 
The second matter dealt with in this bill is weekly compensation. Some employers 
have an agreement with ACC to pay entitlements under the Accident Compensation 
Act. In return, these accredited employers pay lower levies. This scheme encourages 
employers to manage health and safety issues in the workplace. If there is an accident in 
an accredited employer’s workplace, the employer pays the entitlements, the medical 
costs, and any weekly compensation arising from the accident. The employer continues 
to meet payments for the period they have agreed with ACC, which can be up to 5 years 
following the accident. If payments are still needed after that, ACC steps in and picks 
up the responsibility. 
People who work for an accredited employer continue to pay the same ACC levies 
and have the same entitlements as before. Their positio n is just the same as if they 
worked for an employer who was not accredited. It would be unfair for the social 
security system to treat people paid weekly compensation by an accredited employer in 
a different way from people paid weekly compensation by ACC . This bill amends the 
Social Security Act to make sure that people who are paid weekly compensation by an 
accredited employer are treated the same way as people who are in the same 
circumstances but are paid by ACC. This means that weekly compensation, re gardless 
of who pays it, will always be deducted from the person’s benefit payment, rather than 
10 Feb 2015 Social Security Amendment Bill (No 3) 1449 
 
one group of people having weekly compensation payments deducted dollar for dollar 
and another group having weekly compensation payments treated as income.
